1040 E. Grand River Rezoning Request From RE to B-2 – Young Kim, PC
Recommendation, Board Final Action
Mr. Kraft reported that the Planning Commission had held a long discussion
regarding this rezoning request and their decision had been very difficult. He
stated that during their discussions, the Commissioners were split 3-3 on their
decision (with two members remaining silent). Mr. Kraft reported that he
believed that there were two main reasons the Planning Commission had
difficulty deciding on this rezoning.
First, the property is located at the very first intersection west of our town
square (Zimmer and Grand River) and next to some existing B-2 properties. This
means approval would extend the B-2 zoned areas to the intersection. Some
commissioners were willing to expand our B-2 zones beyond what is stated in the
Township Master Plan and future land use map (which states that this type of
development should occur at our town center). Other commissioners were not
willing to deviate from the master plan.
The second problem that the Commission struggled with was that the applicant
had suggested he wanted to also put in a retail shop at this location. The
comments at the public hearing were generally in favor of a greenhouse.
However, at least one citizen asked that the Planning Commission please be
cautious of other uses that could occur under a B-2 zone designation if the
property was sold.
Mr. Kraft stated that, although all the commissioners were generally
comfortable with the proposed use of the property as a greenhouse with a small
retail shop, the Planning Commission cannot consider a use when making its
decision. He said that when the Planning Commission stripped away the use issue
and reviewed the request strictly as a rezoning from RE (where a greenhouse
would be allowed) to a B-2 (where a retail business would be allowed) the
decision about whether it would be inconsistent with the Township Future Land
Use Map and Master Plan and how it would impact the health, safety and welfare
of the surrounding neighborhood, became more clear to many commissioners. The
resulting final vote was 7-1 recommending that the Planning Commission deny
this rezoning request.
Treasurer Fink stated that she thinks it is too bad that the Township’s Planned
Development (PD) zone description did not show more flexibility. If the minimum
size issue could be adjusted, then the proposed use would not have to be
considered in the decision. Unfortunately, this property doesn’t meet the
current requirements for Planned Development zoning.
Supervisor Martin said that she was initially surprised by the Planning
Commission’s decision. She stated that she agrees that putting in a greenhouse
is not objectionable but she also realizes that rezoning the property to B-
2 opens the possibility of objectionable businesses coming in that don’t mix
well with residential areas. She agreed with Treasurer Fink that a PD zoning
would allow more flexible requirements. She also reported that a neighbor who
is zoned Ag-Small Farm had contacted her with concern about what rezoning to B-
2 could allow to operate on this parcel in the future. Supervisor Martin asked
if the Planning Commission had discussed the use of the P D zoning. Mr. Kraft
reported it had not been discussed.
Trustee Wright stated that he feels that the property is perfect for commercial
use.
Trustee Zaban reminded the Board of a previous incident where a rezoning had
been allowed for a specific use and the owner turned around and sold the
property immediately.
Mr. Kraft said that there are already plenty of other commercial properties
along that strip that could accommodate this use. Trustee Wright said there is
only one parcel currently available that is zoned B-2.
Trustee Wright said he feels the Township is hindering possible commercial
development with this decision. He stated that this property is so close to B-
2 parcels on either side that he doesn’t see a problem with rezoning it.
Trustee Wright added that he recognized that neighbors had concerns about what
else could go onto this property in the future but he said there are special
use permits that will give the Township control over this issue if the zoning
is changed.
Mr. Kraft said that the Planning Commission wants to seriously avoid creating a
“strip”.
Supervisor Martin invited the applicant to address the Board. Mr. Todd
Chamberlain, attorney for Mr. Kim, spoke on behalf of the applicant. He stated
that the parcel in question is currently zoned for use as a rural estate.
Because the parcel is slightly in excess of 5 acres, the owner is allowed to
build one house on the property. He stated that this type of development is
probably never going to happen looking at the other current uses along Grand
River Avenue. He said that this property is a prime case for the Township to
reconsider reasonable uses of the property. Mr. Chamberlain said that Mr. Kim
has stated his intended use. He said that he understands that the Planning
Commission does not bind its decision to a use, but argued that the Board will
be able to use special use permits to control future use. He stated that there
is already property zoned B-2 located nearby. He said that Mr. Kim is asking
for an impractically used residential property to be rezoned to something
similar to the character of the other current uses in the area. He stated that
at the public hearing in October, everyone that offered an opinion was
generally in favor of the property being used for a greenhouse. He also said
that there is a benefit to the health and welfare to the community because, if
the property is rezoned, MDOT and ICDC will have jurisdiction. He requested
that the Board part from the Planning Commission’s decision. He added that the
concern the Township has bout future use is the same one they will have when
the surrounding B-2 properties, like Concrete Concepts, are sold.
Treasurer Fink asked if the applicant plans to reside on the property and Mr.
Chamberlain responded that he did not.
Supervisor Martin stated that she respects the Planning Commission process and
she has no intention of overriding their decision. If she were to do anything
this evening it would be to ask the Planning Commission to reconsider the
following:
1)   The Planning Commission has recommended denying the rezoning based on it
resulting in too much of a strip of B-2 properties. She said she understands
their point but asked if we should deny B-2 zoning when the property across the
street and the property next to this property is already zoned B-2. She asked
they please review the Master Plan for just that area.
2)   She stated that the Commission is also concerned about the uses that were
available in the B-2 zone beyond the scope of the proposed greenhouse. She said
she would ask that, at the next Planning Commission meeting, the commissioners
go through every use included in a B-2 zone and make sure that they are all
compatible. If they decide all the uses are not compatible, the Planning
Commission may need to create a new zone or redistribute the uses for the
development of non-obtrusive or less obtrusive commercial enterprises so that
properties could be developed without creating a strip development.
3)   She verified with Mr. Kraft that the description of a nursery in an RE
zone specifically allows, “ growing and raising of commercial plants” rather
than “growing and selling”. She asked if it would be appropriate to modify the
description for a nursery. She said the Planning Commission did something
similar to this. She said that it had been a long process but the Planning
Commission worked through to modify the description of a zone to allow the
development of the Pres Kool property. She asked that they please look at this
option.
Supervisor Martin reiterated that she is not willing to override the Planning
Commission’s decision, especially without giving them an opportunity to look at
the uses in the B-2, B-1, RE and PD districts again. She also noted that
including commercial sales in the description would increase traffic.
Trustee Wright said that there are already other uses allowed in an RE zone
that could potentially increase traffic. He said that, with our current
descriptions, a big operation like the one that Terry Hanks Chevrolet operates
would be allowed if the RE parcel size were large enough. He reminded the Board
that any increased traffic would be on Grand River Ave., not smaller roads like
Sherwood or Zimmer.
Clerk Hiner said that from her experience, increased traffic from a retail
business will definitely impact residents on Glaser Road.
Trustee Wright said that maybe in order to make this request work, the Township
approach the solution in a different way. He said that Supervisor Martin’s
example of the process used with Pres Kool was a good one. The Pres Kool
property was another case where the Planning Commission felt that a proposed
request was a good use of property even though it did not fit under the current
zoning.
Treasurer Fink said that she is concerned about setting a precedent of going
against the Master Plan, but also feels that this is an appropriate parcel for
the type of business Mr. Kim has proposed. She said she thinks it sounds like
the Planning Commission doesn’t have any problem with a greenhouse business but
that they didn’t want to set precedence for deviating from the Master Plan. She
said that the Planning Commission should consider looking at the underlying
problem that may exist with the zoning criteria or the Master Plan that
prevents a business that they all agree is satisfactory from being allowed.
John Jester (Mr. Kim’s consultant from Landmark Technologies) stated that he
had brought a mounted copy of the drawing of the property for anybody that was
unfamiliar. He stated that traffic issues had been considered when the site
plan was developed. He also said that he met with the Township planner in
August and drawn the plan in a manner that it would still be appropriate if
zoning was changed.
Trustee Wright said that the traffic issue is something that could be addressed
in a Special Use Permit. Treasurer Fink responded that the Township does not
contract zone so we cannot consider the use because the owner is not tied to
that plan. Once the property is rezoned, the owner could decide to build a
strip mall instead of a greenhouse and the Township would have no control.
Trustee Zaban asked Supervisor Martin if it was her position that the Board
send this issue back to the Planning Commission. She said that that would be
one of her recommendations. He asked what the Board’s other options were. She
stated that the Board could: 1) vote to approve the Planning Commission’s
recommendations and deny the rezoning, 2) decide not to agree with the Planning
Commission’s recommendation and approve the rezoning or, 3) table its
discussion and request that the Planning Commission reconsider the application.
Supervisor Martin said that she agrees with the Planning Commission that this
rezoning doesn’t agree with the Township Master Plan but she also agrees with
Trustee Wright that a greenhouse is an appropriate use of the property.
Trustee Zaban asked Mr. Kraft how the Planning Commission would respond if the
issue was sent back for reconsideration. Mr. Kraft said that he wasn’t sure. He
said the Commission had already reviewed uses under B2 extensively and their
biggest problem arose when considering the special use allowances. Mr. Kraft
asked if it is an option for the applicant to request a Special Use Permit for
an RE zone and then be granted a use variance. Supervisor Martin said the ZBA
cannot grant a use variance. She said the Planning Commission can recommend
changing the ordinance to allow this request as a special use under an RE zone.
Treasurer Fink added that there are several business that can be considered
potentially more obnoxious than a greenhouse that are currently allowed as
special use under RE zoning including commercial stables, commercial kennels,
and an oil and gas processing facility.
Citizen Wilbrink asked if there was a description of how the applicant’s
nursery was going to operate available for comparison to the description of a
nursery in the ordinance. Supervisor Martin said the Commission might consider
redefining the nursery description in RE.
Trustee Wright said the applicant could consider purchasing the adjacent B-
2 parcel (Concrete Concepts) to operate the retail portion of their business.
Citizen Katie Lo suggested the Board table their decision and ask the Planning
Commission to re-evaluate the request.
Todd Chamberlain requested, if it is the opinion of the Board to send the
request back to the Planning Commission for further consideration, that the
pending application be considered tabled instead of denied before
reconsideration. This will avoid some legal issues that arise once a rezoning
issue has been formally denied.
Trustee Wright made a motion that the Board table the discussion of rezoning
this parcel and send the application back to the Planning Commission for
reconsideration. The motion was supported by Trustee Zaban. Supervisor Martin
asked for discussion. Trustee Zaban suggested that the Board give the Planning
Commission an outline of the Board’s reasons for sending the request back to

Poverty Guidelines Resolution
Supervisor Martin reported that the federal guidelines identifying poverty
income levels had been recently adjusted and, therefore, the Board must now
pass a resolution to adopt the revised criteria into Williamstown Township’s
ordinance. She explained that the poverty guidelines allow property tax relief
to citizens that meet specific financial criteria. She added that this
provision has always existed and that actual income levels are typically
adjusted annually at the federal level to meet changes in economic conditions.
Trustee Wright, supported by Clerk Hiner, moved to adopt by resolution all new
federal income level poverty guidelines into the Williamstown Township
Ordinance.

Hideaway Woods Tentative Preliminary Plat Extension
Mr. Kraft stated that this tentative plat was originally approved in the fall
of 2000 with six (6) conditions. First, there was a question about the city
sewer capacity at this location because you cannot have lots of this size
without sewer hook-ups. The applicant received some leverage on December 10,
2002 when the Honorable Judge William E. Collette granted ten (10) residential
equivalent units (REUs) of wastewater treatment capacity from the City of
Williamston’s wastewater treatment system. Attorney Spagnoulo stated that this
order is not final because there has only been a partial judgment.
Mr. Kraft reported that the Planning Commission has recommended approval of a
12-month extension with conditions 1,3,4,5 and 6 remaining attached (condition
2 of the original approval has been met and does not need to be carried
forward).
Mr. Kraft reported that during discussion at the Planning Commission meeting,
there was a question about how the sewer line will cross adjoining properties.
He added that he did not feel a clear answer was provided. He said that the
Planning Commission also decided not to make a decision on the cul-de-sac
arrangement until the final changes to the plat were made.
Supervisor Martin called for questions from the Board (none) and asked the
applicant if there was any information he would like to add. Carl McIntosh,
representing the applicant, stated that he was comfortable with the Planning
Commission’s decision.
Supervisor Martin stated that she had met with the City of Williamston. The
City said that they feel they have capacity at the plant for the additional
sewer but do not have capacity in their sewer lines near this location. They
have previously experienced backups in this area (2001) and have had to
discharge to the river because of insufficient line capacity. The City said
that when this applicant submits an actual request for sewer hookup, the City
will forward the request to the DEQ with notation that they have had backup
problems.
During their meeting with Supervisor Martin, the City also described previous
problems on Linn Rd. with the sewer extension at Forest of Nottingham
Condominiums. Because the sewer line had been installed before the road, the
City incurred unnecessary costs when installing the road. The City wants to
avoid this situation from happening again by requiring the design for this plat
to include a roadway even if it never is built. If the developer decides to go
forward without a roadway to get to the 10 taps, the City also wanted the
developer to be aware that they would incur a cost for the City reviewing all
the plans again. Supervisor Martin summarized that the City wanted the Township
to be aware that the developer must satisfy several more steps before they
would be eligible for sewer hookup.
Supervisor Martin provided clarification about jurisdiction for these
properties (because they are located in the 425 area). The City will collect
property taxes for the proposed ten (10) properties. In return, owners will
receive water, sewer, leaf pickup, and police coverage. The Township will have
jurisdiction over the properties for issues pertaining to voting, building
inspection, assessing and enforcement of ordinances.
Citizen Al LeBlanc asked where Hideaway Woods was located. Supervisor Martin
responded that it is the development located across from Williamston High
School.
Trustee Zaban made a recommendation, supported by Trustee Wright, that the
Board support the decision of the Planning Commission to allow for a 1-year
extension of the tentative preliminary plat submitted for Hideaway Woods with
conditions 1,3,4,5 and 6 remaining attached (condition 2 eliminated for having
been met). Motion passed unanimously.

the end of the 2002/2003 fiscal year. Trustee Zaban made a motion that the
Board conduct an annual meeting prior to the March 4, 2003 Regular Board
Meeting to begin at 7 p.m. Motion supported by Trustee Wright. Motion passed
unanimously.

said that Williamston Greenhouse had also planned to put up a new sign and
improve the appearance of their building exterior once the construction was

Board but was urged to do so by customers who told her that businesses located

also investigate the possibility for a property tax exemption for 2003 (it’s
too late to apply for exemption in 2002) and added that guidelines are
available in the Township office. Supervisor Martin added that she plans to
include an explanation of the Property Tax Exemption process in the next
newsletter.
Supervisor Martin summarized that, to her knowledge, the Township had never

not be legal for the Township to assist a business using taxpayer money without
some type of matching support from the State. However, she added, the Township
office is willing to do whatever can be done to help.
UNFINISHED BUSINESS
1040 E. Grand River Rezoning Request RE to B-2 – Young Kim, Tabled 12/3/02
Planning Commission Chairman Dan Kraft provided background information for this
request. He stated that the Planning Commission had previously recommended
denying the request because, although the current zoning for the parcel in
question allows for use as a greenhouse, it does not allow for a retail sales
operation. At the December Township Board Meeting, the Planning Commission was
requested to re-evaluate their decision because it appeared that everyone
involved was comfortable with the proposed use but that they were prevented
from allowing the request because they were bound by zoning requirements that
may need to be amended. The Township Board had offered several options for the
Planning Commission to consider.
Mr. Kraft stated that the Planning Commission had reviewed each of the options
suggested by the Township Board and decided that it was most reasonable to
amend the description of the RE zone (the existing zone for this parcel) so
that a greenhouse retail operation could be allowed. The Planning Commission
felt that this was only a slight modification to the description and that the
wording could limit this new provision to the Grand River corridor only. The
Township Planner (Chris Doozen) agreed that this was the best option. This
recommendation will require that a public hearing be held.
Supervisor Martin asked if there were any comments from the applicant. Todd
Chamberlain, attorney representing the applicant for the zoning request, stated
that he appreciated the Board and the Planning Commission’s attention to this
matter. He summarized that he felt the process is moving on a path that will
accommodate the property owner’s needs and, at the same time, incorporate the
concerns of the Planning Commission and the Board. He said that he had learned
of the Planning Commission’s recommendation earlier in the afternoon and had
not had the opportunity to discuss the information fully with Mr. Kim. However,
he stated that his client (Young Kim) is very much interested in having this
process proceed as quickly as possible. He said he understands this to mean
that Mr. Kim needs to file an application for an ordinance change and to do so
expeditiously. Mr. Chamberlain asked that his rezoning request be again tabled
while Mr. Kim’s application is being processed through all the requisite public
hearing steps since the process is moving toward a satisfactory resolution for
both sides.
Supervisor Martin asked Mr. Spagnoulo what the legal requirements were for
repeatedly tabling a request without action by the Board. Mr. Spagnoulo stated
that he presumed Mr. Chamberlain’s concern is based on the fact that if a
request is denied, the applicant has specific timetables to meet in order to
appeal a denial with the Circuit Court. Mr. Chamberlain concurred but said his
applicant had no interest in filing an appeal since the process is moving in a
satisfactory direction. If the Board formerly declines the request, the
applicant must file with the Circuit Court within a 30-day appellate period.
Mr. Spagnoulo asked Supervisor Martin what concerns the Board had with
repeatedly tabling the issue while Mr. Kim’s application moves through the
public hearing process. Supervisor Martin said that the Board had never
repeatedly tabled an issue in her experience and so her only concern was
whether it was legally permitted to do so. Mr. Spagnoulo said that it looks
like there is a way to solve this issue in a manner satisfactory to both the
applicant and the Township but understands that Mr. Kim wants to protect his
right of appeal. He reminded the Board that, after a 6-7 month application
process, there is still a possibility that Mr. Kim’s application to amend the
zoning ordinance to include an RE exception by special use permit may not pass.
If this happens, Mr. Kim will likely ask the Board to vote to accept or deny
his request. Mr. Spagnoulo said that one option, short of litigation, was that
the Township could agree with the property owner to waive the argument of 30
days. Mr. Spagnoulo suggested that the Board table the issue at this meeting
and allow Mr. Chamberlain and him to meet to find an agreeable solution to
address these legal timetable issues. Mr. Chamberlain concurred.
Supervisor Martin asked if there were questions from any other Board Members.
No questions were asked.
Trustee Wright made a motion supported by Trustee Zaban to table the Young Kim
zoning issue again to the February 4, 2002 Board Meeting so that the Township
attorney and Mr. Chamberlain can work out the timetable details. Motion passed
unanimously.
Supervisor Martin stated that Mr. Kim must next file an application requesting
a text amendment to the ordinance. She reiterated that text amendment requests
are reviewed as a whole by the Township one time each year in October.
Applications to be discussed at the January Planning Commission meeting were
due by January 7, 2003. But, she said that if Mr. Kim returns an application to
the Township office by 4 p.m. on January 9, 2003, the Planning Commission has
agreed to include it on this month’s agenda (applications need to be received
with sufficient time for distribution and review by the Township’s planning
consultants). Supervisor Martin provided Mr. Chamberlain a copy of the
application.
Building Use/Expansion
Mr. Howell (Project Manager-Swanson Design) presented the final design proposal
for the remodel/expansion of the Township office building. Supervisor Martin
provided an overview for the reasons the Board had originally decided to
upgrade the building. She said that the building was built more than 30 years
ago. It had functioned very well during its existence but the building was now
out of date and requires a lot of work to be done in order to make it function
properly. For example, the parking lot pavement and lighting need to be
replaced, the bathrooms and entrance/exit doors need to be made handicapped
accessible, etc... She said there are also many areas where the building no
longer meets building code requirements. She stated that these existing
conditions seem inappropriate for a government facility. She added that the
office space has also become increasingly inadequate. She said that the
proposed re-design incorporates the Township’s projected needs for the next 20
years.
Mr. Howell began his presentation by stating that he had been meeting with the
Township since September 2002 and felt he had a good understanding of the
issues faced by the Township. He summarized that the major issues are: 1) the
office space is crowded and inefficient, 2) there is a lack of meeting space,
3) there is a lack of long term storage space in the building and off-site
storage is currently required to accommodate the Township’s storage needs, 4)
the building has no obvious entrance identity, 5) the exterior of the building
is dated, 6) the heating and cooling systems are inefficient and uneven
throughout the building, 7) the electrical supplies are inadequate to
accommodate the computers and other high tech equipment that has been added to
the office in recent years, and 8) the parking lot condition and lighting is
inadequate.
He stated that the Township started with four (4) options for redesign ranging
from a minor remodeling to replace the existing building with a completely new
building. Over the past four months, the project was narrowed to tonight’s
proposal that includes remodeling the current building and putting a small
addition on the front and back of the building. Supervisor Martin added that
Swanson Design was also responsible for the recent Wheatfield Township hall
redesign where many of the same concerns existed.  
Mr. Howell presented a drawing of the proposed floor plan. He described each of
the new proposed building uses (see attached drawings). He highlighted: 1) the
new front and back entrances, 2) new file storage space, 3) new office space
including enclosed space for appropriate offices, 4) fire rated storage space,
5) a new conference room, 6) remodeled restrooms to meet code 7) remodeled and
extended kitchen area, and 8) rental space/meeting space that can be flexibly
adjusted in size.
Next he summarized the site modifications included in the proposal: 1) the
entire parking lot will be pulled up and re-paved and parking capacity will be
enlarged from 50 to 70 spaces, 2) the exterior of the main entry will be
updated to match the new addition, 3) exterior stucco will be added to tie the
building together, 4) the exterior sloped soffet will be removed, 5) the upper
windows in the banquet area will be removed and windows will be placed along
the west wall to improve banquet room lighting, 6) the street sign will be
relocated to a more visible position and 7) new solid (non-glass) double wide
doors will be added to the back entrance.
Supervisor Martin called for questions from the audience. Mr. Spagnoulo asked
if, by making this modification to the building, the Township was no longer
“grandfathered” and now must comply with all handicap rules. Mr. Howell
responded that the Township would now need to comply. Supervisor Martin added
that the Township has several residents that require assistance to use the
current building. Supervisor Martin stated that the plan is for the Township
offices to move to the current banquet hall space on the south side of the
building during the renovation and then move back once the north half of the
building is completed.
Citizen Dexter asked how many square feet would be added to the building and
what the cost per square foot would be. Mr. Howell responded that the two
additions to the front and back of the building total approximately 1000 sq.
ft. The remodel of the remaining building will also add approx. 400 sq. ft. of
useable space. He said that Swanson Design had done an in depth cost estimate
at the request of the Township. As a result, they had calculated an estimated
subtotal cost of $376,659. By adding a 10% contingency they calculated a total
cost $459,825 for non-mandatory tasks. He added that this number does not
include the mandatory parking lot lighting/repaving, roof repair, phone system
and security system upgrades which will have to be done whether the renovation
takes place or not. These mandatory improvement costs will total $88,486.
Therefore, the total cost for essential and remodel improvements is $548,311.
Attorney Spagnoulo asked what tasks were included in the $70,000 site
improvement and maintenance upgrade cost. Mr. Howell responded that this cost
includes taking up and repaving the parking lot and adding adequate lighting.
He added that site drainage will not change.
Citizen Dexter stated that the proposal seemed like a lot of money for 1000
additional square feet of building. Treasurer Fink responded that this project
cannot be looked at simply on the number of square feet being added because the
Township will be gaining much more than 1000 sq feet. She clarified for Mr.
Dexter that this cost covers remodeling the entire building to upgrade many
non-compliance, inadequate and inefficient work areas. She said the Township is
gaining a more modern and useable building.
Trustee Zaban added that in the 15 years he has been involved with the Township
there has been no money spent on the building with the exception of about $300
in landscaping and the cost of a roof repair. He said there should have been
more money spent on the building previously and that the parking lot should
have been done a long time ago. Mr. Howell made a comparison to other relevant
projects based on his firm’s previous experience and determined that the
Township’s estimate was about $20/sq. ft. below the cost of similar projects.
Supervisor Martin reiterated that there are several problems with the building
that absolutely must be repaired including the electrical system (the current
system cannot handle the computer networking needs of the office) and the phone
system (the current phone system is wholly inadequate).
Trustee Zaban added that his biggest concern with the building has always been
security. The lighting in the parking lot is inadequate (the proposed upgrade
includes 6 more lights outside). There will be one main entry instead of two.
There will be an alarm system and better security on the doors (which will have
improved locking mechanisms). Supervisor Martin stated that the Township has
been advised by the Ingham County Sheriff’s Department to have a building alarm
system-especially due to the computer hardware on-site. She added that many
Township citizens will also be using this space as a rental hall. The current
rental fee is only $60 which is an incredible bargain. With upgrades, the
Township will be able to legitimately charge more for space rental.
Citizen Al LeBlanc asked if the entire roof must be replaced during the
remodel. Supervisor Martin said that the roof was re-shingled 2 years ago (the
plan had been to wait for the renovation but couldn’t because of serious leak
problems). Attorney Spagnoulo said that from his perspective (he works with
several Townships) our existing office is not extravagant. Supervisor Martin
asked Mr. Howell to compare the renovation costs without any additions to the
costs to doing a complete remodel (an option considered at one of the early
proposal stages). He said that that option had an estimated cost of $58,000
without including the mandatory changes to the parking area, etc… He estimated
that just remodeling half the building would cost about $300,000.
Citizen Katie Lo asked if the cost of tearing up the parking lot included
hauling the material away. Mr. Howell responded that it did. She asked what the
Building Inspector thought of this proposal. Mr. Aven responded that he thinks
the remodel is long overdue-especially when you have a government building that
is not handicap accessible. He added that it appears to be an excellent cost
proposal for all that will be accomplished. Attorney Spagnoulo asked if there
was concern about having the new additions match the existing building. Mr.
Howell said his firm has a lot of experience addressing this type of problem
and have had good success in the past. Al LeBlanc asked how the heating and
cooling system will be affected by the remodel. Mr. Howell said that the
existing heating and cooling system will remain. He pointed out on the site
drawing where new heat systems will be added. Treasurer Fink added that a zone
heating system is more appropriate for this type of building because there are
spaces that aren’t used at different times.
Supervisor Martin asked for additional questions from the audience or the
Board.
Franz Wilbrink asked how the Township planned to pay for the renovation.
Supervisor Martin said that the Township has been setting aside funds for the
project in the same manner that has been done previously for the Township Park
and the road construction on Mitchell and Vanneter Roads. She added that the
Township’s accountant feels that the renovation can be accomplished without
jeopardizing the Township’s reserve. There will be no need for tax increases.
Katie Lo asked if the new renovation design will eliminate the need for off-
site storage. Clerk Hiner responded that off-site storage would no longer be
necessary and the renovation should accommodate storage for a projected 15
years.
Trustee Wright said that the Board had looked at a number of options and that
the proposal presented tonight gives the Township the most for our investment.
He added that his primary concern was that the proposal incorporate projected
Township needs for the next 20 years. He said that he felt that Swanson had
provided a reasonable cost estimate. Trustee Wright said that by taking a
middle of the road approach, the Township is getting the most for its money. He
said he realizes that it’s a lot of money but he believes the Township needs to
provide an adequate building for its staff and its citizens. He added that the
Board put a lot of consideration into avoiding driving up the costs.
Mr. Howell said that when Swanson prepares an estimate, their goal is to be
within 10% and err on the high side. He said that if the bids come in too high,
the Township has three (3) options: 1) the project can be cancelled, 2) the
Township can decide to pay the higher price or 3) we can re-evaluate the
options within the project and eliminate tasks to bring the project within
budget.
Trustee Wright said that he believes that the costs presented by Swanson are
conservatively on the high side. He said that he’s very comfortable with the
proposal that has been developed. Walt Aven said that it is a good time to
request bids because of the economy and because it is winter so construction
work is slow. He added that money in savings isn’t earning interest. Trustee
Wright added that there are a lot of contractors looking for work.
Supervisor Martin requested a motion on whether to proceed. Trustee Wright made
a motion for the Township to move forward with the building expansion project
as proposed. Clerk Hiner supported the motion. Supervisor Martin called for a
roll call vote.

Dexter Legal Description
Supervisor Martin summarized that Mr. Dexter has approached the Township
because the legal description of his property is not matching up with any
survey of the property. He needs to resolve this discrepancy quickly because he
wants to re-mortgage the property. Mr. Dexter believes that the Township
property overlaps his property by 19 ft. and that the problem appears to be
caused by a survey monument error. Mr. Dexter has submitted an explanation of
the problem prepared by KEBS Surveying on his behalf.
Supervisor Martin said that the Township attorney has reviewed the KEBS letter
and made three recommendations to the Township: 1) an independent survey can be
done by a third party firm to confirm the information presented by KEBS, 2) the
Township can look at the problem practically and accept the memo from KEBS as
fact or 3) the Township and Mr. Dexter can wait for Ingham County surveyors to
re-monument the survey point in question. Trustee Wright asked whether the
county has a schedule that could be accelerated to complete this re-monumenting
as soon as possible. He said it was his opinion that if the County cannot re-
monument soon, then the Township should get it done by a third party.
Mr. Dexter said that the property has been surveyed four (4) times and each
time they come up with a different answer. Until the county redoes the monument
it won’t come out accurate. Vince Spagnoulo said that the Kebs letter uses the
term “may be in question” which is a little loose, making it difficult to make
a decision based on the letter alone. Mr. Dexter stated that if the 19 feet in
question does belong to the Township, then he will no longer be in conformance
with road frontage rules. Supervisor Martin said that the property would be
“grandfathered” in that instance. Mr. Dexter said that when the Township
purchased 41 feet in 1994, the error in the survey should have been discovered.
Attorney Spagnoulo said that he has worked with similar situations. He told Mr.
Dexter that it is appropriate for him to go to his refinancing company, tell
them the situation, and tell them the Township has agreed that when the issue
is resolved it will quit claim any deed over to Mr. Dexter if necessary. Mr.
Spagnoulo said that the Township is able to make that type of promise. That way
Mr. Dexter can get approval by his title insurance company. Mr. Dexter
responded that he didn’t think his title insurance company would agree and
asked if the Township could prepare a letter. Mr. Spagnoulo said that Mr.
Dexter should contact the title company, ask what they need from the Township
and then the Township will do what is right once the correct survey is made.
Treasurer Fink asked if the Township could request the County re-monument this
location ahead of schedule. Clerk Hiner said that she will contact Bob Foltz
tomorrow at the Ingham County Tax Mapping office to inform him of this issue
and request that this location be re-monumented immediately. She will also
forward him copy of the letter describing the history of the problem prepared
by KEBS. Mr. Dexter said there is a proper locatable monument. White Surveying
used the intersection but he should have used the monument 62 feet south.
Vincent Spagnoulo told Mr. Dexter that he could have his representative from
the title insurance company (Bill McGowen, Michigan Banker’s Title) contact him
to clarify the criteria needed. Supervisor Martin said the Township will do
whatever is the correct thing to do.

actually encourages rentals. She said the City of East Lansing had to add this
provision because they have so many student rentals. However, it doesn’t make

forward without any changes.

Bartels-Burn Petition
Supervisor Martin provided an overview of a letter sent to the Township by Mr.
Karl Bartels regarding the Burn Ordinance that was passed last fall as well as
her response letter. She said that Mr. Bartels had called last December to get
a burn permit and discovered that his property was in a restricted area. He was
initially confused because he thought the zoning had changed but now realizes
that only the burn status for his property changed. He has concerns about the
current burn status for Pheasant Run Subdivision. Supervisor Martin invited Mr.
Bartels to address the Board.
Mr. Bartels reiterated that he was indeed initially confused and thought that
the zoning for his property had changed. He said he wasn’t aware that the Burn
Ordinance had changed. He said that his neighbors that signed his petition were
also unaware. Supervisor Martin responded that everyone in the Township was
notified in the October 2002 Township Newsletter. Mr. Bartel’s said he had read
the newsletter but was confused by the black and white map. He said that the
reason he was appearing at the Board meeting tonight was to ask that the
calender system (where burning takes place only on the day that it is allowed)
be eliminated for Pheasant Run Subdivision and their original “call-in” burn
status returned. He added that he believes that the new system is unsafe
because it does not allow for burning to take place on weather appropriate
days.
Supervisor Martin requested questions from the Board. Treasurer Fink asked for
clarification of how Mr. Bartels shares burn space with his neighbors. Mr.
Bartels explained that he and his neighbors accumulate brush at a single
community location. When the pile has reached a sufficient size, he burns the
material at a weather appropriate time. Mr. Bartels added that several times he
has phoned for a burn permit but the weather did not cooperate so he did not
burn. Treasurer Fink agreed that when citizens are restricted to burn on a
specific day, it may not allow burning on the most appropriate weather day. Mr.
Bartels asked if it was a possibility that the rules could be changed so that
he could burn on the weather appropriate day he chooses. Treasurer Fink stated
that she believed it was a possibility.
Supervisor Martin explained that the Burn Ordinance was written to include
specific burn days for subdivisions because, without restriction, it is
conceivable that somebody could be burning every day of the week. This results
in many neighbor complaints. She added that there are many people in the
Township that don’t want the Township to allow burning at all. They find it an
environmentally poor practice, are not happy with the smell or they complain of
physical problems like asthma. The citizens that prepared the Burn Ordinance
believed that if everyone in a subdivision knew which day of the month burning
could take place, they could prepare themselves by burning at the same time or
temporarily leaving their property if they found the smoke offensive. This was
a compromise to accommodate all citizens.
Mr. Bartels said he understands this issue can be a problem in dense
subdivisions but he does not agree that it applies to his subdivision. Trustee
Wright added that the Township held numerous public hearings on this issue and
numerous citizens provided input. He said it would have been good if Mr.
Bartels or somebody from his subdivision had attended to voice their opinion.
Mr. Wright stated that there were many people at those meetings, including
Ingham County’s representative, that didn’t want to allow burning at all
(similar to the policy followed in Meridian Township). Mr. Bartels referred to
a statement in Supervisor Martin’s response letter about residents in the
Township not imposing on the rights of others. He suggested that the ordinance
infringes on his rights. Treasurer Fink said that indeed it does but that’s
because the Township is becoming more and more crowded so the Board has to look
at everybody’s rights. She added that she could foresee this ordinance becoming
even more restrictive in the future. She said if she were to change the
existing ordinance, she might consider allowing burning on days when it was
weather appropriate (instead of on pre-specified days) but she would vote to
limit the number of requests that could be made (for instance to four times per
year). She would not be willing to return to an open policy for burning
whenever a citizen wanted.
Mr. Bartels asked if the petition he submitted with 100% of the neighbors in
his subdivision agreeing with his request held any weight in the Board’s
decision. Trustee Wright asked if the people signing the petition understood
that the changes regarding burning in their subdivision were not due to a
zoning change (as stated on the petition). He said he is concerned that they
may not have understood properly what they were signing. He said that he would
like to speak to a couple of people on the petition to make sure they did.
Trustee Wright added that if 100% of the homeowners in a subdivision want to
change the requirements for their subdivision, then he doesn’t have a problem
allowing the change. But, if one or two of the neighbors do not agree, then
there is a problem. Treasurer Fink stated that the burn ordinance allows for
preparing a petition as a course of action by subdivision homeowners. She added
that she is not sure that Mr. Bartels’ petition meets the format requirements.
Mr. Bartels said he hoped his petition would be enough to initiate discussion.
Supervisor Martin asked Mr. Bartels to clarify the verbage he used to describe
the current burn status to his neighbors signing the petition (noting that the
wording on the petition incorrectly refers to a zone change from Ag-Small Farm
to RR). Mr. Bartels said his verbal explanation was basically that the petition
signatures were being collected to eliminate the restrictions of a calender
date. He added that he reworded his second petition to eliminate the zone
change information before collecting additional signatures from neighbors
outside of his subdivision that may be impacted by his community burn.
Supervisor Martin agreed that the second petition wording was much clearer.
Trustee Wright explained that the Board has been working on a policy for
outlining the format requirements for a petition. He stated the Board needs to
establish those standards to be sure that the people signing a petition are
completely aware of what they are signing.
Citizen LeBlanc asked if the petition were accepted, would the burn rules for
all subdivisions zoned RR change. Trustee Wright said he would not entertain
making an across the board change. Mr. Bartels stated that he was requesting
the change for his subdivision only (where there are about 10 homes on 40
acres). Supervisor Martin stated that the people who signed the second petition
are not in Mr. Bartels’ subdivision so their property has not been affected by
the Burn Ordinance change. Mr. Bartels said he took the second petition to
people outside his subdivision to be sure he spoke with everyone that might be
affected by smoke from his brush pile.
Supervisor Martin said that she hoped the people that signed this second
petition were not under the misimpression that their burn status had changed.
She clarified that the change to the Burn Ordinance prohibited burning on RR
zoned land in subdivision and condominium developments only. Homes in RR zones
outside of subdivisions don’t have the same restriction and they still have the
ability to request a call-in burn permit. Mr. Bartels said that perhaps he
should move his brush pile to the property of a neighbor outside of his
subdivision. Treasurer Fink stated that this might be a good option. Mr.
Bartels added that his existing brush pile is in an ideal location because it
is isolated and has ready access to water.
Supervisor Martin said that the ordinance was written to allow individual
subdivisions to request special consideration if there is 100% agreement among
the homeowners. Treasurer Fink stated that the ability to petition for change
is identified in the ordinance. Mr. Bartels said that he could go back around
and recollect signatures on a revised petition. Trustee Wright said that the
Board has to be sure that the people signing understand what they are signing
to avoid having somebody come in after a change is made and declare that they
didn’t understand. Supervisor Martin stated that this is the first request for
a modification to the Burn Ordinance so it will set a precedent. Trustee Wright
said a lot of time and effort went in by many Township residents and the Burn
Ordinance Committee to prepare the ordinance and careful consideration must be
made before changing it
Clerk Hiner asked if the Board wanted to determine the content of a revised
petition. Treasurer Fink clarified that there is specific instructions for what
should be included in a petition made by a subdivision to alter their
restrictions for burning and that she would like to see the petition
resubmitted in compliance with these items. Mr. Bartels said he would bring the
petition in for review by Supervisor Martin before he goes to his neighbors
again for signatures. Trustee Wright reiterated that the Board is not against
this request, but they want to make sure that it is handled correctly. Trustee
Wright added that if the Board considers making a change for Pheasant Run
Subdivision, the homeowners surrounding the subdivision would likely be
notified as well.
Treasurer Fink reiterated that the Township came up with this very complicated
Burn Ordinance document trying to satisfy everybody’s needs. Supervisor Martin
added that this Burn Ordinance is a compromise. In the old ordinance, citizens
couldn’t even have a campfire without a permit. With the changes included in
the new ordinance, campfires are now permitted. Mr. Bartels reminded the Board
that the procedure he uses for a community burn effectually limits the burns in
his subdivision. Trustee Wright said that this is a very good point and this
fact will make the Board’s decision a lot easier.
Recycling
Trustee Wright reported that the resources that have been available to him for
the last ten (10) years that allowed him to provide a recycling service to the
Township are no longer available (except at a cost that would be prohibitive
for the Township). He presented an alternate proposal for Granger to handle the
Township’s recycling needs. Granger would continue to collect recycling on the
2nd Saturday of each month. He explained that the proposal includes a container
delivery fee, a trucking fee, and a processing fee. The total cost for each
monthly service is $295. He added that this is $105 less than current costs but
does not include staffing. Trustee Wright suggested that the new maintenance
person also supervise recycling. He added that supervision is necessary because
there are a lot of seniors that use the service and some assistance is helpful.
People don’t necessarily recycle properly and if there is contamination, the
load has to go to the landfill which will cost the Township about $100 more. He
added that the opening to the container is high and some people may have a
problem lifting their material. Trustee Wright said that the collection
container would be kept locked except during posted collection hours. People
will still probably leave bags around the storage container during off hours
but they could be processed by the maintenance person. Trustee Wright said the
Township could probably even offer expanded hours. Supervisor Martin said that
she had spoken with Gerald Gorton (who will be assuming the maintenance
position on February 11) and he said he had no problem with working the 2nd
Saturday of every month. Trustee Wright said that people typically drop off
recycling between 11:45 a.m. and 2 p.m. with a final rush at 3 p.m. (near
closing time). Recycling hasn’t been open earlier because the soccer fields are
often in use on Saturday morning.
There was a discussion of where the container should be placed. Supervisor
Martin suggested using the circle drive. Trustee Wright said that there are 5
compartments in the container with some compartments having access from both
sides. He added that the scouts typically collect newspapers with an unmanned
trailer during the Township’s recycling hours. He recommended that if the
Scouts continue, they provide their own supervision. That leaves the Township
to collect magazines, #2 plastic, milk jugs, clear glass, tin, and brown glass
(which only amounts to 10-15 gallons). Trustee Wright said that Granger will
provide signs. He said the Township dumpster is used for anything that gets
rejected. Granger will provide educational handouts.
Trustee Wright said that Saturday, February 8, 2003 will be his last recycling

Poverty Asset Level
Supervisor Martin reported that the Township must approve a Poverty Asset Level
Test in conjunction with the previously approved Poverty Guidelines. This means
the Township needs to determine how much a taxpayer is allowed in assets to
still meet the Poverty Level Guidelines. Trustee Wright asked what a typical
asset level was. Clerk Hiner said she could find no guidelines at the federal
level or with the Township Association. Members of the Board agreed that
homesteads should be exempt from inclusion in any asset level test. Clerk Hiner
said that one vehicle should also be exempted. Trustee Wright asked for
clarification if this process is to set a limit for assets (in addition to
income) that a person cannot exceed before qualification for property tax
exemption. Treasurer Fink explained that the Township has a four (4) page
document that must be completed by anyone seeking to have their property taxes
exempted. There is currently only one person in the Township that has made this
request. Supervisor Martin said that the federal poverty guidelines are very
strict and she doubts that anyone that meets those poverty guidelines will have
many assets. Treasurer Fink said that in order for someone to maintain
financial independence, they should be allowed one working vehicle to be
exempted. Supervisor Martin said that the Board of Review can decide to allow a
partial property tax exemption. Trustee Wright suggested that all assets be
included except an applicant’s home and one vehicle. Supervisor Martin
requested a motion.
Treasurer Fink moved that the Township adopt an Asset Level Test that exempts
the applicant’s home and one vehicle when determining whether an individual
meets the Township Poverty Level Guidelines for property tax exemption. Motion
supported by Trustee Zaban. Motion passed unanimously.
Surplus Property
Supervisor Martin read the following suggested policy into the minutes: “It
will be the policy of the Williamstown Township Board to have the most
qualified person determine the value of surplus properties. The price will be
set with a suggested guideline of approximately 10% of the value of new.”
Supervisor Martin explained that the Township is not allowed to give away or
donate anything removed during the remodeling. It can only be sold or thrown
away. There has to be consistency in how items are sold which is why this
policy has been prepared. She said that she would like the Township to keep a
running list of every item that needs to be disposed of so that Board members
can regularly review the sale prices to make sure that they are reasonable.
Trustee Zaban made a motion to accept the policy as stated. Trustee Wright
supported the motion. Motion passed unanimously.

Building Fees
Supervisor Martin reported that a question has arisen regarding building fees.
When somebody blatantly or unintentionally ignores getting a building permit,
it often takes extra effort by the Building Inspector to track the building
permit down. Walt Aven (Williamstown Township Building Inspector) stated that
according to the original Uniform Building Code, the Township was allowed to
double fees as a penalty in this circumstance. The Michigan Uniform Building
Code, however, does not address this issue at all so if the Township wants to
penalize people for not obtaining the proper permits (and thereby causing extra
administrative time by the inspector) the Board would have to establish this as
a policy. The inspector cannot just double the fees arbitrarily without a Board
decision. He added that this penalty is especially appropriate for contractors
who know the rules. We may need to be more flexible with homeowners who are
unaware of the permit process and when it applies.
Trustee Wright agreed that we should be more lenient with homeowners who are
new to the area but that contractors are well aware of the permitting process.
Supervisor Martin agreed that the Board should set a policy to handle this type
of situation.
Inspector Aven said that the minimum building permit fee is $35 so doubling
would bring the fee to $70. Supervisor Martin suggested that a person should be
given one warning and if they don’t come in to get the proper permit, then
their penalty fee should start being applied. Treasurer Fink added that the
Township should require a deadline to respond. Supervisor Martin asked Mr. Aven
how Meridian Township handles these situations. He said that the situation did
not occur very often but their response varied. If it was a homeowner, they
gave them a warning but if it was a builder (who knows the rules) they doubled
the fee. Supervisor Martin asked how they handled a homeowner that didn’t come
in to get the permit after a warning. Mr. Aven said there was never an instance
where the homeowner didn’t come in and pay the fee once notified.
Supervisor Martin asked Inspector Aven to prepare a written schedule for how
building permit fees and penalty fees should be applied to present at the March
Board Meeting. Supervisor Martin asked that a warning letter be the first step
in the process. Citizen LeBlanc asked if it is possible to add a statement to
the warning letter saying that there will also be a charge for any attorney
fees associated with collecting the building permit fee. Supervisor Martin said
the Township attorney has not completely clarified whether the Township can do
this. Treasurer Fink added that a reminder about building permits should go in
the next newsletter.

Petition Policy
Supervisor Martin presented an informal petition policy prepared by Clerk
Hiner. Clerk Hiner said that she researched policies of other townships and
modeled her proposed version using portions of those that made sense for our
Township’s needs. She added
 
that she kept the draft wording very basic because the policy is not binding so
it should not be complex. She added that if we were preparing a policy for
legally binding petitions, the Township would need a very detailed document.
Clerk Hiner explained that the absolute basic requirements of an informal
petition policy are that the petition be legible, printed on paper, and signed
by at least one person who resides in the Township with their printed name and
address. Therefore, she chose to adopt these three requirements into the draft
Township policy. In addition, she has prepared an attached document which
explains the steps that must be taken to present an informal petition and
offers suggested guidelines for preparing the petition.
 
Citizen LeBlanc stated that these guidelines are important because people have
a tendency to sign anything just to get rid of the person presenting a petition
at their door.
Supervisor Martin said she would not consider any petition valid if there was
not an explanation of what was being signed at the top of the page.
Treasurer Fink said that it would be misleading to tell the public that this
draft informal petition policy is the minimum requirement. She said that if a
petitioner includes only these three items and then brings their petition to
the Board, she would be obligated to turn the petition down because there is no
wording at the top of any page identifying the issue being petitioned.
Trustee Wright said that he feels that the information that has been included
in the suggested guidelines should be made the required guidelines.
Clerk Hiner said that the more guidelines you add to the informal petition
policy the more weight you give to the petition. She said that her proposed
policy presents the minimum requirements and that the attachment titled “Steps
in presenting an informal petition” is the document that would be given to a
citizen to guide them though assembling a petition.
Treasurer Fink asked how the petition process was worded in the Burn Ordinance.
Supervisor Martin read from the ordinance “…the petition should be consistent
with general policies of the Township regarding format and content of
petitions.” Trustee Zaban clarified that, since the Township does not currently
have a general policy regarding format and content of petitions, the topic is
being discussed tonight.
Trustee Wright made a motion supported by Trustee Zaban to approve the proposed
Petition Policy as written. Motion passed unanimously.

Permit Fee Policy
Supervisor Martin read the proposed Permit Fee Policy into the minutes:
“Whenever any work for which a permit is required by the building code has been
commenced without first obtaining said permit, a special investigation shall be
made before a permit may be issued for such work.
An investigation fee, in addition to the permit fee, shall be collected whether
or not a permit is then or subsequently issued. The investigation fee shall be
equal to the amount of the permit fee required. The minimum investigation fee
shall be the same as the minimum fee. The payment of such investigation fee
shall not exempt any person from compliance with all other provisions of this
code nor from any penalty prescribed by law.
   Fee      For expenditures up to and including $5,000.00      $35.00
   For each $1,000.00 or fraction thereof above $5,000.00   $ 5.00
   Re-inspection fee                  $35.00 ”
Supervisor Martin recommended expanding the wording in the first sentence to
state “provisions of the building code.” Trustee Wright clarified that if a
homeowner puts a deck on his property without first getting a permit, he may
pay $35 for a permit plus a $35 penalty. The decision to apply this fee will be
made at the discretion of the Township and will be based on whether the
omission was intentional or due to inexperience. Fees will be applied to
contractors that fail to get the proper permits because they are aware of the
requirements. Supervisor Martin added that citizens moving into our Township
from other areas may be confused because every municipality has different
permit requirements and they may simply not realize a permit is required for
certain tasks. Supervisor Martin suggested that the wording “ an investigation
fee shall” be changed to “an investigation fee may” so that the decision can be
made at the discretion of the Township. Supervisor Martin said that she is most
concerned with the people who have been notified of the permit requirement and
they still fail to come in to get the proper permits. Trustee Wright asked if
the Township has any leverage for collecting permit fees in this case and if it
could be attached to property taxes? Supervisor Martin said that it could not
be attached to property taxes but any new or modified structure involved could
be tagged as a violation to be taken down. The issue could also be taken
through the court process.
Trustee Zaban made a motion supported by Trustee Wright to approve the proposed
Permit Fee Policy with the wording corrected to “provisions of the building
code” and “an investigation fee may” as discussed. Motion passed unanimously.

states that these three recycling centers exist and anyone in Ingham County is
allowed to use them. A copy of this document was included in board packets for
information only-no action is required. Treasurer Fink asked how these
facilities were being funded. Trustee Wright said that originally Ingham County
had planned to start charging a tax on all waste leaving the county and that
they expected the haulers to collect the tax from citizens (the hauler’s
customers) for them. The haulers filed a lawsuit against the County because
they did not agree that they should be collecting taxes on behalf of the
County. Trustee Wright added that the issue was settled and never actually made
it to court. Instead, the haulers agreed to pay the money necessary to run the
program in the form of a donation. They preferred this solution to having the
County force them to collect the tax from their customers.
School Resolution
Citizen Rutger Hoag (Williamstown Township Planning Commissioner) presented the
Township Board with a draft resolution for consideration regarding the position
of the Township on the upcoming school bond issue. Supervisor Martin read his
proposed resolution letter into the minutes:
“Be it resolved that the Township of Williamstown sand against the proposed
Williamston Community Schools Bond proposal scheduled for vote on April 22,
2003:
To preserve the rural environment required in the township Master Plan all
major development in the township must be south of Sherwood Road. However, the
portion of monies collected form this Bond proposal would in effect fund school
facilities north of Sherwood Road being in direct violation of the Williamstown
Township Master Plan.”
Treasurer Fink clarified that the Township Master Plan does not say “must,” it
says “should.” Trustee Wright said that he does not believe the Township should
take a position for or against the bond issue until after it is voted on and
the school board has to come to the Township for approval.
Walt Aven said that school construction projects must be submitted for plan
review and on-site inspections. Supervisor Martin read from the February 2003
Michigan Department of Consumer & Industry Services Bulletin for clarification:
“…the law also provides for inspection by local code enforcement agencies where
the local school board and the local unit of government certify the local
enforcing agency has full-time plan review and inspection staff and are
otherwise qualified to perform these duties in the review and inspection of
school buildings.”
Trustee Wright asked whether just by having the bond proposed and approved by
the voters, does that necessarily mean the Township has to allow development.
Supervisor
Martin said that the School Board must have Township approval for design, but
does not need Township approval to determine whether the project happens or
not.
Citizen LeBlanc said he had read something that suggested that they school
board would also be putting any future additional facilities at the Lockwood
property site as well. Supervisor Martin agreed that this had been stated in
some documents. Treasurer Fink said the schools will have to construct their
own sewer. She added that it will become one of those isolated sewer systems
that the Township is not endorsing.
Citizen Frans Wilbrink said that at one meeting he attended, there was
discussion that a future high school and/or possible 8th/9th grade school could
go on that property.
Trustee Wright asked if the Township Board should meet with the School Board
before the bond issue election takes place. Supervisor Martin said that she had
been contacted by the School Board for dates that they could present to the
Township and she had given them the April meeting dates for both the Township
Board and Planning Commission. Supervisor Martin suggested that this discussion
with surrounding communities should have taken place a year ago.
Citizen Frans Wilbrink said that he felt it would set a bad precedent for the
Board to take a position on the school bond as suggested in Mr. Hoag’s proposed
resolution. Trustee Wright said that he doesn’t believe the Board should take a
position on the School Bond issue until the election takes place.
Citizen LeBlanc asked who would need to approve any proposed sewer system.
Supervisor Martin said that the Michigan Department of Environmental Quality
would be involved and the Ingham County Health Department would also likely be
involved. Treasurer Fink clarified that the Township Board had decided not to
endorse sewer systems because there is a history in the Township of these
systems failing.

Stormwater Phase II
Treasurer Fink presented the final information being submitted regarding the
Township Stormwater Phase II application. She said she had spoken with Kurt
Guter and he had recommended the Township contact our representative (Ms.
Sheryl Bartley) from the
Michigan Department of Environmental Quality (MDEQ) to ask what the downside
would be to the Township submitting a jurisdictional permit. Ms. Bartley said
the downside would primarily affect the MDEQ and not the Township. Treasurer
Fink explained that the Township was originally supposed to file a watershed
permit for stormwater discharge. Part of the Township’s new mandated area is in
the Looking Glass Watershed (we previously were only included in the Red Cedar
Watershed). Treasurer Fink said had also spoken to Norman Kammeraad who is
preparing a similar application for Blendon Township Township. His plan is to
also use the approach of submitting a jurisdictional permit. Applications for
jurisdictional permits were issued on February 26 (12 days before their March
10 due date). Treasurer Fink added that Tetra Tech had resubmitted documents to
the Township with corrected drain information. Treasurer Fink said she believes
the Township can submit a jurisdictional application and still satisfy the
filing requirements adequately. She added that nested jurisdictions include
Ingham County Roads and Ingham County Drains so she is going to list Ingham
County as a potential nested jurisdiction. She will cite the reason as because
they own the roads and the drains.
Treasurer Fink said that the Township is probably going to need to hire a
consultant at some point and recommends Mr. Kammeraad be considered because he
is knowledgeable of this issue and already providing consulting services to
other municipalities. She said that the Township is still technically filing an
empty permit because our application claims that we have no jurisdiction over
anything in or area.
Supervisor Martin said that she has been continually reviewing the stormwater
information that has been sent to the Township office and feels that the
jurisdictional permit process is the best way for the Township to submit.
Treasurer Fink made a motion, supported by Trustee Wright, to transfer all
stormwater documentation made from a watershed permit over to a jurisdictional
permit. Motion passed unanimously.
Citizen LeBlanc asked which two drains were identified in the Looking Glass
Watershed. Treasurer Fink said the two drains were located in Pebblebrook
Subdivision and Pheasant Run Subdivision.

Burn Ordinance Petition
Supervisor Martin reported that Karl Bartels’ revised Burn Ordinance Petition
had been received by mail today. Trustee Wright clarified whether burning of
leaves and grass was permitted by the burn ordinance in Pheasant Run
Subdivision. Supervisor Martin read from the ordinance and verified that it was
permitted.
Trustee Wright said that it is hard to argue with the desires of every single
person who lives in the Pheasant Run Subdivision. He asked what needed to be
done when the houses in the subdivision sell and new people move in if the
Township agrees to grant Mr. Bartel’s request. Clerk Hiner said that if this
request is approved, the issue should be revisited in 2 years. This is the same
schedule for reviewing the entire burn ordinance. Trustee Wright said that the
Township should allow a change in the burn requirements for Pheasant Run
Subdivision to be valid until such time as the burn ordinance is revisited by
the Township. Treasurer Fink asked if the Township wants to accept all the
requests the petitioners have made. Trustee Wright said the Township should
approve the request as long as all burning is done on the community burn pile
as indicated by Mr. Bartels at the February Board Meeting. He clarified that
tonight’s approval would allow for burning in the subdivision’s community burn
pile but does not allow homeowners to deviate from the burn ordinance
individually. Treasurer Fink said that she agrees the Board’s approval should
be limited to allowing burning outside of the burn ordinance in
the designated area only. She added that the community burn pile concept is the
reason why this exception request is agreeable. Supervisor Martin agreed.
Trustee Wright made a motion that the Township approve the Pheasant Run
Subdivision request made in Mr. Karl Bartel’s petition with the following
conditions: 1) individual parcels in Pheasant Run Subdivision will continue to
adhere to the burn ordinance as written, and 2) the subdivision must have a
designated burn area and burning will meet the same requirements as for non-
subdivision lots designated RR. This change is allowed until such time as the
burn ordinance is revised. At that time this request will also be reviewed.
Motion supported by Trustee Zaban. Motion passed unanimously.
