NEW BUSINESS
Complaints-Hofmann 4270 Beeman Road
Supervisor Martin explained that the process for dealing with citizen
complaints is that: 1) a complaint is made to the Township office, 2) the
complaint is investigated, 3) the Township Supervisor writes a letter to the
person in violation and 4) the issue is then brought to the Township Board if
further action is necessary.
 
Supervisor Martin stated that a complaint has been made against the owner of
4270 Beeman Rd. (Mr. Herb Hofmann) by a neighbor at 4300 Beeman Rd. (Mr. Carl
Franks ) about activity not permitted in the zoning ordinance. The complaint
was investigated and Mr. Hofmann was sent a letter (dated 3/25/03) regarding
the zoning violations. Supervisor Martin read the letter into the minutes which
specifically identified two (2) violations: 1) parking of commercial vehicles
on the property (Section 4.01, subsection E of the Zoning Ordinance states that
“the parking of no more than one (1) commercial vehicle with a rated capacity
of over one (1) ton may be permitted on a residential parcel) and 2) noise
disturbance (Section 9.02, subsection A.2, of the Zoning Ordinance states that
“all such activity shall be prohibited between the hours of 8:00 p.m. and 7:00
a.m. Monday through Saturday or any time on Sunday or holidays in such a manner
as to cause a noise disturbance across a residential district boundary”).
 
Supervisor Martin reported that Mr. Hofmann responded to the Township’s 3/25/03
letter in writing and his letter was received at the Township office on Monday,
March 31, 2003. Supervisor Martin summarized the response letter in which he
states that the equipment is not commercial because it is not licensed to drive
on a public thoroughfare and has not been used for any commercial endeavor. He
also states that he only used the equipment after 8:00 p.m. one time and that
he is using the equipment for landscaping his own property. His letter stated
there is other equipment on the property owned by Mr. Jorgenson which will be
removed by April 7. Supervisor Martin said that Constable Dahlstrom has visited
the property and she asked that he report his observations.
 
Constable Dahlstrom stated that he had visited the property on Sunday, March 30
at 3:20 p.m.. He reported that there was equipment at the site but it was not
running at that time. Supervisor Martin requested any questions from the Board.
There were no questions at this time.
 
Supervisor Martin invited Mr. Hofmann to present his position to the Board. Mr.
Hofmann introduced himself and stated that there were three (3) things he
wanted to address to the Board-the accusation that he was running a business
from his home, his equipment and the commercial use of his equipment, and the
noise:
 
1)   Mr. Hofmann stated that he is not running a business from his home. He
said he owns (and stores on his property) a case loader, a 5 yard dump truck,
and a tree chipper/truck combination. He said that the Jorgensen family owns
the bulldozer, grader and trencher currently on his property. The other
equipment Constable Dahlstrom recorded on the property was a Jorgensen truck
(used to move the grader and the dozer) that has now been removed. Mr. Hofmann
said that a friend was storing a plow, salt spreader and sprayer in his pole
barn (which will be gone next week). Mr. Hofmann stated that the equipment he
owns is used for the sole purpose of landscaping his 15 acre property and has
never been used commercially and is not plated for street use. He stated that
he believes he is truly improving his property and invited the Board members to
visit anytime to see what he is doing. He introduced Tom Smith, President of
Grass Roots Landscaping, who prepared his landscaping site plan.
 
2)   Mr. Hofmann said that he had reviewed the Zoning Ordinance book regarding
the definition of “commercial vehicle.” It reads “…all motor vehicles used for
transportation of passengers for hire or constructed or used for transportation
of goods, wares or merchandise and/or all motor vehicles designed and used for
drawing other vehicles and not so constructed for carrying any load thereon…”
 
3)   Mr. Hofmann said that he believes that this definition states that a
commercial vehicle is determined based on use and not on size. He said that
because his equipment is being used for the sole purpose of landscaping his own
property, it is not, by definition, considered commercial equipment. He said he
needs the case loader to build a retaining wall. He needs the dozer and grader
to reseed his back yard. He said that when his backyard reseeding is complete,
the dozer and grader will be gone. He will be left with his loader, dump truck
and chipper which he needs to renovate his yard.
 
3)   In terms of the noise, Mr. Hoffman said that when he moved in from Okemos
last year and was unaware of the ordinance and that he was using the equipment
after an 8:00 p.m. curfew. After Inspector Aven visited his property last year
to notify him of the ordinance, he has been diligent in not using the equipment
after that time.
 
Supervisor Martin asked Inspector Aven for his comments. Mr. Aven said that his
issue with work being done on the property pertains to the grading which is now
in compliance but not complete. Mr. Hofmann said that he is following all the
rules but when an extensive landscape project like he is doing is in progress,
there will be a season where it doesn’t look good. Mr. Aven reminded Mr.
Hofmann that black top debris cannot be buried in the back pond. Mr. Hofmann
said that it will not.
 
Trustee Zaban asked Mr. Hofmann what his proposed timeline was to complete the
entire project. Mr. Hofmann asked Tom Smith (Grass Roots Landscaping-2133
University Park Drive, Suite 700, Okemos, MI) to respond on his behalf.
 
Mr. Smith said he has been advising Mr. Hofmann on the landscape plan for his
property since before it was purchased. The site had been surveyed and he had
prepared the landscape plan for the soil erosion permit that is now in place.
Mr. Smith said that Mr. Hofmann is doing the site work himself but Grass Roots
continues to advise him and provide design work as needed. Mr. Smith said that
he believes the majority of this first phase of site work will be done by the
end of this season. He clarified that this is Mr. Hofmann’s residence and he is
doing the work himself. He said landscaping projects are often ongoing. He
expects the major site work to be done this season but added that Mr. Hofmann
will continue to make ongoing improvements. Mr. Zaban asked if the bulldozer,
grader and trencher would be removed by the end of this season. Mr. Hofmann
said that they would be. He said the trencher will be gone within a month once
the rewiring from the house to the pole barn is complete. The grader and dozer
are there to spread the existing soil and once done, they will be gone. The
loader, chipper and dump truck will remain. Mr. Hofmann said the equipment he
has will allow him to complete the project much more quickly. Mr. Hofmann said
90% of the equipment would be gone by the end of the week. What remains will be
screened by arborvitae.
Supervisor Martin said that Mr. Hofmann can go to the Planning Commission and
request permission to have extra equipment on his property, as long as it is
screened properly and used within ordinance specified times. She added that any
extra commercial vehicles must be screened from the neighbors. She said that
there are remedies to handle situations like this. Since there is a complaint,
the Township must act on the complaint. Mr. Hofmann re-stated that he does not
believe his equipment meets the ordinance definition of commercial equipment.
Supervisor Martin read the definition of “commercial equipment” from the body
of the ordinance: “... equipment rated over one (1) ton.” She said she
understands Mr. Hofmann’s position and that this is a question that needs to be
discussed with the Township’s planning consultant. She said the Board will
consider this point. She said the Township’s planning consultant has already
stated he believes the dump truck meets the definition. Mr. Hofmann said that
his equipment does not meet the definition on page 1/1-9. Treasurer Fink said
that the definition wording in the ordinance is very broad and would include
equipment that moves goods, wares and merchandise whether it is street-licensed
or not. Mr. Hofmann said that goods, wares and merchandise refer to commerce.
 
Supervisor Martin said tonight’s discussion wasn’t a trial but an opportunity
for the Board to hear both sides of the issue first hand. She said that, after
that, she will review the information with legal council and then bring a
recommendation for remedy back to the Board. Supervisor Martin invited Mr. Carl
Franks to present his position.
 
Mr. Franks introduced himself and stated that he lives directly north of Mr.
Hofmann at 4300 Beeman Road. Mr. Franks said that Mr. Hofmann started doing all
this work last year without any permits. He said the main reason they
originally were upset is because he was working until 11:00 p.m. last year and
that he began cutting into their property by 20 feet. Mr. Hofmann had not done
any property survey. Mr. Franks said that even after Mr. Hofmann got the 3/25/
03 letter from the Township, he has shown no respect for the requirements. He
said that this past Sunday, Mr. Hoffman was using the loader and that last
Sunday he was using a portable welder all day long. Mr. Franks said they did
not have one minute of peace last year. Mr. Franks said they don’t care what he
does as long as he does it within the code and, he stated, “we are tired of
looking at his junk.”
 
Supervisor Martin said that the Board has received letters from both parties,
they have listened to both parties speak this evening, and if there is no
additional information, she will next meet with council to decide the best way
to solve this complaint. She said she is confident that a solution can be
found.
 
Constable Dahlstrom asked if the dozer, grader, and trenching equipment could
be stored somewhere else until it is needed. Mr. Hofmann said it would be
needed as soon as weather permits so this would not be practical.
 
Mr. Franks stated that last weekend Mr. Hoffman had a friend in his barn using
a portable welder. He added that even after the landscape construction is done,
there is going to be a noise problem if he is allowed to continue to let people
work in his barn in this way and asked if it was legal for him to do so.
Supervisor Martin said she would address this question with legal council.
 
Mr. Hofmann responded that the Zoning Ordinance specifies a 55 decibal
threshold that he cannot exceed. Mr. Hofmann said he doesn’t want to break any
laws but if he has to shut down on Sundays, the job will take twice as long to
complete because he works full time Monday through Friday.
 
Supervisor Martin summarized that the Board has now heard all the testimony and
she will be going over it all with the attorney so that the Board can make a
determination. She said the Township wants to ensure the Zoning Ordinance is
being complied with and it sounded like Mr. Hofmann is willing to work within
the ordinance. She added that she appreciates all of the information and the
letters and photos from each party.
 
Mr. Hofmann said he had not been made aware of this meeting. Supervisor Martin
said it was customary for citizens on the agenda to receive a copy of the
agenda prior to the meeting providing there is adequate time. She responded
that she had not received Mr. Hoffman’s response letter until Monday, March 31.
If it had not been received, she would have simply informed the Board at
tonight’s meeting that a complaint had been made and that the residents
involved had 10 days to respond. Because Mr. Hoffman’s letter arrived prior to
the meeting, the topic was added to the agenda for discussion at tonight’s
meeting to avoid delay.
 
Other Complaints
Constable Dahlstrom reported there was a fire run to 3824 Beeman Road on March
18 due to a burn pile on a vacant lot around the golf course. The scene was
cleared but there were several more citizen phone calls about burning on the

Text Amendment-PC Recommendation
Planning Commissioner Chair Dan Kraft stated that Mr. Tom Van Camp had
submitted an application for a text amendment to the zoning ordinance to allow
him to have horse competitions without spectators at his arena. The Township
planner had prepared a draft text change and there was a public hearing in
February with no public opposition to the idea. There are four (4) other riding
arenas in the Township that will be affected by this change. Mr. Kraft stated
that the Planning Commission’s recommendation to the Board is that the draft
text amendment be adopted with one change to section G8, which would require
that existing riding arenas bring a permit application to the Township Hall to
be considered by the Township Board.
 
Supervisor Martin said that it appeared that this text change does not apply to
Ag-Commercial property. Mr. Kraft said it may not have been included because
this may already be a permitted use in the Ag-Commercial district. This text
change would now make this use possible by a special use permit for new riding
arenas that ask to hold competitions. When a new riding arena brings a site
plan, they can now request this special use. Supervisor Martin said there are
two (2) other riding arenas in the Township that are located in Ag-Commercial
zones.
 
Citizen Leblanc asked what this text change allows that is different from
before. Chairman Kraft said that this text change allows riding arenas located
next to properties zoned R1, R1-S, RR, RE, or Ag-SF District to use their
arenas for a wider use. The arenas can now hold competitions as long as there
are no paying spectators. Supervisor Martin added that the text change gives
the riding arenas a little more flexibility in the use of their arenas beyond
personal use.
 
Supervisor Martin asked for questions from the Board. Supervisor Martin added
that she had visited Mr. Van Camp’s property while one of these events was
taking place. She said that she was considered a participant by state law
because she was a non-paying spectator. Supervisor Martin said that she also
visited the site three (3) times through out the day to observe the traffic
flow, etc… and found the activity to be very acceptable. She said she couldn’t
tell the event was taking place until she entered the barn. Supervisor Martin
said she plans to contact the Ingham County Road Commission about placing a
“Slow Moving Vehicle” sign at this location.
 
Chairman Kraft summarized that the “private use” paragraph regarding this issue
has been struck from the ordinance and a “permitted use” has now been added
with limitations.
Trustee Wright made a motion to approve the text changes to the zoning
ordinance regarding riding arenas as outlined in the McKenna letter dated March
26, 2003. Motion supported by Treasurer Fink. Motion passed unanimously.
Mr. Van Camp asked what procedure he needed to follow next to receive a permit.
Supervisor Martin stated that he needs to submit a letter of request and the
Board will make its approval decision. Mr. Van Camp thanked the Board, the
Planning Commission, and McKenna Associates for their time and efforts toward
making this change possible.

it was about 75% complete. Supervisor Martin said she agrees that the Township
should deduct any consultant fees and any secretarial fees. The project went as
far as it could go within the ordinance until the drainage issue stopped the
process. Attorney Spagnoulo said the permitees might have made a decision not
to spend the money to go any further. Trustee Wright said that it appears to
him that the applicant has spent the money they paid for the application fee.
Attorney Spagnoulo said that the Township should consider the precedent that
will be set for returning a permit fee for a process so near completion. From a
precedent standpoint, if you give someone a break on a permit, they go through
the 95% through the process and, for whatever reason, they don’t want to go
further you now have a precedent set for returning fees. Trustee Wright stated
that he doesn’t believe the DeWeese’s are entitled to a refund of any of the
fee because it has been legitimately spent. Attorney Spagnoulo said this is
definitely a subjective decision. If the applicant comes back on Day Two,
that’s a different issue. After 8 months of work, you need to be concerned
about precedence. Trustee Zaban said he would just refund the fee after
reducing it by the amount charged by McKenna. Supervisor Martin said she would
investigate this cost and report back to the Board.

NEW BUSINESS
Wetlands Permit Application-Drain Commission
Supervisor Martin explained that the Ingham County Drain Commission (ICDC) has
requested a wetlands permit pursuant to the Township’s newly adopted Wetlands
Ordinance. This is the first application received by the Township. ICRC plans
to re-establish a previously existing wetland and connect it with the Heath
Drain. The wetlands will serve a dual purpose of improving the environment and
collecting, cleaning and discharging storm water run-off from M-43 to the Red
Cedar River. Supervisor Martin explained that ICDC started developing this
project two years ago and they have already received a permit from the Michigan
Department of Environmental Quality. Tonight they are requesting a local
wetlands permit pursuant to the Township’s Wetlands Ordinance. Supervisor
Martin added that there is a provision in the Township’s ordinance that allows
the Township to automatically approve a permit if the wetlands area is
determined to be “non-essential.” The Township’s planning consultant (McKenna
Associates) has reviewed the information provided by the Township’s wetlands
consultant (Wetlands & Coastal Associates) and they agree that the wetlands in
question are “non-essential.” Supervisor Martin invited Deputy Drain
Commissioner Carla Clos to present a description of the proposed project to the
Board.
 
Ms. Clos introduced herself and commended the Township for adopting a local
wetlands ordinance. She added that the ICDC office strongly believes that
preservation and conservation of natural resources is extremely important and
that they are grateful to local governments like Williamstown Township who have
taken the progressive step of adopting a local wetlands ordinance to foster
environmental preservation. She reported that ICDC has had success with
preserving the water quality of the Red Cedar River by preserving wetlands at
other locations. She explained that the proposed project is actually a
reconstruction of a wetlands area that had existed previously until the
property was filled in by a former landowner. She introduced her co-presenters
Blair Webster (ICDC Wetlands Consultant-Water and Woods Ecology) and Alan Boyer
(Engineer-Ledy Design Group). She provided handout information about creating a
healthy aquatic ecosystem with wetlands and information for public distribution
about the positive effect a healthy wetlands area will have on decreasing
mosquito population (a public concern due to the recent West Nile Virus).
 
Alan Boyer explained the technical aspects of the project. MDOT was
experiencing flooding on the south side of M-43 and subsequently petitioned
ICDC to put in a drain. It was determined that some existing drain tile circa
1930 still existed in the area. He added that the Weigandts (adjacent property
owners) had maintained drain tile on their property well but said that the
portion south of Grand River had not been maintained. He identified the land
that drains to the tile on the Township map. He said that they had been able to
locate wetlands on the property south of Grand River (owned by Mr. Buehler).
They could also follow the tile north to Turner Road but the wetland was
degraded. So, in addition to locating the wetland area, they decided to
approach MDEQ about improving it and using it as a basin for flood protection
for M-43 and also as a detention basin. The wetland will contribute to the
water quality going down the drain tile to the Red Cedar River. He identified
the perimeter of the proposed wetland on the Township map and stated that there
will be a water level change of about 2 feet. He said that water will pass into
the wetland, be detained for a period of time, and then pass into the drain
tile and eventually to the Red Cedar River.
 
Blair Webster introduced himself and described his role in locating the
wetlands area and identifying the wetland species present. He explained that
when recreating the wetland, they plan to also increase the plant diversity
from four to sixteen dominant species. He explained that his first task had
been to delineate the existing plant life and then develop a planting plan. He
added that a lot of the newly introduced species flower so the area will be
more aesthetically pleasing.
 
Supervisor Martin invited questions from the Board and questions from the
audience.
 
Citizen Sharon Wiegandt stated that she lives across the street from the
proposed wetlands area. She said the farmer who leases property from them
installed the drain tile on their property about 10 years ago to drain the
farmland and that is the only tile they have been maintaining. She said she
received an easement request by mail last week and was surprised that this was
the first she had heard of the project. She stated that the valley will flood
during spring high water if any more water is directed into that drain. This
will damage her property. She said she is concerned that this project will
cause damage to her property similar to damage to the property located across
from St. Martha’s (where all the trees are dead).
 
Supervisor Martin said that the drain issue will be specifically discussed on
Thursday, May 8, 2003 at the Drain Commission’s public hearing. It would be
good for Mrs. Wiegandt to attend that meeting also to express her concerns. Ms.
Clos provided Ms. Wiegandt with her business card and said that she would be
like to meet with her at her property to specifically address any concerns they
have even prior to the Drain Commission meeting. Ms. Clos added that by
improving the wetlands, there will now be a proper means to convey water all
the way to the Red Cedar River so flooding should no longer occur at the drain
or on the Wiegandt property. The water will now move to the north in a
controlled fashion. Ms. Clos added that by using some of the existing tiles,
ICDC can contain project costs.
 
There were no further questions or comments.
 
Trustee Wright made a motion to approve the wetlands permit application
submitted by the Ingham County Drain Commission. Motion supported by Trustee
Zaban. Motion passed unanimously.
MDOT
Supervisor Martin introduced John Midgley (Director-Ingham County Road
Commission) who attended tonight to provide an update regarding ICRC contracts
and projects to the Board. He said that ICRC will be making a few minor changes
to the contracts this year and that any fiscal year issues the Township may
have can be addressed by making a call to his office. He said that this year
there will not be a cap placed on contract overruns. Supervisor Martin asked
what options the Township has if the contractor’s proposed cost for a project
comes back higher than the ICRC estimate. Mr. Midgley responded that
historically when the contractor’s cost came back higher than the ICRC estimate
(which is the cost used for Township budgeting purposes), ICRC would cover 95%
of the cost overrun and cap the Township share at 5%. He said that ICRC no
longer has the funds to eat this 95% cost. Supervisor Martin asked if the
Township can refuse to proceed with a job if the contractor estimated project
overrun is too high. Mr. Midgley said the Township will be able to go into a
project with an accurate project cost estimate. If the estimate is much higher
than ICRC predicted, and the Township does not feel they can afford to proceed,
the project can be postponed or cancelled. Supervisor Martin questioned whether
Township percentage will be returned if the project comes in lower than
estimated. Mr. Midgley said that the Township portion of any leftover money
would be returned. He added that the ICRC will also be trying to prioritize all
municipal projects so that the project starts soon after the Township makes its
payment. For instance, if Williamstown Township pays for a project in June, the
project won’t be delayed until October.
Mr. Midgely asked the Board if they had any questions or comments.
 
Trustee Zaban asked Mr. Midgley to travel Mitchell Road (which is posted at 45
mph) on his way home from the meeting tonight to see if he agrees that the
speed limit needs to be lowered. Trustee Zaban explained that the Township is
in favor of lowering the speed limit to 35 mph but does not have the authority
to make the change. Since MDOT (or the State Police) has the authority, he was
hoping that Mr. Midgley might get a first hand look at the road and support the
Township’s opinion. Trustee Zaban said there has been a lot of additional
development on Mitchell since the road was originally posted and the high
school enters and exits from Mitchell throughout the day.
This combination is causing the need to reconsider the speed limit.
 
Road Repairs-Recommendation from Committee
Supervisor Martin reported that the Township had received a request from ICRC
to identify which local projects we would like to see done this year.
Supervisor Martin added that the $30,000 match has been restored, so it is in
the Township’s best interest to fund a full $30,000 toward road repair (which
has been already included in the 2003-04 budget). She introduced Brian
Jennings, representative from the Township Traffic Committee, to present their
recommendations.
 
Mr. Jennings explained how the recommendations were developed. He said the
committee uses a software program that evaluates each road’s surface rating,
traffic volume, and the number of years its been on the ICRC “needs repair”
list. The committee members also visit each site. Mr. Jennings said the Traffic
Committee had received a specific request from the Oakleaf subdivision to have
their subdivision considered. He said there was also a request to look at
paving one of the gravel roads in the Township. Mr. Jennings said this request
needs a thorough analysis (including discussion with the residents involved)
before proceeding because it will be expensive to upgrade a gravel road and
could not be paid for out of the Township’s general fund.
 
Mr. Jennings reported that the Traffic Committee’s first road repair
recommendation is to repair the road at Quinlan Acres. This road work was
originally proposed two (2) years ago.
 
The Committee’s second recommendation originally was for Sunrise Drive to be
repaired. However, ICRCs estimate came in much higher than the Township had
projected. Mr. Jennings stated that the discrepancy seems to be due to the cost
of curb and gutter. The Committee had estimated $7-8000 and ICRC’s estimate
came back at $30,000. Mr. Jennings has contacted ICRC to find out why their
cost is so high and to ask whether all the curb work must be done? He suggested
that, if so, the residents of the subdivision help pay for it.
 
Rodeo Trail is the committee’s third recommendation.
 
Clerk Hiner stated that she was surprised to see the Committee report showing
that 300 cars travel through Quinlan Acres in 24 hours. Mr. Jennings said the
Committee uses an estimate of ten (10) trips per household per day. He added
that about 10 years ago, ICRC actually did a count on a subdivision (which they
usually don’t do) and they came up with 9.8 trips per household (which supports
this estimate).
Treasurer Fink asked how often counts are taken. Mr. Jennings said ICRC likes
to take a count every three years but sometimes the data is up to five (5)
years old (at most).
 
Supervisor Martin summarized that the Committee’s recommendation for top three
(3) priorities are 1) Quinlan Acres 2) Sunrise Drive and 3) Rodeo Trail. She
added that the Township has budgeted $30,000 with a $30,000 match from ICRC for
a total available budget of $60,000. From the information provided by the
Traffic Committee, it appears that two (2) of the jobs can be done within this
budget. She clarified that, using the pacer system, the percentage cuts would
be 25% ICRC and 75% Township. She commented that, from the information provided
by the committee, the Township must pay the full amount if for roads rated “1”
and “2”. Mr. Jennings said the roads have to be very deteriorated to be rated
this low. A rating this low means the road has to be completely reconstructed
(which is very expensive) so it is a benefit to the Township to repair a road
once it reaches level 3 to avoid huge future repair costs.
 
Treasurer Fink asked how the Committee determined which roads should be
considered. Mr. Jennings said the ICRC provides the Township with a list to
start with. Since this list is always more than the Township can afford, the
traffic committee prioritizes the list. Treasurer Fink asked why a major road
like Sherwood hasn’t been considered in the past 25 years. Mr. Jennings said
that Sherwood is a county road so they are responsible for prioritizing it. Mr.
Jennings said that if citizens ask the Township about the status of county
roads, it would be best to refer them to Mr. Midgley at ICRC. He added that it
is difficult for the Township to keep track of ICRC’s county road priority list
because it is constantly changing.
 
Supervisor Martin summarized that road projects for Quinlan Acres and Rodeo
Trail will cost $54,300 (without subdivision support). The Township’s 75%
portion would be $40,725. Completing these two (2) projects would be option
one. To do all three projects will cost $84,300 (with a Township portion of $
63,225). If subdivision support is required, residents of Quinlan Acres would
pay about $125 each and residents of Rodeo Trail would pay $522. The cost to
Sunrise Drive residents would be $250-$300 if the county money is divided
proportionally. Treasurer Fink asked if the Township would need agreement from
the subdivision citizens before proceeding. Supervisor Martin responded “yes”
and added that the cost would be billed as a special assessment.
 
Mr. Jennings recommended that the Sunrise subdivision project be delayed for a
year so that the discrepancy between the Traffic Committee estimate and the
ICRC estimate can be clarified. He added that the Township can ask ICRC to roll
the money that would have been assigned to this project to next year.
 
Supervisor Martin said that Quinlan is an old subdivision which has a pass-
through road that many Township citizens use. Rodeo Trail and Sunrise are dead
end roads that are only used by the subdivision owners. She said she thinks it
is appropriate for these two (2) subdivisions to help the Township with repair
costs. She asked the Board whether their opinion is to pay the entire cost for
road repair or should special assessments be made. She added that Delhi
Township Board developed a policy not to repair any roads unless the residents
contribute a portion of the cost. Leslie and Bunker Hill Townships just passed
a millage to use as a funding source for road work. She said it appears a lot
of Boards are moving towards using other funding sources. She said she would
prefer not to go to a millage but to look for alternative funding sources.
Mr. Jennings said there are pluses and minuses with every funding source. With
the millage option, everyone is contributing payment so everyone demands that
their project be considered first. With the special assessment option, citizens
will complain because they are being treated differently from other citizens in
the Township. Mr. Jennings suggested that the process for using alternative
funding sources start now for next year so that citizens have time to consider
what they prefer.
 
Citizen Frans Wilbrink said he thought the original policy was that a
subdivision could pay an assessment to have their road repavement moved to the
top of a priority list. When a subdivision requests road repair and they are
not at the top of the priority list, the subdivision residents can pay an
assessment (like 25%) to have their job prioritized.
 
Trustee Zaban said that his recommendation would be to definitely proceed with
the Quinlan Acres project because the traffic volume is so high on that street
and because it is a through street. He added that $24,000 looks like a bargain
based on the traffic count. He said he believes that some preventative
maintenance (ie. crack filling) is a higher priority than Sunrise Subdivision
based on it’s “number of trips.”
Mr. Jennings said that the Traffic Committee was planning to recommend that any
money left after road project selection be directed towards crack-sealing. The
Committee suggests trying it on a couple of roads to see if crack-sealing
materials had improved in the last 5-10 years. Mr. Jennings added that
subdivisions typically don’t like chip sealing because they get the stones in
their yards. He said that crack filling is estimated to cost $1200 per mile and
that the Committee had recommended two (2) roads in Maple Shade because there
didn’t appear to be any alligator cracking in the surfaces yet (which make it
inappropriate to crack fill).
Trustee Wright made a motion to resurface Quinlan Acres, crack-fill Maple Shade
and Golf View Drives, and roll the rest of the Ingham County and Township
budget for road repairs over to 2004 and ask the Transportation Committee to
study alternate funding options for Township roads and present their
recommendations to the Board for future road decisions. Motion supported by
Clerk Hiner. Motion passed unanimously.
Mr. Jennings asked the Board for some guidelines for the Traffic Committee to
follow. Supervisor Martin said guidelines could be discussed at the Board
Workshop Meeting scheduled on May 20th and recommended that Mr. Jennings plan
to attend. Supervisor Martin thanked Mr. Jennings and the traffic committee for
all their work.
Planning Commission Report
Planning Commission Meeting Minutes
Supervisor Martin commented that the minutes from the Planning Commission’s Red
Cedar Trail Meeting are included in the Board Packet. She said that the
Planning Commission doesn’t have anything to report tonight that requires a
Board vote but that Planning Commission Chairman Dan Kraft would like to
provide the Board with a summary of Planning Commission activity.
Commercial Zoning on Grand River
Mr. Kraft reported that the Board had asked the Planning Commission to consider
the commercial zoning issue along Grand River. Mr. Kraft reported that the
consensus of the commissioners was that there was adequate commercial zoning
available on Grand River. He said the Planning Commission decided that they
would like to see some design standards established. He said the Planning
Commission is also considering a multi-use zoning option.
Supervisor Martin said that the commercial use property in the Township is
restrictive. She said there are many businesses that come, inquire and leave
because there is too much retrofitting that must be done to the ordinance
before they could move in. She said she is pleased that the Planning Commission
is considering a multiuse option. Mr. Kraft said that the next step is for the
Planning Commission to provide their multi-use option to McKenna Associates
(the Township’s planning consultant), and then incorporate the multiuse zone(s)
into the master plan. They are considering Grand River from the east side of
the City of Williamston and west of Zimmer Road (both sides of the City in the
Township).
Mobile Home Park
Mr. Kraft stated that the Township must designate some areas on the master plan
for mobile home park sites. The Planning Commission recommends that a master
plan amendment be made to designate two (2) areas (one on each side of the
Township) so that mobile home parks developers have to work within the Township
use map. Supervisor Martin added that adding the designation to the master plan
is no threat to the current property because if they don’t want to sell to the
mobile home park developer, they don’t have to-the Township is designating
areas that are appropriate. Treasurer Fink asked if the designation would
constitute a map amendment. Supervisor Martin said that the designation is only
applied to the Future Land Use Map in Master Plan.
River Trail Meeting Minutes
Mr. Kraft reported that the minutes reflect a clear signal from the property
owners that a river trail would not be accepted. He said that the Wiegandts and
the Goodmans both have houses within 20 ft of the river. Mr. Kraft said that he
hasn’t met with the Planning Commission since the river trail meeting but he
doesn’t believe they will consider asking the Board for money to pursue this
idea. He said there was some interest at the meeting in preserving the greenway
(similar to what was done prior to development of the Steeplechase
subdivision). He said that Chris Riddle was present at the meeting and had
worked on many greenway projects. He said that green spaces (protected lands-
not trails) increase in value.
Citizen Sharon Weidgandt added that the majority of the people that attended
the meeting were opposed to the trail and it seemed to her that the Planning
Commission was “mystified” by this fact. She encouraged the Township Board to
have the Planning Commission spend their time on things like the existing
Township park on Grand River and other useful projects that the Township can
actually afford. She said that any further consideration of a river trail would
be met with legal action by the homeowners.
Citizen Sam Fowler presented the Board with a letter clarifying the position of
the citizens along the river. The letter had a list of signatures of property
owners (which he did not leave). Mr. Fowler said the Township should send a
follow-up letter to the residents that had received Mr. Kraft’s original letter
so that they don’t have to wonder what is going to happen next. He thinks the
citizens need a letter stating that there was a meeting, the citizens’ voices
were heard, and this is what is going to happen next.
Supervisor Martin said that the letter and meeting were part of an
investigation before starting a feasibility study. It seems obvious to her
that, based on the citizen response at the meeting, the Planning Commission
will make a recommendation not to proceed. The Board has no intent of going
forward without support from its Township citizens. She said that sending a
follow-up letter to everyone that received the original letter is a good idea
and is something that has been done in similar situations in the past.
Citizen Fowler said that he came to tonight’s meeting to ask how much further
citizens that own river frontage need to go to kill this idea. He said the
Planning Commission is saying that this is just a dream but he believes there
is intent because the Township bought an easement on the river front property
before Steeplechase subdivision was put in. Supervisor Martin corrected this
statement, stating that the easement was given by the developer to the
Township. The Township did not pay anything. He pointed out Mr. Farhat has also
come tonight and that he is a property owner in Steeplechase. Mr. Farhat stood
up and said that he would prefer to speak for himself and that he realized he
was buying property that had a river easement at the time of purchase. He said
that, based on the meeting and the discussion at tonight’s Board meeting, he is
no longer concerned that a lot of money is going to be dumped into a river
walk. He added that he was surprised to hear that two (2) property owners (out
of 100) were actually in favor of the trail. He stated that the citizens in the
Township are already worrying about road costs, school improvements, library
construction, etc… He said he thinks there are plenty of places where money
needs to be spent instead of developing a river trail.
Treasurer Fink said that calling the using the word “feasibility study” in the
letter was a misnomer. It was just an idea and that people wanted to see if
anyone else shared the same vision. The word “feasibility” caused people to see
it as something more and this was not intended.
Trustee Zaban said it would be great if the 100 Township citizens that are now
not going to have to fight development of a river trail, could redirect their
energy into improving the park. Mr. Fowler said there was a lot of support at
the meeting from property owners to improve the greenway by cleaning the river
banks, etc…
Burn Ordinance-Board Policy (Size, Weather Conditions)
Supervisor Martin said she would like the Planning Commission to clarify that
the size for brush fires in the Township Burn Ordinance. NIESA has suggested
brush fire specifications of 4’x4’x4’. She said she has also included an
Interim Township Policy for the Board to consider adopting for six (6) months
until the until the Burn Ordinance is formally amended
Treasurer Fink moved to adopt the Interim Township Board Policy for Burn
Permits to restrict the size of brush piles as identified. Motion supported by
Trustee Wright. Motion passed unanimously.
Treasurer Fink asked if the campfire provision of the Burn Ordinance allowed
for a citizen to keep adding brush after the campfire has been started. She
referred to a neighbor who owns an R1 property and is not taking out any
permits for burning before he does so. Supervisor Martin suggested that
Treasurer Fink put her question in writing and attend the Planning Commission
meeting when the Burn Ordinance revisions are going to be addressed. Supervisor
Martin added that the Township will never be able to control everything.
Treasurer Fink said she feels that the campfire provision has given citizens
the right to burn whenever they want without any limitations. She said that
their needs to be a better definition of campfire (she added that she would be
happy to write it). Clerk Hiner said there will always be someone who will find
a way to get around an ordinance and we shouldn’t over-regulate which would
impose on all citizens. Supervisor Martin said there were two (2) fires in the
Township recently that got out of control. One of those fires was burning
without a permit. Both property owners were fined by the fire department.
Supervisor Martin added that there is also a question about whether the
Township can deny permits based on weather conditions. She said that she and
Treasurer Fink are looking in to it. Trustee Wright recommended that the
Township could ask citizen Andy Provenzano to provide his expertise about
weather conditions and burning.
Citizen LeBlanc commented that 2-3 weeks ago there was an article in the
Detroit newspaper about two (2) Townships that had recently enacted a “No
Burning” ordinance. Citizen Brian Jennings suggested that the Township contact
the MDNR because they have an existing website about this issue so the Township
could push the jurisdiction responsibility onto that agency.

Supervisor Martin reviewed the items included in the consent agenda packet. No
corrections were identified. Trustee Zaban moved to approve the Consent Agenda.

PUBLIC COMMENT FOR NON-AGENDA ITEMS
Supervisor Martin invited comments from the public for any non-agenda items.
Citizen Nick Cannarile (4513 Petoskey Drive-Pebblebrook) stated that homeowners
in his area are concerned about speeding on Sherwood Road near their
subdivision but wasn’t sure where to report the problem. Supervisor Martin said
it was good to let the Township know so the concern could be passed on to the
Ingham County Sheriff’s office. He presented one resident’s (not his own)
written suggestions to address the problem: 1) Decrease the speed limit to
25mph, 2) Post a “Speed Limit Enforced” sign as a deterrent, 3) Ask police to
patrol the area more often during peak work travel hours, 4) Post a “Speed
Kills-Slow Down” sign as a deterrent, 5) Resurface the road because people
might be driving faster to smooth out the rough ride.
Supervisor Martin explained that the State Police Department sets the speed
limit based on the speed that 85% of vehicles are traveling (defined as “normal
traffic”) and that it is very difficult to get them to lower a speed limit.
Trustee Wright commented that Trustee Zaban has been lobbying for a similar
speed reduction on Mitchell Road (which has a high school entrance and exit)
for many years without success. Supervisor Martin said that the Township can
request a portable electronic speed sign be placed at that location. The
Township will likely be put on a waiting list because there are only two units
available for this area. The Township can also request more police monitoring.
Several comments indicated that the police do have some presence at this
location already.
Trustee Zaban asked Mr. Cannarile if he could ask homeowners at the next
Pebblebrook Subdivision meeting if they would be willing to pay another mil in
order to have a police presence in the Township. There are currently only two
police cars available to patrol a large area. Supervisor Martin suggested Mr.
Cannarile also personally write a letter to Sergeant Vicky Harrison at the
Ingham County Sheriff’s office stating his concerns and asking for her
suggestions. She said he should encourage the rest of the residents in his
subdivision to do this also.
NEW BUSINESS
Yard Maintenance Proposal-Zach Hiner
Williamston High School student Zach Hiner presented the Board with his
proposed Eagle Scout project. His plans are to create a volunteer program to
help senior citizens in the City and the Township with yard work that has
become too difficult for them to manage. He said he first came up with the idea
last fall when he and a friend helped an elderly person who was unable to
remove leaves from her property. She couldn’t burn her leaves anymore due to
the new burn ordinance. He realized that there may be others in the community
that could use assistance. Mr. Hiner said his plan is to gather a list of
volunteers and assign them to projects as they come up in a manner similar to
the way Mr. Larson coordinates volunteers at the food bank. Mr. Hiner said his
role would be to recruit the volunteers and administer the program.
Mr. Hiner asked the Board if they felt there was a need for this type of
service in the Township. Supervisor Martin said that she definitely sees the
need, especially after a storm when a lot of debris must be cleared. Treasurer
Fink suggested Mr. Hiner contact the senior center for their input as well.
Mr. Hiner asked support from the Township in two ways: 1) Would the Township be
willing to advertise the service through a short note in an upcoming next
newsletter and, 2) Would the Township be willing to take requests from citizens
and direct them to him. He will then follow through from there. Supervisor
Martin responded that the Township would be willing to advertise the service in
a newsletter and suggested the he provide a pamphlet with information that
could be available at the counter. The Township will also take requests from
citizens on his behalf.
Supervisor Martin asked how long he anticipated the service to continue? Mr.
Hiner said he plans to continue the project for the next two years (while he is
in scouts) and then cross-train some of the younger scouts to take the project
over. He will encourage them to make the project their own by expanding and
improving the service as they work toward their own Eagle project.
Treasurer Fink, Trustee Zaban and Trustee Wright stated that they were
definitely willing to support this type of program.
Supervisor Martin asked Mr. Hiner when he anticipated being ready to begin. He
said he plans to be ready for this fall. Supervisor Martin said that the next
newsletter is tentatively scheduled for September 1.
Digital Orthophotography with the Drain Commission
Supervisor Martin introduced Greg Minshall (Engineer-Fitzgerald Henne
Associates) to describe the use of Digital Orthophotography for mapping
purposes on behalf of the Ingham County Drain Commission (ICDC). The ICDC has
decided to use this technique to develop a base map for drains in Ingham
County. Mr. Minshall explained that he started working with Mr. Lindemann on
the project three years ago. ICDC has been awarded a 50-50 grant to create the
map of the county using digital orthophotography. This will be a 2-3 phase
project. He said that the first phase of the project required building a good
base map/ They began by drawing section corners in the county using GIS (which
is accurate to within a few centimeters). The Corps of Engineers has actually
completed the first phase which included taking aerial photos of the entire
area referencing the GPS locations which were marked by “X” targets painted on
the ground. The photos that are generated are 100 scale (each pixel represets a
6” x 6” square). Mr. Minshall said they also plan to overlay contours at 2’
intervals so the map can be used to identify high points and low points.
Mr. Lindemann is asking the communities that are going to benefit from these
new maps to participate in the cost of the project. The maps are not design
grade so, for instance, a Township cannot give the map to a consultant and ask
them to design a sewer from it. However, Townships can take a developer’s
drawing (at the same scale) and lay it over the map to see how site contours
are going to affect a project. Mr. Minshall said there are 2 primary phases of
the mapping project and the first phase is now complete. Townships can now plot
their own copies of the map or request a plot from Fitzgerald Henne as needed.
He said that the cost for the project is the best it could be because the
project was done county wide and because the Corps of Engineers is providing a
50% matching grant. Supervisor Martin commented that upgrades (like splits,
etc..) could be laid onto the map once a year. Mr. Minshall said that tax
descriptions could also be added to the properties.
Supervisor Martin asked the schedule for payment being requested by the Drain
Commissioner For instance, since Phase 1 is already complete, does he want the
Township to approve money for the project immediately? Mr. Minshall said that
the reason Mr. Lindemann moved forward quickly (without first approaching local
governments for financial support) was due to the deadline requirements of the
Corps grant. ICDC borrowed the money from the county to pay for Phase 1 and now
need to pay it back by the end of the year. Mr. Minshall said that Phase 2 will
start with the federal fiscal year (October 1, 2003). He added that the Corps
has stated that they have the additional money available but that is not
guaranteed. The second deadline for Phase 2 would be a commitment by Oct. 1,
2003. Mr. Minshall said that a Phase 3 would include tasks like overlaying a
wetland map, or flood plains map (FEMA is currently remapping so floodplains
have not been included in the first phases).
Treasurer Fink asked if the maps are not design grade, what is the Drain
Commission planning to use them for? Mr. Minshall said that Mr. Lindemann is
going to start requiring developers to provide engineer grade maps (from the
county base map). The engineered map can then be imported into the base map.
Trustee Wright commented that a year ago Marvin Fouty did a similar
presentation for the Board. Supervisor Martin clarified that his presentation
was for a GIS based map. Trustee Wright asked the cost of that proposal. Mr.
Minshall said the cost may have been less but that the digital orthophotography
map will be more accurate and include contours and drain information.
Trustee Wright said that he recalls that the Planning Commission liked what
they saw at the GIS presentation but had decided to wait until the County made
a decision on the method of development for the county map. He added that it
appeared that the County has its plan now in place. Mr. Minshall added that
Sidwell maps are not as accurate as the newly developed maps. Trustee Wright
said that, over a period of time, accepting to participate in the cost of
developing this map could save the Township much more than its going to cost.
Treasurer Fink asked if the map would satisfy documentation needs. Mr. Minshall
said that, for instance, the map would be fine for delineating a wetlands area.
Treasurer Fink asked if Mr. Lindemann planned to map the outfalls from the
Phase 2 Stormwater Outfall Program. Mr. Minshall said that Mr. Lindemann had
spoken to him about doing so.
Supervisor Martin said that she finds it encouraging that Lansing, East
Lansing, Delhi, Doug Stover from Equalization, Tri-County, etc.. were all
present at the recent meetings to discuss this concept. She added that it looks
like everyone is jumping on board and will be sharing the cost for this. She
added that it is good to see planning being done on a more overall basis.
Trustee Wright asked Supervisor Martin what Chris Doozan (Township Planning
Consultant-McKenna Associates) thinks of the mapping system. Supervisor Martin
said that he thinks it is good and that they can work with it. Mr. Minshall
said that Autocad maps can be downloaded by any computer. Supervisor Martin
said that ICDC plans to make a presententation to all the Townships in Ingham
and Tri-county. The more that agree to contribute to the cost, the lower the
cost to the Township could potentially be. Mr. Minshall said that tonight is
the first municipal Board presentation he has made so far.
Trustee Wright asked Mr. Minshall if ICDC was looking for a financial
commitment tonight. Mr. Minshall said he doesn’t need a commitment tonight but
would like the Board to consider it and get back to him. Trustee Wright said it
looks like something Williamstown Township would be interested in
participating. Treasurer Fink said some of the outer municipalities don’t have
the tools to map required by the storm water program so they should also need
to join. Mr. Minshall added that he would be willing to return to Williamstown
Township to answer any remaining questions and encouraged the Board to contact
him anytime.

NIESA Agreement
Supervisor Martin reported that Williamstown Township had been recently
forwarded an agreement for signature by NIESA. This agreement would be in
addition to the Articles of Incorporation that the Township entered into with
NIESA years ago. She introduced Mark Adams (attorney representing NIESA) and
Charles Galbraith (Locke Township Treasurer, Locke Township representative to
NIESA, and Chairman of NIESA) who have attended tonight to provide background
information and answer questions about the new agreement. Mr. Galbraith said
that he appreciates hearing the Township’s concerns and the plan is to address
those items that are worrisome to the various parties in a revised draft. He
added that Trustee Zaban had suggested they attend tonight’s meeting to
alleviate and address concerns the Board might have about signing the new
agreement.
Mr. Galbraith explained that the Townships already collect tax money on behalf
of NIESA and then pass it through so there is no change to what will be
required of the Townships in the new agreement. According to Mr. Galbraith, the
City of Williamston is concerned because they collect the money but have no
control over it. Also, because the City has a DDA and a TIFA district, some of
the NIESA taxes they collect don’t actually go to NIESA. Money that the voters
voted for when they approved the NIESA millage (and that citizens think are
going to NIESA) is going to TIFA or the Downtown Development Authority. State
statute allows the City to distribute the money this way. Treasurer Fink
expressed surprise to hear this was possible. Mr. Galbraith stated that he
admits that as the bylaws and Articles of Incorporation were being formed,
nobody thought about emergency service funds being captured. He said the idea
behind this new agreement was that there be “like terms” for everybody
contributing. He said that in NIESA’s quest for uniformity, they were hoping
that all the contributing parties (especially the City) would be willing to
sign the new agreement.
Supervisor Martin said she sees no benefit to the Township entering into this
new agreement. Trustee Zaban asked the speakers to explain the difference
between this agreement and the NIESA Articles of Incorporation. Mr. Adams
responded that the Articles of Incorporation were constructed around the basis
that the municipalities always have the final decision about who provides fire
and rescue service to their citizens. For example, there is currently one unit
that chooses to contract with the Perry Area Fireboard and NIESA pays the bill.
The primary purpose of this new agreement is to define the language “on similar
terms” by designating service districts. Mr. Adams added that there is a need
for the language to be cleaned up. The issues that make this clarification
necessary have evolved over the past six (6) years due to all the disparaging
interests. There was an agreement with the City of Williamston at one time
(1999) but it was never signed. Treasurer Fink asked if there had also been a
written agreement with Williamstown Township. Mr. Adams said that Shirley
Graham represented the Board at the time and the agreement was verbal.
Supervisor Martin explained that the City’s main problem is that their TIFA
funds are captured by the DDA. Unless the DDA elects to return the NIESA
portion of those funds to the City (so they can be forwarded to NIESA) the City
would have to take the money from their general fund to replace it. Mr. Adams
stated that it’s a benefit to NIESA and to all the units involved if the time
spent dealing with all the different agreements could be reduced. Time could be
better spent on planning and other important issues.
Supervisor Martin itemized her problems with the new agreement proposed by
NIESA. First, she said, she does not want to enter the Township into a thirty
(30) year agreement. Mr. Galbraith suggested that fifteen (15) years might be a
more reasonable timeframe since that is also the life of the NIESA millage.
Supervisor Martin said she also does not like the idea of an annual charge. She
said the Township has no intention of ever charging the citizens more than what
the Township turns over in millage. She added that she would also have a hard
time signing something that could commit the Township to fees when there is no
cap on what NIESA can charge. Mr. Adams said that the “user rate” wording was
inserted to try to meet some of the objections of the City. Supervisor Martin
said that Townships do not have TIFAs and DDAs so the contracts should be
worded differently. Treasurer Fink said that she feels the Township needs a
contract with NIESA but she doesn’t think we need this contract. Mr. Adams
explained that if each of the four (4) Townships agreed to sign the uniform
contract, then the City would also likely sign so the problem (regarding “on
like terms” and the captured DDA money) would be solved.
Supervisor Martin asked why the state contract reads “the authorities may
establish service districts” but the wording used in the NIESA Articles of
Incorporation is “the authorities shall.” Mr. Adams responded that the two
documents are essentially stating the same thing. Supervisor Martin said that,
for instance, Pebblebrook Subdivision may want to use Meridian Township’s
service. She asked whether the Township has the authority to contract their
entire service out ? Mr. Adams said that the Township could make that choice.
He added that the most important thing isn’t the term of the contract but the
ability to terminate it. The contract is terminable with fifteen (15) months
notice.
Supervisor Martin reiterated that she would like to see the Township contract
language worded differently from the City because the Township has a very
different structure. Mr. Adams asked whether it was fair for some portions of
the City to be allowed to pay less than the rest of the participants.
Supervisor Martin responded “no” but said that state statute does allow for
TIFA districts so the way the City money is being dispersed is legal. Mr. Adams
said NIESA believes that if they can come forward with clear, concise, uniform
agreements from all the remaining parties, then the burden will be on the City
to explain why they are not conforming. Supervisor Martin said she must
evaluate the agreement on its face value to this Township and without regard
for what the City is doing. Mr. Adams asked if the Township could send a
representative to help work out the language with NIESA so that it would be
acceptable to the Township. He added that Locke Township also voiced concern
with the “30 year” language and have recommended 15 years instead. He said that
Wheatfield has no problem with the current wording. Treasurer Fink asked how
this new agreement is going to prevent the TIFA money from still being captured
at the City. Mr. Adams responded that under the new agreement, NIESA will
assign a cost and the City will have to make up the difference of what is
captured by the DDA from their general fund. He added that Webberville made an
agreement with their DDA and now that DDA just sends all the captured money to
NIESA. Supervisor Martin said the Township doesn’t need a lot of the clauses in
the new agreement because they don’t apply. Mr. Adams said that because this
was a new statute at the time of formation, NIESA was one of the first to use
it. Under state law, NIESA has authority to do anything (including collection
of fees) their members can do if the authority is delegated to NIESA. This new
contract will clearly delegate the power to NIESA. He added that NIESA can
operate without the delegated powers, but they have more authority to collect
fees if they have the contract.
Treasurer Fink stated that NIESA already appears to have a separate agreement
with the Village of Webberville so they already will not have uniform
agreements with everyone. Treasurer Fink asked Mr. Adams to clarify the
definition of “uniform”. Mr. Adams said he expects that the City will sign the
Township Agreement and then add a couple of additional clauses. He said it is
really only paragraphs 4,5 and 6 that are potentially different between the
Township and the City agreements. He added there will be some “tweaking” in
paragraph 9 and possibly elsewhere.
Supervisor Martin stated that the Township’s contribution to NIESA went from
$28,000 out of general fund money to $171,000 per year being contributed by the
taxpayers of Williamstown Township due to the NIESA millage. Her understanding
was that this increased cost would be offset because there would no longer be
charges for ambulance and fire responses in the Township (since fees have
already been paid for out of our taxes). Mr. Adams said that before the
millage, the ambulance service was making money which was used to subsidized
fire service. He said there have been fundamental changes in society like
decreases in Medicare reimbursements and requirements for volunteers to be
certified in advanced life support certification. The cost of the service has
gone up considerably. Treasurer Fink said that it appears the Township is now
paying 5.5 times more for than before the millage with no added service except
another ambulance. Mr. Adams said that is not correct because there were
already ambulance fees. Treasurer Fink said that the people have been
misinformed. Trustee Zaban said that it is good for the Township Board and
NIESA to have this dialogue so that these specific concerns can be addressed.
Supervisor Martin said that this broader topic will be discussed further at a
Board Workshop. Right now the Board needs to have someone help hammer out the
wording of the agreement with Mr. Adams.
Treasurer Fink asked whether it was difficult for NIESA to respond to fire
ordinance complaints. Mr. Adams said that NIESA does not have the legal
authority to issue penalties for a citizen failing to follow local fire
ordinances. Mr. Galbraith said that NIESA has tried to recommend the NFPA
ordinance as a uniform ordinance for the area (this is what Meridian Township
currently uses). Treasurer Fink asked how NIESA responds to an illegal fire.
Mr. Adams said that if NIESA knows it is a permitted fire (because they have
been notified by the Township) they don’t respond. He added that ordinance
enforcement is a local police issue. Treasurer Fink said that people will call
911 if they see fire. Mr. Adams said if NIESA determines it is a permitted fire
that is out of control, they respond. If the property owner does not have a
burning permit, the fire department will charge them for the response. NIESA
does not have authority to tell them they have violated the Township’s burn
ordinance. Treasurer Fink clarified that NIESA only responds to a fire if it
has gotten away. She added that she would like to see a uniform ordinance. Mr.
Adams said that NIESA has discussed circulating one but Townships like Locke
and Leroy have no interest in having a burn ordinance.
Employee Policy (updated)
Supervisor Martin said it was necessary to update the manual because there have
been some changes since the last update including addition of a Cemetery
Sexton, a full-time Township/Cemetery Caretaker and a full time secretary.
Trustee Wright clarified that the recommended changes have been highlighted in
bold.
Treasurer Fink questioned the statement “all paid time off must be used within
the same calendar year” (page 6). Treasurer Fink asked if will be the
Township’s policy to pay employees for time off not used. Supervisor Martin
stated that she would prefer that the employee be required to use the time off.
Treasurer Fink said she thinks the policy should be to use it or be paid off
for the accrued time.
Clerk Hiner said the fact that time off is accrued needs to be clarified in the
policy. She said she could agree with a use it or lose it policy if all the
vacation time was issued to the employee on January 1 so they have the entire
year to decide when to use it. With an accrual plan, the employee has to wait
until the last pay period in December to receive their full two weeks of
accrued vacation time. Therefore, she does not think the proposed policy is
appropriate. Supervisor Martin said that her concern is that employees not
accumulate more than two weeks of vacation at any one time. Trustee Wright said
that “calendar year” should not be used in the wording. Treasurer Fink
clarified that Trustee Wright prefers to track vacation by employed year.
Supervisor Martin asked Clerk Hiner how she would word this item in the manual.
Clerk Hiner said she thinks the employee should be able to carry a portion of
their vacation hours over to the next year or the Township should have a “cash
out” clause. She added that because the Township is a small office, there
should be a clause that states employees cannot take more than one week off at
a time.
Supervisor Martin said she would agree that an employee can accumulate time as
long as they do not accumulate more than two weeks. If this is the policy, the
Township can notify an employee when their accrued time is going to reach the
maximum and encourage them to arrange for time off by a certain date. Trustee
Wright suggested that vacation time be stated as 80 hours instead of two weeks.
Supervisor Martin said a worksheet can be prepared so that full time employees
are aware of when they will reach the two week maximum (accrued vacation hours
also appear on each paycheck stub). The employee just cannot accumulate more
than 80 hours-once they reach 80 hours, no additional time will be accrued
until some is taken. Treasurer Fink clarified that this will be an incentive
for employees to use their time. Clerk Hiner said the Township could also
consider cashing out vacation time at a reduced rate. Trustee Zaban suggested
that the details be fleshed out at a workshop. Supervisor Martin said she would
like to address the issue tonight. Inspector Walt Aven asked if an employee is
required to give two weeks notice. Supervisor Martin said that the Township is
an at-will organization so the employee does not have to give notice.

Rezoning Request from Ag-C to R-1-S at 1435 Epley Rd-Templeton
Planning Commission Chair Dan Kraft reported that the public opposition to this
request was overwhelming. The original request came before the planning
commission 6 months ago when a neighbor complained that a road was being
constructed and litigation is pending on this issue. Mr. Kraft reported that,
based on the public concern at the public hearing and the recommendation by the
Township planning consultant (McKenna Associates), the Planning Commission
recommends denial of this request. Mr. Kraft added that rezoning would be
inconsistent with the Master Plan, would result in a spot zoning in a rural
part of the Township, and would be allowing special privileges to the applicant
(in addition to several other reasons noted in the Planning Commission minutes)
the Planning Commission voted to deny the request.
 
Supervisor Martin commented that there were no positive considerations listed
in the Planning Commission minutes to support the decision rezoning request.
Mr. Kraft agreed and noted that several of the items in the minutes are
statements of fact and cannot be considered either positive or negative.
  
Trustee Zaban referred to item (h) of the Planning Commission minutes and asked
if the 1320’ road that has been constructed exceeds the zoning ordinance 660’
maximum length requirement. Mr. Kraft responded that the subdivision ordinance
requires that a cul-de-sac road cannot exceed 660’. He added that, evidently, a
1320’ road has already been constructed. Supervisor Martin clarified that it
has been constructed as a private driveway at this point. Mr. Kraft said he
believed that, if the rezoning were approved, the property would be able to
accommodate 32 residential lots with frontage requirements accommodated.
Supervisor Martin clarified that this item then is a statement of fact and not
a positive or negative comment. Mr. Kraft concurred. Trustee Zaban reiterated
that the zoning ordinance requires a maximum road length of 660’. Mr. Kraft
concurred.
 
Supervisor Martin invited the applicant to address the Board. Mr. Bob Templeton
(445 Highland Ave. East Lansing) stated there has been litigation initiated on
this property and the Supervisor has been listed as a witness so he request
that the issue be tabled until the litigation process is complete. Mr.
Templeton said there was never an intent to split the property into 32 parcels
and that the reason he requested rezoning is that the Road Commission
requests that for a county road to be created, the road service more than 2
parcels. He said the engineer did draw the drawing with a 1320’ road including
a cul-de-sac (660’ +660’).
Mr. Templeton said another point he wants to make is that the current zoning
requires a minimum of 120 feet of frontage for that zone. For a real road, his
understanding is that the frontage requirement is 160’. He said that if that
property was rezoned and split using the current roadway plan, the splits would
be of no more density than the nearby properties. He said, to clarify, if you
take the piece of land he owns there and split it up into 6 parcels, the splits
would be 10 acres in size. Supervisor Martin corrected him stating that the
property being requested for rezoning is only 38 acres so you couldn’t create 6
ten acre parcels. Mr. Templeton agreed.
 
Mr. Templeton said that another point he has is that this property is similar
to the properties owned by Bob Hilty and Dwight Kamp. He said they were both
prior Planning Commission members and the zoning on their properties was
changed while they were on the Planning Commission. He said he thinks his
property is similar to their property so his zoning request should also be
allowed. He asked if a comment section was allowed after the Board responds to
his point. Supervisor Martin said not usually but, if he has more to say, he
can speak again.
 
Supervisor Martin responded to each of Mr. Templeton’s points. First, she asked

Mr. Templeton responded that it is all tied up together. Trustee Wright said he
fails to see how the litigation pending between two private citizens has
anything to do with a rezoning request. Mr. Templeton said the road way is part
of the litigation. Treasurer Fink clarified that maybe Mr. Templeton is
concerned that a decision made at this Board meeting could impact his pending
litigation. Mr. Templeton said he is not a lawyer but a decision tonight may
impact the litigation. He said he would leave the decision on whether to table
the rezoning request up to the Board. Supervisor Martin clarified that it is a
personal civil litigation between a citizen and Mr. Templeton and not

He responded that it is not at this time. Supervisor Martin said she is not
positive that there is a need to table the decision. She asked Mr. Kraft if, as
chairman of the Planning Commission, he saw a conflict of interest for her to
consider tabling this decision because of the pending litigation that names her

Supervisor, acting as chairman of the Board, and voting on the rezoning request
being a benefit to either litigant. The Board agreed that they were ready to

Supervisor Martin clarified that even though the applicant stated that there
was no intent to split to 32 parcels, the rezoning will allow it so the
property owner will have the right to split in the future. Therefore, the Board
has to consider this as a future possibility. Supervisor Martin said she didn’t

Mr. Templeton said that Ingham County Road Commission uses 160’ for its rural
road specifications. Treasurer Fink said that R-1-S district was not intended
to be put in rural areas. She said it was intended that R-1-S and R-1 districts
be located closer to the City where hook-up to sewer and water would eventually
be available eventually. Trustee Wright said he doesn’t understand why the

parcels split-there are other options for rezoning that make more sense. Mr.

Zoning Ordinance Revision-Addition of M-43 Access Management District
Planning Commission Chairman Dan Kraft reported that MDOT had provided the
Township with recommended access guidelines for access management along the M-
43 corridor and was encouraging local municipalities to adopt these guidelines
to better manage future commercial growth. The Planning Commission worked with
McKenna Associates to adapt those guidelines to our Township’s needs. The
Planning Commission is proposing an overlay district that would only apply to
the M-43 corridor and properties within 300’ of the corridor. In some
instances, it will limit the access points to Grand River to lower the
likelihood of traffic accidents. Mr. Kraft said there had been a 2 step public
hearing; the first meeting was held 2 months ago and then the final version was
deliberated on by the Planning Commission on June 17, 2003 with a final
recommendation that the Board adopt the M-43 overlay plan for the M-43
corridor.
 
Supervisor Martin clarified that this overlay does not impact parcels zoned
residential. Mr. Kraft concurred that this access management plan will affect
business or subdivisions when they move in. Supervisor Martin explained that
she had worked on this corridor study with representatives from MDOT and the
surrounding communities. The goal is to plan for 50 years down the road so that
we can avoid traffic bottlenecks like Meridian Township currently experiences.
She said that when businesses come in, they will need to provide service drives
and accesses from one business to another so traffic doesn’t have to move back
out onto Grand River. Supervisor Martin said that right now the Township does
not have the sewer capacity or the desire to commercialize Grand River but this
will help us manage the future. Treasurer Fink asked if it is going to affect
existing small businesses that won’t be able to connect up to the access
drives. Supervisor Martin said in that situation, easements can be installed.
This will be an overlay to our zoning ordinance.
 
Trustee Zaban made a motion to include the proposed text amendment for an M-43
Access Management District as an overlay to Article 25A of the Zoning
ordinance. Motion supported by Trustee Wright. Motion passed unanimously.
