Planning Commission
Vice Chair Rex LaMore summarized the meeting for the Board. A Public Hearing
regarding wireless communications facilities was held. The Planning Commission
recommended adoption by the Board with minor changes. The Election Committee
formed and met to discuss the election of officers. There are major changes
this year with the election of Chair Fielek and retirements of Trustee Wright
and Commissioner Cook from the Commission and possibly more changes due to the
election in November. The Township has an excellent Planning Commission and
look forward to working with the new appointments by the board.
The Commission is also addressing an item requested by the Zoning Board of
Appeals regarding review of potential splits for parcels on Haslett Rd and
Shoeman Rd. The Commission is continuing review of the Master Plan. The
Economic Analysis chapter is being updated to establish the value of
agricultural use within the Township and the need for protection of this use.
Wireless Communication Facilities.
Vice Chair LaMore reviewed the reason for the recommendations. The State
changed the prerogatives of municipalities to regulate wireless facilities and
developed standards for by right use and special use along with changing the
review time for towers for both current and new facilities.
This could have an impact on the base of the tower footprint. These revision
recommendations are a result of this directive from the state.
The recommendation is to adopt the revisions with the removal of the word
option.
Trustee Wright moved the Williamstown Township Board approve the recommended
revisions to the Williamstown Township Zoning Ordinance Concerning Wireless
Communications Facilities in compliance with the new legislation signed by
Governor Snyder regarding Public Act 110 of 2006 with the removal of the word
“option”.
Seconded by Trustee Williams
Discussion: none
Motion approved.
Unfinished Business
Mitchell Road Speed
Supervisor Martin reminded the Board of approach by Mr. English and
Commissioner Schafer regarding the speed on Mitchell Rd. Chief Hall met with
the Road Commission and Supervisor Martin contacted the Township’s legal
counsel for information on the precedence of the playground issue that Mr.
English had spoken to.
Chief Hall also checked with the State Police regarding the playground issue.
Neither the Road Commission, Legal Counsel or the State Police were aware of
precedence using the school athletic field as part of the definition of
playground as a means to allow the Township to control the speed limit. Though
the speed limit on Williamston Road and Vanneter Rd. is 35, an official
investigation may recommend that they be raised to 45 mph. Chief Hall stated
that from a law enforcement perspective, the department has not seen major
issues to date on Mitchell Rd. The speed limit is 30 mph during beginning and
ending school hours. The Police Department will continue to watch this area and
with good enforcement current speed limit should be safe.
Road Maintenance Proposal
Treasurer Eyster has put together a policy and proposal for budgeting.
Treasurer Eyster explained the report last month gave background information
that the road committee used for their recommendation. Need to look for
additional funds for resurfacing the other through and subdivision roads within
the Township.
It is highly recommended to address resurfacing as it is most cost beneficial
to resurface before needing reconstruction. The road commission will make a
recommendation which roads should be resurfaced each year.
Treasurer Eyster reviewed the funding proposal presented to the Board for
consideration. The proposal recommends that any adjusted fund balance over
$1,000,000 be allocated with 50% towards road capital outlay and 50% for
infrastructure. This would set aside funds for special projects. The amount set
aside would change yearly based on the adjusted fund balance. Anticipate having
funds over $1,000,000 to set aside yearly. Big expenditures are not typical.
This process sets asides the funds that will roll over at the end of the year
and promotes savings for future expenditures. This can be adjusted if it
appears too much money is accumulating in a fund. If put aside for
infrastructure now, the Township shouldn’t see a big draw down of general
funds. Policy can be changed if it is not working as anticipated. Road
committee would make yearly recommendations.
Discussion:
The draft proposal looks good.
Please review prior to the next board meeting.
New Business
Budget 2013-14
The budget approval process has begun. The proposed budget was added to your
packet without major changes. Most changes will be due to increase in grounds
maintenance at the park and cemetery. Please review for the next meeting. Clerk
will be working on insurance. Departments need to meet and look at their
respective budgets.
Anticipated timeline for budget review: Public hearing will be in February with
a vote in March. Revisions need to be complete by January for the Public
Hearing.
Meridian Police Contract 2013-15
Proposed two year contract was in the packet. Only changes are yearly and
hourly amounts were increased. Everything else remained the same. Police
committee met with Chief Hall and Lieutenant Fraiser to review the contract.
Overall comments were positive. The Committee looked at the budget allocation
and it was recommended to approve the contract and lower assessment to $120
residential and $200 for commercial. Trustee Hayes and Treasurer Eyster serve
on the police committee. The projected budget for police expenditures shows if
it was reduced to the suggested assessment and maximum expenses of cost that
would be covered. This did not include county funds at this time until the
audit is completed with the County. Suggest asking the county to do the audit
early next year. Thought Meridian would approve the contract at the November
meeting. Once county completes audit, county funds can be added back in to the
total fund amount.

within the township. This is the highest density residential district within
the township. Asked for a time line to come into compliance, however the owner
has not submitted one as of this date. The Board is in agreement to turn this
matter over to the Township Attorney. The Right to Farm Act only protects farms
that are in districts were farming is allowed.

1235 Grand River Rd.

zoning district does not allow non-commercial use. Owner has not responded to
letters requesting compliance.

Attorney.
168 Haslett
Owner is out of compliance of the Zoning Ordinance with a non-commercial

February 27, 2013
Williamstown Township
Board of Trustees Meeting Minutes
February 27, 2013
Call to Order
The Williamstown Township Board of Trustees convened at 5:00 pm. at the
Williamstown Township Hall located at 4990 Zimmer Rd., Williamston, Michigan.
Supervisor Mickey Martin called the meeting to order and reviewed the agenda,
consisting of one item, discussion of the proposed Zimmer Road bridge over the
Red Cedar River.
Roll Call
Present: Trustee Imhoff, Clerk Gaffner, Treasurer Fielek, Supervisor Martin and
Trustee Hayes
Absent: Trustee Eyster and Trustee Williams
Public Comment
None
Closed at 5:02.pm
Discussion
The original Zimmer road bridge railing design is standard concrete with
horizontal metal tubing. Members of the Township Board and Planning Commission
were interested in possible options that might be more aesthetically in line
with the rural character of the Township. The Ingham County Road Commission
provided three options for the Township Board to consider, in lieu of using the
original design.
1.   A tinted application sealer at an initial Township cost of $500-$1,000 and
continuing maintenance costs of $8,000-$10,000 every 5 years.
2.   “Form Liner” option, modifying the concrete railing walls with a pattern,
with a Township cost estimated between $20,000 and $50,000.
3.   A “Texas T Railing” with a Township cost of $30,000.
Board members, along with Planning Commission chair Rex LaMore, discussed the
three options presented and the costs associated with the options and decided
none of them really demonstrated the true character of the Township and the
costs associated with the options were more than the benefit provided.
Trustee Hayes moved that the board approve spending up to $10,000 for a bridge
railing design that would be more in line with the rural character of
Williamstown Township, so long as a desgn change did not delay the Zimmer Road
project. Any change in design would require approval of the Township Board.
Motion seconded by Clerk Gaffner
The Motion Passed
Trustee Hayes moved to adjourn at 5:45
____________________________
Ernie Gaffner, Clerk

The Citizen Academy begins in the fall and runs for 9 weeks. Youth Academy
begins Thursday the 14th, with 3 Township students participating. The Academy
runs for 2 hours a night for 6 weeks. Most students participating are
interested in law enforcement. The department has activated on-line reporting.
There is a link on the Meridian Township site to allow a report to be submitted
on line which is then addressed by the shift Sargent. Provides an alternative
for callers that don't feel they need to see an officer. This is available to
Township residents. The Township can provide a link to the Meridian site for
this feature.

the minimum patrol hours per the contract. On-line reporting is factored in as
part of administrative cost. If this led to an investigation, additional
charges may be incurred.

May 22, 2013
Williamstown Township
Special Board of Trustees Meeting Minutes
May 22, 2013
Call to Order
The Williamstown Township Board of Trustees convened at 2:00 p.m. at the
Williamstown Township Hall located at 4990 Zimmer Rd., Williamston, Michigan by
Supervisor Martin.
Present: Supervisor Martin, Trustee Imhoff, Clerk Gaffner, Treasurer Fielek,
Trustee Williams and Trustee
    Eyster
Absent: Trustee Hayes
Trustee Eyster presented information concerning a recommendation from the
Ingham County Department of Transportation and Roads (ICDTR) for Germany Road.
Before any bids can be obtained for the recommendation, the Township Board
needs to approve having the ICDTR seek bids on their proposal for Germany Road.
The county recommendation is for 2 inch asphalt paving and CIPR on the half
mile east of Meridian Rd, and CIPR and single course chip-sealing the 1.1 miles
from west of Hart rd to Zimmer Rd which together totaled $190,000. This would
break down to $104,000 for the Hart to Zimmer Rd portion and $86,000 for the
half mile east of Meridian Rd section. The ICDTR has determined that if CIPR
and paving is done on the half mile east of Meridian Rd, there should be some
ditching and culverts in that area to improve the drainage. Most of the cost is
in labor by ICDTR to install the culverts and do the ditching. ICDTR requests
that the culvert pipe cost be included in the project cost, but it should be
less than $3,000 and does not raise the total estimate ($190,000) previously
given. This would include 8 new driveway culverts and a cross culvert (pipe
cost only) for the half mile east of Meridian Rd. All labor to be done by ICDTR
crews and is not included in the cost and will be provided by ICDTR, which
includes ditching and culvert installation in the half mile east of Meridian Rd
and labor for Chip sealing the 1.1 mile from west of Hart to Zimmer Roads. All
CIPR, and paving in the half mile east of Meridian Rd, must be done by a
contractor(s).
Trustee Eyster stated that the Township will not know the exact amount of funds
available until the audit for 2012-2013 fiscal year is completed in August or
September. According to board policy, $45,000 to $50,000 additional funds
should be available for road work in the summer of 2014. If the total cost for
the contract through the County is under $190,000 the Township could pay for it
by using the funds currently available ($159,449.50) with the remaining
$30,550.50 taken from road funds that would have been spent in 2014.
Clerk Gaffner moved that the Township approve having the Ingham County
Department of Transportation and Roads seek bids for the recommended Germany
Road repairs.
Second by Supervisor Martin
Motion approved.
Trustee Imhoff moved for adjournment
Second by Treasurer Fielek

Ernie Gaffner, Clerk

Code Enforcement
Supervisor Martin explained that a Code Enforcement Ordinance would allow for
ticketing and allow Meridian Police to help with code enforcement. The Police
Department would note violations when patrolling, inform the Township, and the
Township would send the standard 10 day letter out. If continued non-
compliance, a ticket could be issued. This then goes directly to court as a
civil infraction. Funds collected as a result of the tickets would go to the
Township. Chief Hall is agreeable to this service as part of the patrolling.
Meridian currently does a sweep twice a year for unlicensed cars,etc. in
Meridian Township and could provide the same service here.

Question of minutes: none.
Special Use Permit (SUP) sign application
PC Secretary Eidt reviewed the application of Stamprite Supersine’s sign
proposal.
Applicant is proposing to erect a sign of 143 sq. ft. that would display stock
quotes along with a panel for CG Financial. The primary concern of the
commission was the size. Maximum size of 48 sq. ft. is allowed per the
ordinance. There was sentiment of some Commissioners to work with the applicant
on a compromise of the sign size. During the Public Hearing Chair LaMore
pointed out the ordinance is reasonable, varying from the ordinance would
create a domino effect to increase size of signage, and does not fit the vision
of the Master Plan. The Planning Commission recommends denial of the
application.
Rob West of Stamprite Supersine addressed the Board: The property owner had
purchased the existing sign, felt it was too small for the site, and had
received comments that the size should be increased. This design is honoring
the customer’s request and would model the stone work of the pillars on Grand
River. Applicant does not believe there would be a domino effect due to the
cost of this size sign. The site does not have a clear area for site visibility
for the small size of the existing sign. The Planning Commission felt the
proposed sign was too large and the applicant/owner would consider a compromise
in the size.
Questions/Discussion:
·   Speed seems to a problem with reading the sign.
·   At the Public Hearing Mr. Peterson stated the ticker sign is a branding
method. The larger sign would allow more space to be able to read.
·   Maybe ticker not feasible for this site.
·   Suggest adding address number.
·   Speed and ticker sign combination seems to be a real hazard.
·   Another sign located in Haslett is larger and still not readable.
·   Moving sign seems to distract from the business name.
·   Board not in the position to negotiate the size of the sign.
·   Larger size would require a variance. Concern over questions that need to
be addressed with granting a variance for this proposal.
·   Current sign is at maximum size as allowed in the ordinance.
·   Meridian Township granted a request for a larger sign due to building
location behind other buildings. Larger lettering would allow it to be seen at
a glance. Valid concerns over size of sign.

Code Enforcement
Jerry Richards, the representative from Manick and Smith, presented a draft
Code Enforcement Ordinance to the Board for review. Township Attorney, Gary
Bender, reviewed the draft with Mr. Richards and his additions are included in
the draft language. Civil infraction language was included for each category
along with language to give broad options for enforcement along with methods of
addressing violations, prosecution and enforcement. Mr. Richards requested
direction of the Board regarding addressing vegetation issues. Mr. Richards
raised specific areas of concern and articulated areas to address in code
enforcement. Code enforcement does not need to be limited to areas that are
addressed in the draft. Meridian Township Police can work with the Township on
uniformly enforcing the code. The current complaint basis for enforcement does
not work well, while the Police Department has the ability to canvas the whole
Township to ensure equal treatment of residents. A procedure policy would be
created to track progress.
Discussion included:
·   Junk cars: some can be abated and charged, while others would be given a
citation and proceed to court.
·   Blight ordinance was reviewed and is adequate. Could be uniformly enforced
without necessarily adding to staff or cost. The Blight Ordinance is similar to
Meridian Township’s. Propose a uniform process of enforcement. A draft policy
was shared with the members of the board and reviewed regarding the process
whether a complaint comes in over the phone or observed by the Police
department.
·   Could announce to residents a sweep of the Township for code enforcement.
This could be done a couple of times a year.
·   If the board chooses to have a vegetation ordinance this could be done
similar to Meridian. Meridian’s sweep occurs through the police department and
building staff.
·   Williamstown Township would be more involved with the police department.
Verification of the police finding would occur before a letter went out from
the Township. Communication would go back to the police department of when the
letter was sent so that they are able to verify that it was abated or proceed
to write a civil infraction.
·   A brief set of rules of the zoning ordinance would be provided for the
police to follow in enforcement.
Board Discussion:
·   Vegetation ordinance: Subdivisions such as Pebblebrook and Larkin Estates,
would appreciate a vegetation ordinance.
·   Concern over differentiating between large parcels, structures, footage,
etc. Can exempt certain types of vegetation. Consider heights and distances
·   Would like to see what other communities are doing regarding vegetation.
Consensus over having some type of vegetation regulations included in the
Blight Ordinance or as a Vegetation Ordinance.
·   Process of civil infraction: Some will be ignored and can still end up in a
court situation. Municipal violations bureau could be formed.
·   Suggest having a form that is used for complaints. Goal is for uniform
enforcement.
·   Advantage with police coverage.
·   Complaints can be made from outside the Township.
·   Make sure ordinance is in line with Township values.
·   Need to change the Ordinance to include the language addressed by the
attorney.
Next step: Mr. Richards will return with language regarding vegetation. Will
need to get other Ordinances updated with required language for enforcement.
Notification should go out to residents.
A Township official or their designee could determine if an infraction needs to
be turned over to the attorney for further action. .

Website and revised mission statement. CADL is working in local schools and for
the past few years has sponsored a “Book Battle” for 6th grade students,
encouraging the reading of books from the library. The library provides several
technology services, including use of computers, printing, scanning, and
downloading of books and instruction classes for those desiring to know more
about the use of technology. There is a proposal on the August 5th primary
election for the renewal of 1.56 mills to support the operation of CADL. During
the past 12 months there were more than 62,000 visitors to the local library
and Williamstown Township has 1,640 CADL card members.

$195,000. She advised the Board that there are 50.3 miles of County Secondary
roads in the Township and the cost to resurface these roads is $32,000 per
mile. If the Township were to establish a program for the resurfacing and
maintenance of the 50.3 miles on a 7 year program, it would require an
assessment of approximately 1 mill. The majority of Board members voiced their
opinion in support of holding public hearings to obtain information from the
Township residents and find out if there was enough support to put a road
millage proposal on the ballot at a near future election. It was agreed to
begin providing information to the Township residents concerning the condition
of the roads, the cost to maintain them and what could happen to the roads if
they are not maintained.

Burn Permits
Supervisor Martin stated that while working on making requests for Burn Permits
available on the Township website, she was made aware of the fact that the
Township burn ordinance does not allow the residents of a residential dwelling
located in an industrial zone to obtain a burn permit. The ordinance is
specific about not allowing for commercial burn permits but does not allow for
an exception for residence within the same zoning.
Trustee Hayes moved the Williamstown Township Board approve the granting of
burn permits to nonconforming residents living in industrial zones B-1, B-2 and
I-1, when residents make application and follow the guidelines set forth in the
Township “Burning Permit Application.” Burn permits will not be granted to
residents in these same zones if the residence parcel also includes a
commercial exposure.

Road millage
Board is looking at putting a road millage on the ballot for road maintenance
and repairs.
Supervisor Martin stated the Board is considering a ballot proposal for a
millage dedicated to road maintenance and reviewed the report. There are four
classifications of roads: State Roads, County primary, County Secondary, County
Secondary Subdivisions. Twp. funds are not used for State or County primary.
Act 51 requires a match for secondary county road improvements, which the
Township has provided.
There are three types of road preservation: Reconstruction, Hot in place
recycle, (typically in subs and is contracted out) and micro-surface over chip
seal. In the past seven years the Township has spent $500,000 and the County
$195,000 on Township secondary roads. Cost affiliated with each type of
preservation was reviewed along with the recommended maintenance schedule and
the possibility of some roads converting back to gravel.
The Board road policy was reviewed as well as funding for road improvements.
The amount of money the Township may receive from new state funding may provide
approximately $8,000. At this time the Township cannot maintain the roads in
acceptable repair without further funding.
Trustee Eyster reviewed the tables in the report showing the initial cost to
bring roads up to standard, maintenance cost of secondary subdivision roads and
secondary roads, the sources of funding and potential new funds from a millage
over a 10 year period. The report is fairly detailed so that when it is
finalized, residents will have a clearly written detail of the Township’s
needs. Without funding the Township would need to revert some roads back to
gravel. There are roads that are currently in need of reconstruction.
Clerk Gaffner requested residents sign up to receive a copy of the report and
excused himself to make additional copies.
Supervisor Martin addressed the amount of property taxes that are collected for
the Township is 2 %
(Approximately $182,000). Over 5 years the total collected from residents of
Williamstown Estates totaled approx. $19,500. The board would like to hold a
Town Hall meeting sometime in July to review a potential ballot proposal.
The Board welcomed comments from those in attendance:
Kurt Guter: 4045 Cygnet, Williamston Estates along with other residents of the
subdivision.
(Crawford, Genova, Cooper, Hillard, and Tebeau) They noted their support for
funding measure to be placed on the ballot. Suggest simpler information that
can be shared on the website with the detailed report available.

The Williamstown Township Board of Trustees convened at 10:30 a.m. at the
Williamstown Township Hall located at 4990 Zimmer Rd., Williamston, Michigan by

Discussion of Placing a Proposal to raise funds for Township road preservation,
reconstruction and maintenance.
Board Comments:
      Due to continuing inflation, is 1.5 mills enough to preserve the Township
Roads?
      It is understood the money being sought is for secondary roads, including
subdivision roads.
If the County receives taxes from Township residents, and the county
commissioners cut back on the amount of funds allocated for specific budgets,
such as police and roads, why should the Township have to increase taxes to
take care of those areas and not put pressure on the County to use the taxes
the Township gives them, in the Township?
The proposal should designate what amount of the tax increase will be used for
secondary roads, and what amount will be used on subdivision roads.
Can the proposal specify an amount to be used on County Primary Roads and not
just secondary and subdivision roads?
Motion by Clerk Gaffner: Moved the Township Board approve placing a proposal on
the November 4th ballot for Township Road preservation, reconstruction and
maintenance with a 1.5 mill limit as presented and amended.
   Second by Trustee Eyster
   Motion Approved
Williamstown Township Ballot Proposal November 4, 2014
Shall the limitation on the amount of ad valorem taxes which may be levied by
the Township of Williamstown, Ingham County, Michigan, against taxable property
in the Township be increased by up to 1.5 mill ($1.50 per $1,000 of taxable
value) for a period of ten (10) years, 2014 through 2023, inclusive, for the
purpose of providing funds for secondary road preservation, reconstruction and
maintenance, and shall the Township levy such millage for these purposes? If
approved and levied in its entirety, the estimated revenue that the Township
would collect from this 1.5 mill is $328,342 in 2014.
11:38 Trustee Fielek moved for
adjournment                                        Second by Trustee Eyster

Site Plan SUP 3800 Vanneter
Commissioner Weston reviewed the letter dated April 10, 2015 from McKenna
Associates. Residents attended the public hearing and raised concerns with the
expansion to a 12 bed facility. Concerns included: parking, generation of
trash, use of basement for an apartment and number of residents for this size
lot. He noted that the ZBA granted the variances due to administrative error of
the building permit approval process. The applicant has attempted to address
the concerns of the consultant and the neighbors.
Chris Lobb, attorney for the applicant addressed the Board. He noted that the
Harns have operated a 6 bed facility at this location for 17 years. McKenna
Associates letter dated April 10, 2015 recommended approval, based on
information provided from the applicant, for the Special Use Permit to increase
the facility to 12 beds. The 12 bed facility use is identified as a Special use
in the R-1 district, and is noted as such in McKenna’s letter as well as
addresses the need for affordable housing for a growing segment of the
population outlined in the Master Plan. Residential use abuts three sides of
the property and agriculture abuts the fourth.
The applicant addressed the consultant’s recommendations for the Site Plan
conditions and obtained the variances needed. As part of the variance approval,
an evergreen screen and fencing will be added as approved by the ZBA. The
consultant recommended less parking and the applicant revised the site plan to
accommodate his recommendation along with the addition of the Evergreen screen.
Complaints were lodged by residents of parking in the street during the Public
Hearing.
July 15th: The Planning Commission recommended denial despite the
recommendation of the consultant based on comments of the neighbors regarding
parking issues, use of living quarters by an employee’s family,
Handling of trash, and activities of residents and staff. The motion for denial
gave four reasons: Compatibility with the neighborhood, parking, size of
facility for lot and the apartment. Applicant is aware of need for SUP for
apartment. There will be no one living in the lower level. Staff person with 2
small children currently living in the lower level are moving.
Fair housing issue was not addressed by the planning commission. The board
needs to consider this when making a determination as the Federal Fair Housing
Act is there to protect discrimination against those with disabilities and
provides for financial incentive to accommodate a need within the community.
Applicant added staffing and have not personally worked at the site for some
time so in order to obtain financial viability going forward there was a need
to request the expansion. The Harns feel they have satisfied the concerns of
the consultant, McKenna and Associates and the ZBA and that this is a
reasonable request and should be approved.
Supervisor Martin opened for questions:
   Trustee felt the facility was well maintained, and that public parking is
allowed on the street.
   Reasonable to approve need for senior housing. Residents have a right to be
present.
   Supervisor Martin again asked if there were questions from the board:
   Questioned the need for the apartment. According to the architect the
expansion of the basement was made for storage and a break area.
   With 24 hour care employees work in 24 hour shifts. Building inspector
stated the basement is not approved for a bedroom facility.
   Tom Reder with Bergman associates: Architect for the Harns. Stated there was
living quarters in the lower level and it will be corrected. In his opinion
there is an escape for the bedroom. Has not been inspected for code compliance.
He stated an egress window is in place. Added on to the basement with an egress
stairway when the addition was done. Additional stairway added for staff. If it
is not used as an apartment there is not a compatibility issue with the zoning
ordinance.
   Financials show that 10 residents are needed to cover cost. The applicant
was aware of the intention to increase beds when they made application for the
addition. The owners were at a breakeven point without the addition.
   Chris Lobb noted the Smith case: his contention that board has to approve
the SUP to be economically viability. Also looking at the FFA (Federal Fair
Housing Act) along with the compatibility issue of Zoning Ordinance.
   Gary Bender, Murphy & Spagnoula, Township attorney, noted that the Smith
case does not state this in particular- have to look at industry locally not
just the owners cost.
   ZBA approved the variance for the lot coverage due to Township
administrative error.
   The applicant has addressed the nine factors outlined in McKenna’s letter,
the zoning ordinance and master plan.
   The owners had not received complaints from the neighbors until the public
hearing (PH) was held for the special use permit (SUP).
   There were unusual circumstance for approval for the variances. The variance
was only issued due to administrative error without proper oversight. The ZBA
took ownership of the Township’s mistake and hence granted variance. Do not
feel the request would have been granted otherwise. The ZBA made it clear their
decision was not to be construed that they approved the SUP request.
   The Township was not aware of a family living in the lower level at any time
prior to the application for the SUP.
   Board belief that the Township follows the Master Plan.
   Applicant’s attorney does not feel the Township can turn down the request.
   Notice must be given to residents living in lower level.
   Applicant was aware at time of building permit application the intent for
expansion of beds. The process for the SUP should have been the first step.
   Applicant’s attorney stated there was a lack of knowledge on the applicant’s
part of the process.
   Live in is an employee of Williamston Compassionate Care.
   The expansion of the business would require an understanding of the process
and going through the appropriate channels. Applicant acknowledges that it was
not well thought out and presented.
   Impact of expanding the facility is not compatible with the neighborhood.
Clerk Gaffner moved the Williamstown Township Board deny the Site Plan and
Special Use Permit for 3800 Vanneter Road, as the Township Board has determined
that a special use proposal does not comply with the standards and regulations

Wallace-Special Use Permit Go-Mini Rentals
Trustee Williams moved the Williamstown Township Board approve the Special Use
Permit for the Go-Mini Storage system. The approval will help serve a growing
need for temporary service at a location that is already providing on site
storage. Approval is subject to the following conditions:
1.    No more than 104 Go-Mini Storage Units will be stored on site
2.   Go-Mini Storage Units will be locked at all times
3.   Rented Go-Mini Storage Units will not be stored on site
4.   Go-Mini Storage Units will not be stacked on site

·   Concerns about the height of trees being purchased by the owner to comply

Board that a new motion be drafted to include Board member concerns and brought
back for discussion at the January 2016 meeting.
Harns – Williamston Compassionate Care Special Use Permit
Trustee Williams moved the Township Board approve the Williamston Compassionate
Care special land use application, calling for expansion to accommodate up to
12 residents, based on the following findings:
1.    By virtue of having obtained lot coverage and set back variances, the
building is in compliance with zoning ordinance requirements.
2.   Measures have been implemented by the applicants to address neighbors’
concerns and achieve compatibility with adjacent uses.
3.   A need for a facility of this nature exists in the area.
4.   The facility will have no greater impact on public services and traffic
and roads than a typical single family home.
This recommendation of approval is subject to the following conditions:
1.   An affidavit, in a form suitable to the Township, shall be recorded by the
applicant confirming that the basement shall not be used as living quarters.
2.   An additional two parking spaces shall be constructed by May 1, 2016, as
proposed on the site plan.
3.   A copy of the adult foster care license from the State of Michigan shall
be submitted to the Township, including a copy of all renewal licenses.
Seconded by Trustee Eyster.
Discussion:
·   Once the special use permit is approved by the Board, Harns can then submit
the license
·   With the addition of beds, the code went from residential to commercial
·   As part of the licensing process with the State, a final check will be made
by the fire marshal
·   Initial license is for six months, then renewal is every other year
Motion approved

Red Cedar Renaissance
Commissioner Giese reviewed the actions of the Planning Commission and the site

Planning Commission recommended approval by the Board of the site plan
contingent on Ferguson/Continental Lansing’s commitment to remove the log jam
(fallen trees) in the river at the northwest corner of the Township park, and
on the Township being recognized for its efforts on behalf of this project.
Jason Hockstock, Eric Iversen and Tom Stover (land owner) presented an overview
of the project. The compensating cut will create protected wetlands and flood
plain. Mr. Stover plans to begin work soon to restore property to farming. The
applicant has agreed to clear the log jam in the northwest corner of the
Township park.

NEW BUSINESS
USGS/Ingham County Water Study
Garry Rowe described the proposed well-water testing project that will involve
testing about 20 Township residential wells for bacteria and for several heavy
metals. The 17 wells that were tested in 1983 will be retested. Testing has
been completed in Aurelius Township. Mr. Rowe asked for Township help in
communicating with residents. Individual test reports will be provided to
residents whose wells are tested and a report of findings will be presented to
the Township. The Ingham County Drain Commission will provide major funding.
Township funding will be up to $600.
Trustee Williams moved the Township Board approve the participation in the
USGS/Ingham County Groundwater Study at a cost not to exceed $600. This Study
will provide information useful to Township residents on the quality of the
Township wells.
Seconded by Clerk Mitchell.
Discussion: None
Motion approved.

Absent: None
Public Comment
None
Closed at 7:10 p.m.
Presentation
Gary Rowe presented his findings of a water test study conducted of the
groundwater quality in Williamstown Township. It was a follow up study to the
1986 county grant project. The current study compares results from 1986 with
2017. Mr. Rowe states tests done this year show an overall rise in some
elements (such as Boron) and a decrease in others (such as Arsenic). At this
time, the State of Michigan does not have a Boron water safety standard. There
is a Boron brochure available with recommendations for the residents regarding
this health advisory. Testing is continuing in other Ingham County townships.
The report was presented to the Board. A copy of the report is available from
the Township.

October 12, 2016 Synopsis
WILLIAMSTOWN TOWNSHIP
BOARD OF TRUSTEES MEETING
October 12, 2016 Synopsis
The Williamstown Township Board of Trustees held its regularly scheduled
monthly meeting, October 12, 2016 at 7:03p.m. with Supervisor Bloomquist,
Treasurer Cutshaw, Clerk Steinberg, Trustees Imhoff, Williams, Hayes and Eyster
present. The Board approved the consent agenda, consisting of the minutes of
the September 14, 2016 Board meeting, payroll report, treasurer’s report,
accounts payable, revenue and expenditure reports, building inspector’s report,
and police report. The Board heard the quarterly police report from Chief Hall
and, from the township’s audit firm, a summary of the latest audit report. The
Board approved the Planning Commission’s recommended revisions to the
Subdivision Control Ordinance and approval of the Whitcraft pond site plan. The
Board tabled the recommended changes to the Zoning Ordinance sign regulations
and the denial of the Verizon Tower Special Use Permit/Site Plan. The Board
also acted on a FOIA appeal, reviewed budget changes for FY 2017-2018, reduced
the police assessment to $100 per residential unit and $175 per commercial
unit, accepted donated funds for a park picnic table, and approved expenditures
for township soccer fields. The meeting adjourned at 10:25p.m..
The next meeting of the Board is Tuesday November 15, 2016 at 7:00P.M. in the
Township boardroom at 4990 Zimmer Rd.
Township website: http://www.williamstowntownsip.com
Mark Steinberg, Clerk

WILLIAMSTOWN TOWNSHIP
BOARD OF TRUSTEES MEETING
DECEMBER 14 2016 Synopsis
The Williamstown Township Board of Trustees held its regularly scheduled
monthly meeting Wednesday December 14, 2016 at 7:00 PM at the Township hall,
with Supervisor Bloomquist, Treasurer Cutshaw, Clerk Steinberg, Trustees
Eyster, Williams, Kane and Duffy present. The Board approved the consent agenda
consisting of the minutes of the November 15, 2016 Board Meeting and the
following reports: accounts payable paid, accounts payable for approval,
revised payroll check report, payroll paid, revenue and expenditure reports,
Building inspector’s report, Treasurer’s report and Police report. The
following Board actions were taken: approved a Zoning Ordinance Amendment
regarding Open Space Preservation in Section 8.03 (C); approved a modified site
plan for the Verizon Tower on 1690 Haslett Rd for an overhead canopy in lieu of
an enclosed building; sent the proposed Sign Regulations revisions to the
Planning Commission for further review and revision;. approved the purchase of
a Snow Blower to be used in the parks cemeteries and other Township properties;
approved a variance to the Township Burning Ordinance to allow burning of brush
piles on Parcel No. 33-03-03-01-400-005; tabled a draft fireworks ordinance for
discussion at the January 11 Board meeting; and scheduled a workshop on the
2017/2018 budget at 6:00pm on January 25, 2017 at the Township Hall.

boardroom at 4990 Zimmer Road.

Board of Trustees Budget Workshop Minutes
January 25, 2017
Call to Order
The Williamstown Township Board of Trustees convened a budget workshop at 6:04
p.m. at the Williamstown Township Hall located at 4990 Zimmer Rd., Williamston,
Michigan. Supervisor Bloomquist called the meeting to order and reviewed the
Agenda. Supervisor Bloomquist led the Pledge of Allegiance.
Roll Call
Present: Supervisor Bloomquist, Trustee Kane, Trustee Duffy, Treasurer Cutshaw,
Clerk Steinberg, Trustee
Williams and Trustee Eyster (via Skype).
Absent: None
Public Comment
None. Closed at 6:06 pm.
Budget Workshop
The purpose of the workshop was to provide Board members an opportunity to
review and discuss a draft budget and related materials concerning the
Township’s fiscal year 2017-2018 beginning April 1, 2017. Materials discussed
included:
·   Draft budget
·   Employee benefit summary
·   Staffing recommendations
·   Road and Infrastructure funding policy
·   Financial administration policies
·   Escrow accounts
·   Costs of administering tax collections
In context of detailed discussion, the Board selected several items for further
review this calendar year. These included:
Policy issues
1. Infrastructure budget (how determined?)
2.   Benefits for elected officials
3. Employee benefit policy
4. Contract policy (assessing, IT, planning, legal, insurance
5. Recycling
6. Roads
Budget issues
1. 911 revenue
2. Dues
3. Park fees
4. Internet and phones
5. Capital outlay
6. Office repairs
7. Codification
Strategic planning
1. Videotaping board meetings
2. Tax collection administration fee
Public Hearing
A date for a public hearing on the 2017-2018 budget will be set in the near
future.
Public Comment
None. Public comment closed at 9:07 pm.
Supervisor Bloomquist adjourned the workshop at 9:08 pm.

UNFINISHED BUSINESS
Policy Review
Three topics were presented for discussion. Trustee Eyster prepared background
information on budget policy and road policy.
Budget Policy - - In recent years the Board has maintained a substantial
reserve account so as to assure adequate resources in the event of emergencies.
In context of developing the budget for FY 2018-2019, the Board will consider
reducing the maximum Fund Balance so that additional funds can be allocated for
roads.
Food Purchase Policy – A draft policy was presented, intended to clarify when
the Township will and will not approve food purchases and will be brought back
for approval in December.
Road Policy – Despite anticipated increases in Township allocated funds and
funds available through the Ingham County Road Department, funding for roads in
the foreseeable future will not be adequate to meet road maintenance needs. The
Board was asked to consider various methods for applying available funds in
ways that maximize the volume of roads maintained while being fair to all
residents.
Budget Review
Supervisor Bloomquist presented a preliminary budget for review and input by
Board members. The budget will reflect a 3% increase for the staff. The
supervisor is recommending soliciting bids for pre-audit services.

Trustee Williams moved the Williamstown Township Board approve the Cemetery
Committee move forward on the purchase of fence for the South property line up

December 13, 2017 Synopsis
WILLIAMSTOWN TOWNSHIP
BOARD OF TRUSTEES MEETING
December 13, 2017 Synopsis
The Williamstown Township Board of Trustees held its regularly scheduled
monthly meeting on Wednesday, December 13, 2017 at 7:00 PM at the Township
hall, with Supervisor Bloomquist, Treasurer Cutshaw, Clerk Steinberg, and
Trustee Kane present. Trustees Duffy, Eyster, and Williams were absent. The
Board approved the consent agenda consisting of the minutes of the November 8,
2017 Board Meeting , the Minutes of November Planning Commission Meeting and
the following reports: accounts payable paid, accounts payable for approval,
payroll paid, revenue and expenditure report, November revenue report, building
inspector’s report, the Police report and acknowledged receipt of the
Treasurer’s November report . The following additional Board actions were
taken:
Approved the Food Policy revisions to be incorporated into the Financial
Policy.
Approved Resolution 117 to waive the collection of fines for late filing of
Property transfer affidavits.
Approved the pre-payment of $10,000 for the Williamstown-Locke Drain to be
expended from 401-101-982.
Approved the expenditure of a maximum $4400 for the budgeted recommended
upgrades to Township Computers and software to be expensed from 101-191-980 and
728 (elections), 101-215-980 and 728 (Clerk) and 101-253-980 and 728
(Treasurer).
Approved the expenditure of $2036.88 for the remaining balance for the drain
assessment from GL 101-441-813 (Drains-at-large).
The next meeting of the Board is a regular Board meeting on Wednesday, January
10, 2018 at 7:00pm in the Township boardroom at 4990 Zimmer Road.
Township website: http:/www.williamstowntownship.com. Phone 517-655-3193.
Mark Steinberg, Clerk

UNFINISHED BUSINESS
Mitchell Road
Trustee Duffy moved that the Williamstown Township Board petition, in the form
of a resolution, the Ingham County Road Commission and/or the Ingham County
Board of Commissioners stating the board’s support for lowering the speed limit
on Mitchell Road with the following points to be included in the resolution:
1. The speed limit should be reduced to 35 MPH.
2. Mitchell Road’s proximity to Williamston Community Schools, specifically
Williamston High School, makes 45 MPH an unsafe speed limit.
3. A current Support letter from Meridian Police Chief Hall
4. Williamston Community Schools Board of Education submitted a letter to the
township expressing its members unanimous support for the speed limit
reduction.
5. A request that any new speed study should be conducted while school is in
session
6. A new petition from Mitchell Road area residents
7. Letter of support from County Commissioner Randy Schafer and State
Representative Sam Singh
Seconded by Trustee Williams
Discussion
State law has changed, making the Township’s position less controlling. Would
be useful to enlist support from various constituencies.
State Police response to informal request was shared with Board members
Motion passed. Budget Policy
Trustee Duffy moved the Williamston Township Board approve the amendments to
Budget Policy 12 to add more funding to Township roads with the addition of a
definition for special projects. Seconded by Trustee Williams.
Discussion:
?   The Policy amendments would reduce budget reserves and increase funding
available for roads.
?   Is the new reserved amount ($800,000) higher than needed?

Treasurer Cutshaw, Trustee

Nays: None. Motion passed. Budget Review

Williamstown Township
Board of Trustees Meeting Minutes
Call to Order
The Williamstown Township Board of Trustees convened a meeting at 6:00 p.m. at
the Williamstown Township Hall located at 4990 Zimmer Rd., Williamston,
Michigan. Supervisor Bloomquist called the meeting to order and reviewed the
Agenda. Supervisor Bloomquist led the Pledge of Allegiance.
Roll Call
Present: Supervisor Bloomquist, Trustees Kane, Duffy, Eyster and Williams,
Clerk Steinberg and Treasurer Cutshaw.
Public Comment for agenda and non- agenda items
None
Closed at 6:03PM
Meeting Purpose
The purpose of the meeting was to discuss Board members’ visions for the near
term future of the Township, and to discuss related ideas and strategies. No
policy decisions were made.
Suggested initiatives:
Update zoning ordinances to better conform with current residential and
commercial needs
Record all Board and Planning Commission meetings
Improve playing surfaces on the soccer fields
Prepare the township hall to serve as a shelter in the event of weather
emergencies and other emergencies, in coordination with other appropriate
agencies
Placing signage (message board) on Grand River Ave to inform people of upcoming
events
Support for older adults:
Development of affordable housing for seniors
Host a 5-k fundraiser
Help in hauling junk to the township’s spring clean-up
Protecting and enhancing revenue streams
Enroll with MiClass (an investment pool for township funds)? Need to clarify
our liability if the system crashes or for any reason we cannot access our
funds.
Collection of the tax administration fee. In discussion, concerns seemed to
outweigh support.
Recycling/sustainability
Plan for permanent recycling at the township – if this involves obtaining fill
material, will need a way to assure appropriateness of this material
Possibility of converting neighborhood streetlights to LEDs
Install repository for medications in the township hall
Further cooperation with the City of Williamston
Possible joint Master Planning
Overlay zone for transition area on Grand River Ave east of the city
Collaboration on the blue water trails project
Public comment for agenda and non-agenda items
Opened at 7:58pm
Nancy Williams spoke in support of signage, senior housing, and help with
spring clean-up.
Closed at 8:01pm
Meeting adjourned at 8:03pm

Public Hearing: Marijuana Opt Out Ordinance
Supervisor Bloomquist opened the Public Hearing by noting that the Township
Board was considering adopting an ordinance opting out of approving
recreational marijuana facilities in the Township. This action, if adopted,
would not restrict personal recreational use as approved by the passage of
Proposal 1 in November. Before taking action, the Board wants to solicit
comments from residents. Supervisor Bloomquist asked that comments be limited
to 3 minutes, per established policy.
The following individuals made comments in person:
Andrew Stickle (speaking on behalf of his family farm, 5271 N. Williamston Rd.,
Williamston) – Supports the Township opting in to medical and recreational
marijuana. His family is interested in starting a grow operation on their
family farm and potentially employing people as well. He also provided
supplemental written materials.
Adam Spina, 401 Winding River Road, Superintendent, Williamston Community
Schools – Supports opting out of marijuana growing in the Township due to
potential impact on Williamston students.
Edward Shand, 1388 Milton Rd., – Supports opting out of recreational marijuana.
He doesn’t support recreational but is ok with medical marijuana, properly
controlled, for the protection of children and some adults.
The following residents submitted comments via e-mail:
Irene Foor-Bridges, 4030 Meridian Rd., Okemos – opposed to having recreational
marijuana facilities in the Township.
Mickey Martin, 1561 Germany Rd., Williamston – supports a decision to opt out
of recreational marijuana in the Township. Can be reconsidered once the State
decides implementation strategy.
Jonathan Brandt, 4725 N. Branch Rd., Williamston – asks the Township leadership
to prevent any marijuana dispensaries in the Township.
Rebecca Scott, 4301 Courtside Dr., Williamston – supports the Township opting
out of recreational marijuana, citing potential safety and addiction issues.
Howard Gregson, 1015 Gulick Rd., Haslett – Does not support the Opt out
ordinance if facilities can be restricted to commercial districts. Could be an
economic benefit to the Township.
John Merrill, 4223 Vanneter Rd., Williamston – Supports the Township not opting
out of marijuana facilities. The Township should honor the vote of the citizens
to allow recreational use.
Public Hearing Closed at 7:20 p.m.
Planning Committee Report
Gerald Eidt, Chair of the Planning Commission, recapped the meeting held
November 28, 2018. The Commission approved the election of the current Chair,
Gerald Eidt, Vice Chair, Rob Stanford, and Secretary, Jocelyn Brown-Timm. A
public hearing is scheduled for January 23, 2019 for Jackson Metal Cleaning.
The Commission reviewed draft language for use of an automatic pool cover in
place of a fence. The Commissioners want more information about the use of
automatic covers and what other communities are doing to address this issue. A
motion was passed to table this issue until the January 23, 2019 meeting.
Discussion will continue regarding Zoning Ordinance language for farm animals
and event centers at the January meeting. Board Trustees asked questions about
solar regulations.

Red Cedar Compensating Cut
Planning Commission Chair Gerald Eidt discussed the reasons for the Red Cedar
Compensating Cut, specifically the requirements about where excavation can take
place for this project. Alan Boyer,LSJ Engineers, gave a presentation about the
Red Cedar Compensating Cut for the Red Cedar (Frandor) Development. Excavators
will place approximately 10% of the excavation, or 16,000 yards into Summit
Cemetery for fill at the rear of the cemetery. DEQ already issued the permit
for this site and it is good for another 18 months. The County Drain office
permits are expected soon. Work will begin this fall, weather permitting.
Ideally, the project would be completed by Spring. Jason Hockstok of
Continental/Ferguson, LLC, and Tom Stover of Burton Holdings expressed
appreciation to the Township for helping to facilitate completion of the
project.
Clerk Steinberg moved the Williamstown Township Board approve the revised site
plan for the Red Cedar River Compensating Cut in Williamstown Township with the
following conditions:
That discussions regarding an easement for the non-motorized trail continue;
That a grading permit is required;
That the project be evaluated for compliance with floodplain regulations;
That a copy of the revised Ingham County Drain Commission soil erosion control
permit be provided;
That a copy of the MDEQ/EGLE permit #WRP 001072 specific to the compensating
cut area be provided.
That the area be planted with native wetland seeds.
Seconded by Treasurer Cutshaw.
Discussion:

(Addressed in the plans)

tree ordinance)

There will not be a loss of farmland.

Waiver of Meeting Pay
At the September 5 special meeting the Board voted to not pay Trustees for the
special meeting. Clerk Steinberg reported that the vote should not have been
taken, for two reasons. First, Boards can’t add action items to a special
meeting agenda unless all board members are present (two were absent). Second,
theBoard cannot, by law, reduce compensation for board members, and the
Township is bound by the salaries set by the compensation commission.

discussion and action.

Dangerous Buildings Ordinance
Clerk Steinberg moved the Williamstown Township Board postpone action on the
Dangerous Building Ordinance until the November Board meeting.
Seconded by Trustee Duffy.
Discussion: 
Gary Bender, Township Attorney, addressed several concerns stated during public
comment:
The owner of record gets notified by certified/return receipt; it is in the
ordinance.
The Hearing Officer’s determination can be challenged.
The definitions of the Dangerous Buildings tracks with State Statute.
The Blight Ordinance is not a remedy, as it doesn’t talk about buildings, only
land, cars, trash, etc.
The Dangerous Building Ordinance is the appropriate remedy for a dangerous
building.
The ordinance is used as a method to force the property owner to deal with the
issues related to their property.
It helps protect the health, safety and welfare of the community.
There are three methods of appeal. If the Township does not set up a Dangerous
Building Board of Appeals, then it goes to the Township Board for appeal.
Old barns may be covered under the right to farm act; therefore, it would have
to be researched under the GAAMPS laws.
Trustee Eyster suggested that in Section 9 of the proposed Ordinance the
Township should add that the Board may not consist of members of the Board of
Trustees or employees of the Township.
Motion passed.
Cyber Insurance
Trustee Williams moved that the Williamstown Township Board purchase cyber
liability insurance as an add-on to the Township’s general insurance policy, at
a cost of $853.00 for the current fiscal year.
Seconded by Treasurer Cutshaw.
Discussion: There was discussion about whether or not the Township needs this
coverage considering that it has back-ups, etc. Township information sources
have indicated a rise in data hacks and ransomware attacks on public entities.
A previous Township breach was discussed and the implications, including legal
and costs, should resident or employee confidential data be breached.
Roll Call Vote:
Ayes: Trustee Williams, Supervisor Bloomquist, Trustee Eyster, Clerk Steinberg,
Treasurer Cutshaw.
Nays: Trustees Duffy and Kane.
Motion Passed.
Discussion
Lighting Policy:
Trustee Eyster and Treasurer Cutshaw brought forward their recommendations for
handling requests for Township-paid streetlights. They suggested development of
special assessment districts for lighting. In lieu of street lighting, a
government entity could consider reflective additions to signage, such as
reflective tape. DTE indicated it would cost approximately $2100 to install a
streetlight. The proposed policy will be brought back to the Board for a vote
at the November meeting.
Road Millage:
There will be a public forum on Thursday, October 17 at 7:00 p.m. to gather
input from residents on a potential road millage. The recently commissioned
road report is on the Township website for people to read prior to the forum.
The Township Board is considering putting a millage proposal on the ballot in
March 2020. The Board encourages residents to get the word out to other
residents. There is also an article in the Williamston Enterprise advertising
the forum. Treasurer Cutshaw addressed what has happened with money earmarked
for road repairs in the past and how that money is accounted for now.
Basically, all monies earmarked for the roads are only spent on roads. The
County has not always been able to fulfill their part of the contract. Any
monies not spent in a given year are rolled over to the next year to be
utilized. If a road millage is passed, the law states that the money raised can
only be used for road expenditures.
Well and Septic Revisions to Code:
Currently the well and septic code is a “point of sale” system where the
wastewater systems are checked for conformance with requirements. Michigan is
the only state that doesn’t have a statewide system for wastewater. Ingham
County is considering doing away with the point of sale system and going
instead with a ten-year inspection schedule. The Ingham County Environmental
Health Department will ultimately be presenting the proposed revisions to the
county commissioners for adoption. The Township would like to have a public
meeting for the residents before that time so that our resident’s comments and
concerns can be included in the deliberations.
Reports – Departments and Committees

2 mils for 8 years to purchase equipment.
River Grant: Three Saturdays are planned for river log jam clearing, this
Saturday, October 19 and 26. The City of Williamston is submitting a grant for
a launch site and parking in downtown Williamston. Williamstown Township is
checking into a possible launch site at the park at Meridian Road.
Township Hall: The Township is currently getting estimates for the replacement
of the back doors and air wall curtains in the Township Hall.
Cemetery: We have received some complaints regarding the cemetery. Supervisor
Bloomquist stated that the Township has adopted procedures in response to
clarify expectations and improve communication. The Township encourages
residents to contact the Township in a timely manner with any concerns.

to the public in light of the Covid-19 pandemic. After receiving a recent email

temporarily Suspended as well.

Elections:
Clerk Cleveland reported that Williamstown Township currently has 4,624
registered voters, up from previous years. For the November 3rd election the
Township had 1,200 in person voters, 2,628 absentee voters, for a total of
3,828. Voter turnout in the Township was about 82%. The Absent Voter Counting
Board (AVCB) completed their tasks at about 5:00 a.m., November 4th. The
Clerk’s office is still working on reports and election wrap-up. At this point,
it looks like everything went well. The Deputy Treasurer, Kim VanErp, and the
Supervisor’s Assistant, Sharon Anway, were extremely helpful with election
tasks in the office leading up to Election Day.
River Clean Up:
The team is still working on the small log jams. Work is expected to be
completed around the end of November, weather permitting.
Covid 19 - Office:
Given the uptick in Covid-19 numbers, Township employees will start working
from home whenever possible, starting next week. Office hours will be limited,
but residents needing to come in person can make an appointment. For residents
needing to pay their taxes, if paying by cash, we prefer they go to Independent
Bank to pay, but cash will still be accepted at the Township. Staff will be
staggering schedules and forwarding phone calls. The logistics are still being
worked out, but there will be a reduction of Wednesday hours to close at 4:00
p.m. instead of 7:00 p.m.

meeting.

December 2, 2020
Williamstown Township
Board of Trustees Special Meeting Minutes
December 2, 2020
Call to Order
The Williamstown Township Board of Trustees convened a virtual meeting at 6:00
p.m. on December 2, 2020 via Zoom (meeting ID 861 7143 5739) due to the COVID-
19 virus. All Board members present were calling into the meeting from
Williamstown Township, Ingham County, in Michigan. Supervisor Bloomquist called
the meeting to order and reviewed the Agenda. Supervisor Bloomquist led the
Pledge of Allegiance.
Roll Call
Present: Supervisor Bloomquist, Clerk Cleveland, Treasurer Cutshaw, Trustee
Creagh, Trustee Steinberg, and Trustee Eyster.
Absent: Trustee Duffy
Public Comment for agenda and non-agenda items
Opened at 6:02 pm
None
Closed at 6:03 pm
Oath
All Board Members present took the Oath of Office for the new four year term.
Strategic Planning Review
Educational Opportunities:
Supervisor Bloomquist discussed educational opportunities for Board of Trustees
members as well as Planning Commission and Board of Review members. The
Michigan Townships Association (MTA) has a New Officials Training taking place
for Board of Trustees members in December and January. All are encouraged to
attend to learn about up to date laws and best practices related to Township
governing. The Township office will order current the up to date version of the
Authorities and Responsibilities of Michigan Townships from MTA for each Board
member.
Supervisor Bloomquist queried the Board about areas of interest with regard to
special topics Board members would like to learn more about. Zoning was
mentioned as one possibility.
New Trustee, Keith Creagh, asked for a one on one meeting with Township
officers in order to understand better their roles in governing the Township.
Board members discussed doing a tour of the Township’s properties and physical
assets, once it is safe to do so, in order to gain understanding on what the
Township owns and maintains.
The Board discussed developing an “ethics” resolution for outlining ethical
expectations for the Williamstown Township Board. Other Township have done this
and found it to be helpful guidance for their Board members.
The Board also discussed the general role of Board members and the importance
of working together as a Board.
Website, Branding and Social Media:
Supervisor Bloomquist informed the Board the staff has been discussing the
Township’s branding (logo, etc.) and began the process of identifying ways that
the website could be improved as well as other ways the Township (staff and
Board) could improve communication with its residents. A committee is being
created to study these issues and make recommendations to the Board.
Parks:
Supervisor Bloomquist provided background on the Township park and the update
of the Parks and Recreation Master Plan, which is currently before the Board
for adoption. Board members had previously been asked for comments on the
updated plan. The Board discussed various aspects of the park upkeep including
doing a controlled burn, maintaining the park drive, and grant opportunities.
Considerations for the future could include trail development/expansion, river
respite along the trail, educational opportunities at the park, expansion of
active uses, and potential designation of Branch School as a state historic
site.
Resident Educational/Engagement Opportunities:
As part of a Community Block Grant the Township was awarded educational
opportunities were developed for residents with topics that included
alternative energy solutions, composting, rain gardens, etc. Some programs have
been held including the Branch School open house, the Art Tour, the Photo
Contest, and more, however many have been postponed until the Covid virus is
under control. Potential future opportunities include promoting Township
businesses, community art projects, and more programs of interest to residents.
Cemetery:
The Township recently expanded the cemetery for natural burials and it is in
the process of landscape design. Drives are also slated to be resurfaced/
repaired in 2021. Other items under consideration is the re-creation of the
metal arch that once was at the main entrance, expansion of the barn for an
office, and restoring damaged headstones.
Policies:
The updating of the employee manual was started but needs to be completed so
procedures can be put in place to ensure consistent implementation and fairness
to employees, particularly in the areas of pay and duties. Other policies will
be developed regarding meetings and (possibly)social media for the Board to
review. The Township will also be review policies regarding road funding and
maintenance, as well as the Neighborhood Road Policy.
Budget Review
The Board began its review of the 2021-2022 budget. Supervisor Bloomquist
explained the current understanding of what the Township’s revenue and expenses
might be in the upcoming year. Board members will be discussing this at each
regular Board meeting. A public hearing will be held early next year, followed
by the final adoption of the budget. Board members and residents are encouraged
to reach out to Supervisor Bloomquist with any questions or concerns related to
the budget.
Chromebooks:
Among items under consideration is Chromebooks for Board members use that would
be loaded with Township policies, ordinances, meeting packets, etc. for easy
access.
Roads: The Township is currently working with Mannik Smith to make
recommendations on road maintenance for 2021. Review of road funding,
maintenance, and neighborhood road policy will be taking place soon. The
Township also has the ability to adopt an ordinance that would limit truck
routes on certain roads, which will also be discussed.
Sustainability:
Under discussion is the creation of an Environmental Committee which could
review ordinances for the protection of the environment and promotion of
sustainability to help the Township lessen its carbon footprint. The committee
could also help provide education on environmental issues to Township
residents. This will be discussed further at the January Board of Trustees
meeting on January 13, 2021.
Public comment for agenda and non-agenda items
Opened at 7:50 pm
None
Closed at 7:51 pm
Adjournment and Review
Trustee Steinberg moved to adjourn the meeting.
Seconded by Treasurer Cutshaw.
Meeting adjourned at 7:54 pm.
 
Minutes approved by:

Meridian Police Update – Chief Plaga
Chief Ken Plaga, Meridian Township Police Department (MTPD) gave the police
report. The annual police report will be provided to Williamstown Township next
month. Increased calls for service and increase in domestic and mental health
calls attributed to Covid-19. Billable hours are down and injury accidents are
up slightly. Meridian Police are working with Community Mental Health on a
pilot program utilizing technology in the field to interface with counselors
for crisis help. Two new officers have been added with two more being added
soon. Two new radar signs have been purchased and they can be requested
electronically on webpage or by email for deployment at problem areas.
Discussion: Chief Plaga was asked about concerns with accidents at the
Williamston Rd./Sherwood Rd. and Zimmer Rd./Sherwood Rd. intersections.
Supervisor Bloomquist has already reached out to the Ingham Country Road
Commission regarding Zimmer Rd/Sherwood Rd and will follow up; Chief Plaga will
also reach out to them.

Williamstown Township
Board of Trustees Meeting Minutes
Public Hearing for Red Cedar Manor Special Assessment District
Call to Order
The Williamstown Township Board of Trustees convened a virtual meeting at 6:00
p.m. on January 14, 2021 via Zoom (meeting ID 872 8284 7983) due to the COVID-
19 virus. Supervisor Bloomquist called the meeting to order, reviewed the
agenda, and stated the reason for the meeting/public hearing. Supervisor
Bloomquist led the Pledge of Allegiance.
Roll Call
Present: Treasurer Cutshaw, Trustee Creagh, Trustee Duffy, Trustee Steinberg,
Supervisor Bloomquist, Trustee Eyster, and Clerk Cleveland. All Board members
called in from Williamstown Township except Trustee Eyster who called in to the
meeting from Northport, Florida.
Public Comment for agenda and non-agenda items
Opened at 6:05 pm
None
Closed at 6:06 pm
Supervisor Bloomquist outlined the proposed road improvement plan for the Red
Cedar Manor Special Assessment District (SAD) and shared the improvement map on
the screen.
Public Hearing
Opened at 6:08 p.m.
The following residents asked questions or made statements regarding the
Special Assessment District:
Jim Brinker: Mr. Brinker wanted to know the amount each property would need to
pay for the SAD. Supervisor Bloomquist shared the breakdown on the screen and
explained that it is approximate until the work is completed.
Melissa Wood: Ms. Wood requested a list of petitioners and stated that she
objects to the project.
Terry Smith: Mr. Smith requested the approximate timeline for the project and
asked if it would be completed in 2021. Supervisor Bloomquist explained next
steps and approximate start dates, indicating that it would likely be completed
in 2021. He also asked for an approximate interest rate.
Debra Borgman: Ms. Borgman asked about the interest rate and when we will know
what the rate will be. Supervisor Bloomquist explained that the Township will
not know for certain what the interest rate would be until all the paperwork is
completed and it is accepted. However, when the Township looked at the millage
rate for the recent road millage proposal the rate was three percent.
Gary Wright: Mr. Wright asked about how the payments are made by the residents
affected. Treasurer Cutshaw explained that it would appear as a Special
Assessment on the Winter tax bill that is mailed in December each year. Once
the Special Assessment is paid off, it would no longer be listed on the tax
bill.
Public Hearing closed at 6:27 p.m.
Public Comment for Non-Agenda Items
Opened at 6:28 p.m.
Melissa Wood: Asked about other roads in the Township that would be repaired
this year.
John McLaughlin: Mr. McLaughlin explained that the roads need to be fixed and
the residents need to pay for them. He stated the Township set up a policy to
allow for the SAD to happen so the subdivision roads could be repaired.
Sharon Day: Ms. Day offered appreciation to the Township Board for the work on
behalf of the residents of the Township.
Closed at 6:32 p.m.
Supervisor Bloomquist thanked the residents for their participation and
statements in both the Public Hearing and Public Comment.
Adjournment
Trustee Duffy moved to adjourn the meeting.
Seconded by Treasurer Cutshaw
Meeting adjourned at 6:33 p.m.

recommendations which includes pay increases for the Supervisor, Clerk, and
Treasurer, from $29,700 to $31,000 annually. The recommendation is for a single
increase for the period of April 1, 2021 through March 30, 2023.
They also recommended pay increases for the Trustees from $5328 to $5400
annually, plus the existing $65 monthly stipend for any Trustee who attends
more than two authorized meetings in a month. A review of the past two year’s
data by the Commission showed minimal use of the meeting stipend. Mr. Conroy
shared that the Compensation Commission felt the slight increases are well-
justified based on increased cost of living and the difficulty of continuing to
work and keep the Township going through the pandemic.
No residents asked questions or made statements during the Public Hearing.
Trustee Creagh moved to close the public hearing.
Seconded by Trustee Eyster.
Public Hearing closed at 7:23 p.m.

Opened at 7:24 p.m.
None.

Meridian Police Update – Chief Plaga
Chief Ken Plaga, Meridian Township Police Department (MTPD) gave the police
update. Chief Plaga reported that over the past 5 years there were 14 accidents
at the Sherwood Road and Zimmer Road intersection, and 9 accidents at the
Sherwood Road and Williamston Road intersection. Roughly half of those
accidents were single car. A traffic study will be conducted at those
intersections to determine if they warrant making them 4 way stops. Chief Plaga
reported that overall billable hours are down due to Covid-19 and a majority of
billed hours were the two large structure fires in the last quarter. Drunk
driving arrests are increasing in the area in general, but not specifically in
the Township. Four new officers are being hired. Assistant Chief Brad Bach is
retiring on May 14 and they are looking to promote from within for his
replacement.
Planning Commission Update – Chair Eidt
Chair Eidt reported that the commission was pleased to welcome Trustee Creagh
as Township Board representative. Two public hearings were held March 24th and
proposed ordinances have been forwarded to the Board for action - Cluster
Zoning Amendment for Article 25/Planned Development and Event Barns Amendment
for Article 8/Site Development Standards for Specific Uses. Supervisor
Bloomquist will put the proposed Amendments on the Township website for the
public’s review. The commission reviewed the site plan for Ark LLC/Odd Fellows
Contracting and approved the meeting schedule for 2021/2022. The commission
received the initial draft of farm animals on non-farm parcels proposed
amendment and formed a sub-committee for further review. The Planning
Commission will continue review at the May meeting.

goes on for an extended amount of time. A previous NIESA Board member said that
it was illegal to use public funds to feed public employees. Other local
departments, such as Mason and Leslie, were able to feed their people with no
problem during the multi-department fire call. Chief Yanz will research to see

currently for new CPR equipment. Trustee Duffy will update the board on the
April NIESA meeting at the May board meeting.

the Williamston put-in down to the MDOT park, only one portage was necessary.
There is a new log jam forming west of the Township park. He reported that the
prescribed burn company did a great job of controlling the fire and burning
just what was intended. Prescribed burn kills off invasive species that are
more susceptible to fire. Supervisor Bloomquist reported she could not find
trees for an Arbor Day project but could perhaps try an Adopt a Tree project.
Supervisor Bloomquist had a meeting with Tri-County and Ingham County Parks
regarding signage on the river and their wish to include all municipalities on
signage design and placement.
Roads: Trustee Eyster advised that there are three main roads that were not

swampy and partly gravel. The road most prevalent with houses is Epley Road.
Supervisor Bloomquist advised that Red Cedar Manor engineering is nearly done
and RFPs should be going out soon. Meadowdale is going to move forward with
letter of intent to determine if the residents will move forward with work on
Meadowdale Dr. Subdivision roads have been getting worse as time goes on.

CADL Yearly Update – Julie Chrisinske
Capitol Area District Library (CADL) Head Librarian, Julie Chrisinske, gave an
update on the library. During the Covid-19 pandemic numerous new services and
protocols were developed such as door side service, a computer appointment
system, and Grab and Go bags of books and movies. Demand for online services
increased, and additional online content and programs were created. She
reported that they were also able to help students by providing Internet
hotspots to local schools. They are hoping to open by appointment on June 1,
2021.
ACTION ITEMS
Event Barns Zoning Ordinance Amendments
Trustee Steinberg moved the Williamstown Township Board postpone action on the
proposed Zoning Ordinance amendments regarding Event Barns to the June 9th,
2021 meeting.
Seconded by Trustee Duffy.
Discussion: Supervisor Bloomquist reported that information regarding the
Ordinance was posted on the website and comments were received. Items discussed
were possibility of an assessment, density of event barns within an area, hours
of operation and capacity, and effect on the roads with the increased traffic.
Supervisor Bloomquist stated, according to the way the proposed ordinance is
written, there are approximately 135 properties that would be eligible to have
an event barn. McKenna brings in information from all over the state and that
is taken into consideration when writing the ordinances. Board members would
like feedback from municipalities with event barns. Multiple Board members
stated that balancing the rights of property owners to have the event barn and
the rights of neighbors is an important to maintain.
Prior to the June 9 meeting Board members will reach out to other
municipalities with a list of questions to ask them. The Planning Assistant
will develop a list of questions and disburse it to the Board members.
Questions would include number of events allowed, acreage requirements,
operation hours, location, setback requirements, and any issues they have had.
Motion Passed.
Cluster Zoning Ordinance Amendments
Trustee Creagh moved the Williamstown Township Board postpone action on the
proposed Zoning Ordinance amendments regarding Cluster Housing to the June 9th,
2021 meeting.
Seconded by Clerk Cleveland.
Discussion: The matter of the term “affordable” being a HUD term was discussed
and it was explained that this was unintentional. The term “affordable” could
be removed from the ordinance and the intent would still remain. Board members
requested to have the revisions out prior to the June 9 th meeting to give time
for resident questions or comments.
Motion Passed.
Newsletter
Clerk Cleveland moved the Williamstown Township Board approve expending up to
$2000 for the cost of design, printing, postage and mailing a Township
Newsletter with Foresight Group.
Seconded by Trustee Steinberg.
Discussion: Supervisor Bloomquist explained that the Township last sent out a
newsletter in 2019 with the summer tax bills. This year the idea is to have a
newsletter designed and mailed out prior to the summer tax bills because of the
change to the Spring Cleanup, which would provide important information about
the Township. It would include information on the common questions asked by
residents such as building permit requirements, fence regulations, burning
regulations, and reminder of services offered by the Township. This would be
something for the residents to keep and refer to as needed.

has had eight fire fighter candidates pass the hands-on exam and are waiting on
their written exams. Two other candidates have completed both and are now full-
fledged fire fighters.
