people going down the river in kayaks and canoes since the cleanup project was
completed. There is a new obstruction in the river and cleanup is being worked
on before it gets larger. A plan is being developed for the house and park, and
sources of revenue for the house and the park are being investigated.
Roads:  Supervisor Bloomquist stated that two additional subdivisions have
asked for estimates on fixing roads utilizing the Special Assessment District/
Neighborhood Road Policy. Meetings are set with the two neighborhoods and if
they decide they want to move forward, the neighborhood would then do petitions
for a Special Assessment District. Supervisor Bloomquist advised that Red Cedar
Manor is waiting for completed RFPs to move forward with their road work.
Elections: Clerk Cleveland reported that Okemos Schools had two millage
proposals for the May election, and both passed overwhelmingly. Okemos Schools
will reimburse the Township for the cost of the election. The Township had 24%
voter turnout with 88% of ballots being absentee ballots. The election has been
certified and the Township has not been chosen to be audited.

The Williamstown Township Board of Trustees convened a virtual meeting at 7:02

virus. Supervisor Bloomquist called the meeting to order, reviewed the agenda,

Present: Supervisor Bloomquist, Trustee Eyster, Clerk Cleveland, Treasurer

Public Comment for agenda and non-agenda items
Opened at 7:04 PM
David Kenney, 1553 Epley Rd.: He previously emailed Jim Howard with questions
and concerns about event barns. He wants anybody that stands to gain from event
barns to abstain from voting.
Jennifer Tubbs, 5915 Shoeman Rd.: She has concerns about noise, from her
experience and indicated that farmers aren’t doing event barns, that people are
buying properties with barns to start event barn businesses. She suggested
limiting event barns to 5 events per year. From personal experience she knows
how disruptive event barns are, including making roads are more dangerous from
drinking & driving. If the Board moves forward, proximity to density is more
important than distance.
Sam Zuke, 6116 Shoeman Rd.: Mr. Zuke has DJ’d more than 1000 events. He said
police were usually called because of noise and it is not reasonable to expect
a one-time customer to care about the noise or anything else. From May –
October expect events every Thursday through Sunday.
Julie Byelich, 850 Gulick Rd.: Her acreage backs up to huge property that could
be an event barn. She has small children whose rooms face the farm and is
concerned about noise, etc. After hearing others who live next to event barns
talk about their property being trashed, she can’t imagine dealing with that
herself.
Jeff Sweet, 5915 Shoeman Rd.: Mr. Sweet is a teacher. He enjoys time with his
kids and family and the peaceful use of his property including bonfires and
outdoor movies. He has concerns about event barns include DJ noise and 300
people leaving at night.
Jordan Byelich, 850 Gulick Rd.: He sent an email to Jim Howard. Concerns about
the event barn include: challenges with traffic, noise, liability when people
wander onto his property, how it will be regulated and that the Township office
would be closed during events.
Closed at 7:23 pm.

Planning Commission Annual Report
Presented by Rob Stanford, Vice Chairman of the Planning Commission
Vice Chair Stanford stated he appreciates comments about Event Barns and said
it would be helpful to have these comments at Planning Commission during the
planning stage. The Planning Commission spent 18 months working on the Event
Barn ordinance and they did not get any comments from residents about Event
Barns. They reached out to a number of event barn owners, people that had used
them and neighbors of event barns.
The May 26th Planning Commission meeting included a public hearing for site
plan review and special use permit for Barkham Creek Farms on E. Haslett Rd.
According to Planning Consultant, Chris Doozan, from Mckenna, the site plan met
the ordinance requirements. The Planning Commission recommended to wave the
paving of the parking lot, lighting requirements and dust control. The
applicant submitted a revised landscape plan for screening from the neighboring
property.
The Planning Commission continued discussion of farm animals on non-farm
parcels. Vice Chair Stanford invited residents to attend upcoming Planning
Commission meetings which are announced on the Township website.

DISCUSSION ITEMS
Event Barns- Based on feedback from residents, each member of the Board was
charged with contacting Townships with event barns to give the board a sample
of any issues that Townships have experienced and what their ordinance language
includes. Items of concern and/or interest:
Location only allowed on state highway
Limited to existing barns
More limited hours
Limited number of events per year to 6-12
Lowered maximum attendance
No amplified music
Not permitting event barns
Setting a density standard for neighbors
Daytime only
Trash complaints
Limited special use permit would require renewal
Increase in traffic on local roads
No complaints in Rives Twp. (only one event barn has been permitted)
Language to insure it is a secondary use to farming
Limiting alcohol use
Monitoring activity became an issue due to complaints
Limit of zoning districts as well as acreage
It was suggested to bring back the issues to the Board at the July meeting to
discuss next steps by the Board.
Ethics Policy-Revised draft was submitted to the Board based on comments
received.
Discussion:

in the office on a regular schedule.

design a new website. Bids have been requested for a new auditor. NIESA has

wages. NIESA is intending to request funding from the participating
municipalities as well. Concern was expressed over the continued cost of
additional pay in the future for staff. Question about the practice of billing
Township residents when insurance does not cover the full cost, as other

Parks: Trustee Steinberg updated the Board regarding the priorities of the

Police Update - Chief Plaga
Chief Plaga reported that the department conducted traffic stops at the west
end of Sherwood Road near Meridian to try to curb speeding in that area. A
speed study and traffic survey will be conducted at the Zimmer Road/Sherwood
Road intersection to determine what steps might be taken to reduce accidents.
Extra hours are down for this year to date. Due to summer activity those hours
may go up. Once the department is fully staffed, they plan to participate in
Ingham County's Violent Crime Initiative. Chief Plaga reported that
diversity of officers is a priority and while the national average for female
officers is 12.5%, they are currently at 25%. They are once again holding the
Citizens Academy and encourage residents to participate and learn more about
how their department operates.

DISCUSSION ITEMS
Event Barns - Supervisor Bloomquist expressed appreciation for the residents
who have come forward to state their views on this subject. Based on the
interest shown, she suggested a committee be formed with two Board members and
two Planning Commission members to look at everything that has been gathered
and discussed to this point and solicit more input from the community. The
Board members will be Trustees Cutshaw
and Creagh, and the Planning Commission members are yet to be determined. The committee will provide recommendations
to be provided to the Planning Commission to hold a public hearing and
gather further input from the community before final recommendations are made to the
Board.
Joint meeting with City- Supervisor Bloomquist explained that it was Township's
turn to host the meeting last year but since that meeting was cancelled due to
Covid-19 the Township will be host this year. August 18
th or 25th is the proposed date for the meeting.
Reports - Departments and Committees
NIESA: There have been two NIESA meetings since the last board meeting and in
his absence, Trustee Duffy provided a summary via email. Both meetings centered
around wage increases for EMTs and Paramedics to bring them more in line with
other local municipalities. Director Yanz and Deputy Chief Pfiester
expressed concerns that if this action wasn't taken soon, not only will they
lose more staff, but they won't be able to
recruit new trainees to replace the lost staff members. The wage
increases were unanimously approved.

DISCUSSION ITEMS
Fire Insurance Withholding - Supervisor Bloomquist explained that whenever
there is a fire, and the loss is more than 49%, the township can receive escrow
funds from the impacted homeowner’s insurance to ensure that the building loss
is rebuilt or removed. Supervisor Bloomquist reached out to the township
insurance representative, Jason Orton, regarding the escrow of funds through
this program. By adopting the resolution, the Township would be added to the
state list of participating communities. Insurance companies access these lists
after a fire to determine if a portion of the insurance funds needs to be sent
to the township. It was noted that homeowners would have access to these escrow
funds to assist with rebuilding, etc. Most municipalities in Michigan
participate in the Fire Insurance Withholding. This applies to any property –
commercial/residential. The next step for the Township Board would be to
complete the enrollment process. The Board is in consensus to move forward and
take action on the resolution.
Joint Meeting with City - This meeting will take place on Wednesday, August 18,
2021 @ 7:00PM at the Williamstown Township Hall. In the past it has been a
large round table discussion that included participation from important
community stakeholders including: the City Manager, Williamston Schools, CADL,
Senior Center, and City Council representatives. Possible topics to address
could include the joint river clean-up, Summit Cemetery, ARPA Funds, planning
commission, and subdivision projects. A reminder will be sent to all parties.
The public is invited. Information has been provided on the website and it will
be posted at the Township office.
DNR Forestry Program Grant – This was shared with the Township Parks and
Environmental Committee. The Environmental Committee was in favor of moving
forward. The goal would be to have a forestry area in the Grand River township
park. It would serve both an aesthetic and educational purpose. It could be a
forestry demonstration that our residents could both learn from and consider in
light of climate change. It would be beneficial to bring some membership of the
two committees together to plan.The Board is in consensus on moving forward
with the grant process and will bring it back to the September Board meeting.

NIESA: No report from Trustee Duffy.
Parks: Trustee Steinberg shared the parks membership list is going to be
expanded. They are looking to align with Rotary to clean the minor log jams out
of the river. With flowers currently in full bloom, residents are encouraged to
visit.
Elections: Clerk Cleveland shared that Perry has an upcoming mileage in
November. Opting out is still under determination because there are only 245
residents in that school district within the Township. It’s important to note
that Williamston Township is a part of 7 different school districts. We may be
able to amend our agreement with Shiawassee County to opt out for this election
and consider what options would be available for the Perry voters.
Environmental Committee: Trustee Eyster shared that this committee established
a vision and mission statement. The committee wants to look at future
demonstration and lecture events to inform Township residents around
environmental issues, awareness, and considerations for informed decision-
making. Ideas are currently being generated and must tie into the two developed
statements that center around air, land, and water. Once the topics are
determined, event planning would begin. The timeline would encompass the next
couple of years.
Logo Design: Clerk Cleveland and Supervisor Bloomquist met with Lynn Brown of
Mid-Michigan Consulting to begin the Township’s Logo work. The meeting gave her
a sense of who we are as a township. Ms. Brown is working on a variety of
concepts/templates and will be bringing these ideas/draft designs back to
Supervisor Bloomquist, Clerk Cleveland, and the rest of the Board, for feedback
and consideration in a couple weeks. The logo could be utilized in a variety of
ways and on multiple items – ex. signage, letterhead, apparel, possibly even a
flag, as this was wish by past Board members.
Greenhouse Gas Committee Audit: Supervisor Bloomquist noted the EPA has a

This may be something to consider for the township, as it would provide a

planning. It’s possible that an outside source (e.g., university intern) could
also be considered or utilized to complete the audit.
Roads: The Red Cedar Manor project is on hold until 2022 due to drainage work

DISCUSSION ITEMS
Social Media Policy Draft: Clerk Cleveland has been meeting with the Resident
Engagement Committee regarding the development and establishment of a township
social media page (ex. Facebook) for residents to learn about township issues,
provide event visibility, or special notices. The consensus of the committee
was to move forward with this initiative without allowing comments on Township
posts. If approved, this policy would not only provide an alternate way to
communicate with residents, but also provide an additional point of connection
beyond current communication methods (ex. newsletters, the website, or the
Williamston Enterprise). The initial implementation and planning of the
Township Facebook page would include protocols for permissions to post and
intentional planning on how events/information would be posted. During board
discussion, perspective was shared on the time commitment required of township
staff to maintain a Facebook page. Clarification was sought regarding a
Facebook membership group vs. a page. It was confirmed that it would be a
Facebook page. It was suggested that the Board might consider the option of
having residents’ comment on posts, with a disclaimer stating that pages/posts
are not actively monitored. Concern was expressed that not responding or
acknowledging comments may lead to negative perceptions by the community that
the Board is unresponsive. It was shared that the Township could have email and
phone contact information shared on each post as an avenue for residents to
provide feedback or have questions answered. Board members are encouraged to
further review the draft and have comments to Clerk Cleveland by September 30,
2021 so that revisions may be considered before the October Board Meeting.

Audit Review
Brenda Seelman, from Clark Schaefer Hackett CPAs and Advisors, presented a
review of the Williamstown Township Audit issued for year ending March 31,
2021. The Township received the highest rating the auditors can award. Ms.
Seelman provided highlights of the report with regards to the Township’s
current revenue and expenditures, as well as the capital assets and general
fund balance. Additionally, she provided a summary of the Township’s net
position, which has seen an overall increase. Auditor recommendations were
reviewed and implemented upon completion of the report in September.
Police Report
Lieutenant Bart Crane from Meridian Township Police presented police activity
in the Township. Lt. Crane’s report highlighted the billable hours for the
township are in line with past hour and call patterns. Most calls were related
to automobile accidents and welfare checks. There has been a slight increase in
calls regarding gun shots being fired, however this is typical with the onset
of firearm hunting season in November. Lt. Crane shared details about their
Citizens’ Academy being held at the Meridian Township Police Department in
Okemos. He reported one Williamstown Township resident is currently attending.
He reminded residents that on October 30, 2021 the police department will be
hosting a Halloween Open House from 10:00am -1:00pm. All township residents are
invited to attend; pre-registration is required.
Interest was shared from the Board regarding asking the resident who is
participating in the Citizens’ Academy to share their learning and experiences
at an upcoming meeting. Inquiry was made regarding the slight increase in
arrests for the month of September. Lt. Crane cited that the arrests were
related to traffic stops and outstanding warrants.
The Board praised the work of the department and their resident welfare checks.
Lt. Crane provided additional details on the role of a police officer during
mental health calls and noted that Crisis Intervention and Mental Health
Training have been at the forefront of law enforcement education. Police
officers are often the first line of support. Meridian Township Police works in
partnership with Community Mental Heath (CMH) on all calls. Officers travel
with an iPad that allows police and/or the resident with direct contact with a
CMH counselor should support or immediate services be needed.
Lt. Crane also shared information about a Senior Citizens Program where elderly
residents can sign up with the police and share contact information for check-
ins. This service can occur a variety of ways from the resident receiving a
call from police, or the resident calling the police or cooperating partners.
If a senior citizen doesn’t respond, the officer will then provide an in-person
check.
Planning Commission
PC Chair, Jerry Eidt, provided an overview of the Commission’s most recent
meeting on September 22, 2021. He shared a summary of the Public Hearing
regarding the draft language for proposed text amendments to Section 8.02 of
the Zoning Ordinance to allow certain farm animals on non-farm parcels. The
Commission discussed and questioned aspects of the draft, as well as considered
feedback from public comment. A Public Hearing date was set for Site Plan
Review and Special Use Permit for Williamston Storage Center. The Commission
also addressed fence heights and lot coverage in non-residential districts, as
well as a review of the current Township Ethics Policy and collection of
Commissioner signatures. The Planning Commission appointed a committee to
nominate officers for upcoming the year. Chairman Eidt announced the
resignation of Commissioner Rex LaMore, and voiced his appreciation of Mr.
LaMore’s time and expertise over the years.
The Board asked for an update on Event Barn progress. Treasurer Cutshaw shared
that there have been two meetings of the Planning Commission subcommittee and
this is proving to be a complex issue. They have had two speakers address their
group who are well-versed in these types of venues. Legal and law enforcement
perspectives and considerations have been provided thus far.

Logo Review – Graphic Designer Lynne Brown continued to work with Supervisor

first and second choices. The top two logos will be put into action on sample

“Serving Our Neighbors.”
Social Media Policy Revised Draft – The Board expressed their approval for the
updated draft. Minor suggestions and edits will be made. A final draft will be
brought back to the Board in November for vote and adoption.
Roads – This committee met and drove the local roads and a determination was
made that Epley Road is in extremely poor shape and is in need of improvement.
Supervisor Bloomquist sought consensus from the Board for Mannik and Smith to
ascertain what needs to be done on Epley. She reminded the Board that bid
packets are forming now to initiate the process for 2022. In addition to Epley,
the township is working on determinations for Red Cedar Manor, Meadowdale, and
the cemetery drives. The committee hopes to have a final recommendation to the
board in November.
Medical Marihuana Regulations – Supervisor Bloomquist shared that with recent
court cases, townships are able to regulate Caregivers. Caregiver facilities
can turn into grow facilities which are not allowed in the Township. Lt. Crane
from Meridian Township Police shared that it is a multifaceted and lucrative
issue that communities are facing. The Board is in agreement to move this issue
to the Planning Commission for further review and processing.
Budget Workshop October 20th – Supervisor Bloomquist shared that the budgeting
process for the next fiscal year will be starting on October 20th. While no
binding decisions will be made at the meeting, the Board will discuss ARPA
funds, special projects, strategic planning, and developing a capital
improvement plan for the next 3-5 years.

perspectives in Williamstown Township. At the committee’s next meeting Fire

public safety perspective. The Committee would also like to hear from our
Township Building Inspector, Tim O’Neil, as well as seek insights from an

DISCUSSION ITEMS
Permanent Recycling – Reclaimed by Design has reached out to the Township
regarding the possibility of moving forward with the earlier (2015) plans to
provide permanent recycling service. If agreed upon, this plan would replace
the current contract with Granger. The Township would be responsible for the
site improvements in order to implement this plan. ARPA funds could be used/
considered, as this project is an expansion of a service. The Board expressed
interest in moving forward and suggested that a cost analysis would be
beneficial. Supervisor will bring some data and financials to the next Board
meeting.
Roads/Restricted Road Use – Residents have raised concern over the use of our
local roads as short cuts for non-local traffic. Commercial truck routes could
be designated and marked/posted accordingly utilizing county primary roads.
This would lessen the impact of commercial trucks on our local roads and
increase safety for pedestrian bikers/walkers. Enforcement questions were
shared. Supervisor Bloomquist will bring back language and a process for moving
forward.
Budget – Changes to the budget have been made based on the Oct. 20th Board
Workshop. Payroll and department recommendations will be made next month. It
was confirmed that ARPA funds have been deposited in the Township’s bank
account. Community input will be sought on plans for these funds within the
guidelines set forth by the Federal Government.
Police Services – Our contract with Meridian Township Police (MTP) expires at
the end of 2021. MTP wants to continue to provide service to the township,
however the current contract may need to be amended due to reduced staffing of
officers. The Board will need to determine considerations for reductions in
service. As/when officers are added, the patrol hours may be reinstated at an
hourly rate. The Board would like to consider the cost estimates for different
hourly patrol plans, as well as Chief Plaga’s perspective on the most impactful
safety services provided MTP.
Reports – Departments and Committees
NIESA: Treasurer Cutshaw attended the October Meeting. The NIESA Budget was
reviewed, as well as their efforts to capture their DDA funds from Webberville.
Hourly wages and staffing shortages were discussed. A project under
consideration is facility remodeling to accommodate overnight volunteers/
officers.
Parks: The City of Williamston received a grant for a kayak launch in 2022.
Clearing out major log jams ahead of this installation would be helpful. There
was also discussion around the annual care and maintenance for the township
soccer fields located at the Grand River Park. The Board is in support of
Supervisor Bloomquist exploring guidance and proposals for this work.
Environmental Committee: The committee discussed next steps with regards to the
recent DNR grant approval. They have established a 2030 goal for being carbon
neutral and are creating goals to achieve this. Solar energy for township
buildings, as well as cemeteries and the park are being considered. The
committee is seeking input from the Board. The Board supports moving forward
with a proposal.
Joint Committee on Event Barns: Trustee Creagh shared that the work continues
and significant revisions to the recommendation are occurring.

Streaming of Township Meetings – Supervisor Bloomquist will be seeking bids for
streaming services to be provided to the Township for future meetings. There is
consideration being given on joining MiDEAL. As noted on Michigan.gov –
Department of Technology, Management, and Budget – “MiDEAL is the State of
Michigan's extended purchasing program that allows Michigan cities, townships,
villages, counties, school districts, universities, colleges and nonprofit
hospitals to buy goods and services from state contracts. Membership for the
Township would be $180.00 annually. Local governments benefit directly from the
reduced cost of goods and services and indirectly by eliminating the time
needed to process bids.”

final date that taxes can be paid at the Township Hall is Monday, February 28th
from 9am-5pm for collecting taxes only. After the 28th, Ingham County will take
over the tax roll.

Public Hearing for the Police Assessment Roll
Trustee Creagh moved to open the public hearing for the Police Assessment Roll.

The Public Hearing for the Police Assessment Roll was opened at 6:04 p.m.
Melody Wallace: She stated she is opposed to $900 in the budget for a
newsletter. Also, she couldn’t find the contract with the Meridian Township
Police Department online and stated the contract should have gone out to bid if

Williamston’s police department wasn’t considered for this contract and if the
contract we have with Meridian Township allows the Township to vacate the
contract.
Maureen Maloney: She had a question about how the police reduction will work
and if there would be a subsequent reduction in assessment for residents.
Frans Wilbrink: He stated the Township should bid out police services each time
a contract is near the end. Commented on the absence of Board members at the
meeting. Stated the Township should reduce the assessment.
Supervisor Bloomquist explained how the police contract works and why the
Township chose to stay with Meridian Township. She also explained the police
assessment and how the Township will need to determine if a reduction in the
assessment is appropriate.

Treasurer Cutshaw moved to open the public hearing on the 2022-2023 Proposed
Budget.
Seconded by Trustee Creagh.

the salaries of the elected officials after the budget is adopted. He wants to
review the police contract. He pointed out an error in the budget.
Melody Wallace: She had more questions about the police contract.

to attendees and will correct the budget for the Board meeting on March 9th.
Supervisor Bloomquist, Treasurer Cutshaw, and Trustee Creagh addressed the

She addressed the question about Compensation Commission, explaining that the
Compensation Commission meets every two years and their recommendation is
automatically adopted (by law) unless the Board rejects their entire

DISCUSSION ITEMS
Permanent Recycling Update
– Supervisor Bloomquist recommended moving forward with the agreement for
professional services from Mannik and Smith Group (MSG) in preparation for a
proposed Permanent Recycling site at the Township Hall. The results of this
work will provide the Township with engineering advisement and site
improvements necessary to ensure its feasibility and success. In addition, MSG
will also help prepare the EGLE grant application to aid in offsetting the
costs to the Township. The Board noted that in an effort to not miss the
deadline for the grant application and because the requested project fee was
over $1,000 it should become an Action Item.
Trustee Creagh moved the estimated fee from The Mannik & Smith Group to provide
assistance with a grant application for a proposed recycling center be moved up
into Action Items.
Seconded by: Trustee Eyster
Motion Carries.
Reports – Departments and Committees
NIESA –
Covid runs have decreased over the last several weeks. There was little action
on the Webberville DDA efforts. Station 62 still waiting on cost estimates. New
Board Members were elected: Dorothy Hart is Chairperson, Tommy Pratt is Vice
Chairperson, and Kevin Duffy is Secretary.
Board of Review –
Supervisor Bloomquist shared that there are currently five petitioners
scheduled. The process begins next Monday, March 14th. There are also five VA
petitions and two Poverty Exemptions. Each Board member has gone through
training this year, as in the past. Supervisor Bloomquist anticipates that it
will run smoothly.
Treasury Department –
Winter Tax season was completed on February 28th. Approximately 60-70 tax
payments were delinquent and have been sent on to the County for collection.
Treasurer Cutshaw also shared information on a new state program called
Michigan Homeowners Assistance Fund (MIHAF) which helps homeowners by providing
funds to prevent homeowner mortgage delinquencies, defaults, foreclosure, loss
of utilities or home energy services and displacements of homeowners
experiencing financial hardship. The hope is to assist up to 8,000 residents
within the state. She has shared this information with residents, when
applicable.
Parks and Recreation Committee –
Supervisor Bloomquist shared that the committee discussed the request of Matt
Phelan, coordinator for the Williamston Sting Girls’ Softball Club. It is the
committee’s desire to treat each team who requests field usage equally. Current
Board policy that states reservation fees for practices and games. It was
suggested that the Board review the policy and procedures of our park fields at
next month’s meeting. To help inform the conversation, it was suggested that
both the Parks and Recreation Committee and Mr. Phelan bring important
information and data to the next Board Meeting, including, but not limited to:
-   the number of players/teams who participate in the club
-   how many members are township residents
-   club membership costs
-   plans for how the club could improve this asset of the township and
community
-   field rental data from the past several years
-   costs for field maintenance
-   current teams who use the township park fields and their fees (ex.
Williamston Soccer Club)
The Parks and Recreation Committee continues to explore hosting a Harvest
Festival at the Grand River Park in the fall. Preliminary planning includes
having food trucks, small races, music, games, and activities. The goal is to
introduce the park to more residents.
Environmental Committee –
The committee continues to work on the Forestry Grant. They have identified all
the plants that will be used for the project. Planting will begin on April 23rd
and 24th. On the 23rd, 440 bare root plants will be planted, mulched, caged,
and watered. On the 24th, 2,000 acorns will be planted. In May there are 85
containered plants scheduled to be planted. They hope to include as many
children and families as possible in the endeavors and are also seeking
participation from organizations like the Boy Scouts.

Opened at 9:03 PM
Closed at 9:03 PM
Adjournment and Review
Trustee Duffy moved to adjourn the meeting.
Seconded by Trustee Creagh
Meeting adjourned at 9:04 p.m.

Park Field Rental Policy –
Treasurer Cutshaw reviewed the park comparison price list and field management
plans from surrounding and similar municipalities. It was noted that across the
area, policies and prices varied greatly. The Board shared agreement that the
township’s current park rental policies and fees are fair and not unreasonable.
They also recognized the efforts that the local softball club are putting forth
to become established and organized. They noted the importance that athletics
provides for encouraging positive interactions and improved mental health for
our youth. The Board is supportive of encouraging the utilization of our fields
and are willing to collaborate with the club in the future. This support would
require a thorough long- term plan that encouraged the development of the park
assets. This will be communicated to Mr. Phelen.

Supervisor Bloomquist reminded the Board that this important work will be May

Reports – Departments and Committees
NIESA –
Trustee Duffy shared that Station 62 is fully paid off. The NIESA attorney
drafted an agreement with the Webberville DDA to be discussed on April 14,
2022. Committee appointments were made.
Parks and Recreation Committee –
Trustee Steinberg shared information on the proposed fall festival plans. It
will take place on October 16th. There will be the 5K race in the morning
coordinated through the Williamston Rotary. There will be Township sponsored
events later in the day that may include food trucks. Other discussion items
included Grand River Park signage which continues to be in development. There
will be a Volunteer Day to stain the pavilion. The date will be determined
soon. The Grand River Park driveway review is still in process. 
Senior Center –
Determinations for their Board of Directors will be in May. Trustee Steinberg
shared his excitement in all that is occurring at the center and the positive
direction of the upcoming plans.
Redistricting –
Clerk Cleveland shared and reviewed Williamstown Township’s redistricting and
polling place changes to be implemented for the August 2nd State Primary and
November 8th General Election. These changes were recently determined by the
Williamstown Township Local Election Commission. Furthermore, Clerk Cleveland
noted that these changes are a result of our most recent census. It provides an
opportunity to review our precincts for efficiency and effectiveness. Our
township services four school districts which can lead to ballot splits, which
can be costly. With our new precinct boundaries, school splits will only occur
in Precinct 2. Changes have been approved by Bureau of Elections and have been
applied in the State of Michigan’s Qualified Voter File. Clerk Cleveland
reminded the Board that all district number have changed and that every
township voter will be getting new Voter Information/Identification Card with
these updates. Residents can expect additional communications regarding these
changes and what to expect in the Williamston Enterprise, the township website,
and our Facebook page. Voters can find additional information at Michigan.gov.
Environmental Committee/Forestry Grant –
Trustee Eyster shared that our local Scouts will be out on April 24th to plant
acorns at 9:00am. April 30th is bare root planting. May 7th will be larger
trees. She shared her pleasure at the opportunity this planting experience will
provide and emphasized the idea that this event is an investment in our young
people who will be able to come back someday and say, “I helped plant this
forest.” Sign-ups for this event continue to be distributed.
County Broadband Survey –
Treasurer Cutshaw reminded the Board that this important survey is out and that
the county needs resident input and perspective. The data collected will help

Communities developed by MSU Extension and Michigan Department of Treasury.

planning for Michigan communities.

appointed Treasurer.
Forestry Grant – The grant closes at the end of August. Trustee Eyster will
work with the committee to write the final report as stipulated and due in
September in order to receive reimbursement. Committed project volunteers have
been watering the trees all summer long. In a recent assessment of the newly
planted forest, by Jim Miller, it was estimated that of the 520 trees planted
24 were dead and approximately 25 are distressed, but have signs of life.
Overall, he and the forest grant consultant were pleased at the progress and
impressed at the overall plant health maintained over this hot summer.
Elections – Clerk Cleveland shared that the August Primary went well. She
celebrated the Election Inspectors and Chairs outstanding service to our
township residents. Collectively, they processed 1810 voters. 67% of that total
were absentee and the other third were in-person voters divided between the two
precincts. The election has been certified by Ingham County as of August 10,
2022. Next, it goes to the State for certification. An unforeseen issue
experienced was at St Katherine’s/Precinct 1. The AC was not working well and
the precinct was very warm. With the significant increase in Absentee Voters,
the Board discussed the purchase of a second tabulator for the Absentee Voter
Counting Board (AVCB). Clerk Cleveland shared that she has been advised by the
vendor to wait until the new version coming out in 2023 is available for
purchase. Also, the Township would be unable to obtain a tabulator in time for
the November election. In the meantime, it has been suggested that the Township
borrow a tabulator from the City of Lansing, if available, for November General
Election. The Board agreed that the AVCB needs the access and processing speed
to tabulate the number of ballots that the township is expected to receive for
the upcoming election.
Recycling Update – Supervisor Bloomquist reminded the Board that this month’s
recycling focus is metal from 9am until 3pm. Anything that contains freon will
require a $20 fee. September’s recycling focus will be trash and latex paint
(for a fee). She provided an update on the status of the Permanent Recycling
Grant and indicated that we are still awaiting a determination of award.

August 24, 2022
Williamstown Township
Board of Trustees Meeting Minutes
Special Meeting and Public Hearing for Red Cedar Manor Special Assessment
District
August 24, 2022
Call to Order
The Williamstown Township Board of Trustees convened the Public Hearings for
the Red Cedar Manor Special Assessment District. Supervisor Bloomquist called
the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m., reviewed the agenda, stated the reason for
the meeting/public hearing, and led the Pledge of Allegiance.
Roll Call
Present: Supervisor Bloomquist, Treasurer Cutshaw, Clerk Cleveland, Trustee
Eyster, Trustee Duffy, and Trustee Creagh. Quorum established.
Public Comment for non-agenda items
Opened at 7:01 pm
None.
Closed at 7:02 pm
Supervisor Bloomquist outlined the reason for the public hearing is due to the
bid cost exceeding 10% of the estimated cost and to hear objections to the
proposed assessment roll Red Cedar Manor Road improvement project.
Public Hearing for the Red Cedar Manor SAD
Trustee Creagh moved to open the public hearing for the Red Cedar Manor Special
Assessment District.
Seconded by Trustee Duffy.
Motion carried.
Opened at 7:03 p.m.
The following residents asked questions or made statements regarding the
Special Assessment District:
Nancy Parmenter, 4358 Congdon Dr.: Questioned the longevity of the road surface
project and the cost, as well as sought clarification on the driveways and
shoulder components of the plan.
Jim Brinker, 21 Oliver Dr.: Sought clarification on the portions of the
project, specifically driveways, that were removed from the original proposal.
Dave Sachau, 4424 Wilfors Dr.: Questioned if additional costs would be added to
residents’ property taxes as an additional assessment or as a cost from the
Drain Commission.
Supervisor Bloomquist read correspondence from Mr. Sachau dated August 23, 2022
that included several questions raised by both him and various residents of Red
Cedar Manor regarding the road project.
Melissa Wood, 4432 Wilfors Dr.: Expressed her observation that the adapted
proposal is different than what was originally planned for. She concluded the
cost is more and outcomes of the project are less than what residents approved.
Additionally, she asked for a new petition to be circulated among residents
with a new plan and revised costs.
John Sarafin, 4394 Wilfors Dr.: Sought clarification on cost differences for
concrete and asphalt driveways. He asked for information on how contractors are
chosen for projects and the bid process.
Raymond Borgman, 28 Oliver Dr.: Sought information on costs related to traffic
control, sewers, mailboxes, and slope restoration.
Pat Smith, 4363 Wilfors Dr.: Wanted information regarding parking for residents
during construction.
Sharon Carter, 4431 Congdon Dr.: Expressed her concern on the longevity of the
materials being used for the road construction project, the implications for
weather and delays in supply chain management, her appreciation of the Special
Assessment process, her understanding that projects can change, and her desire
for a revote in light of new project information. She also expressed concerns
regarding how the Board could make a decision with so many unanswered questions
and concerns, as well as her hopes for a Plan B for residents to consider.
Supervisor Bloomquist also read a letter from Sharon Carter dated August 18,
2022 that listed project questions and requested a new vote in consideration of
the changes to the plan and costs.
Steve Selinger, 4434 Congdon Dr.: Agreed with Ms. Carter desire for a revote.
He also sought confirmation on if the road would be widened during the project.
Jeremy Berger, 4411 Wilfors Dr.: Shared that, as a new resident to the
neighborhood, he was unable to vote. He did not resist the decision of his
neighbors, however now he questions the bidding and timeline process, how
projects are funded, and the reason for the culvert replacement.
Supervisor Bloomquist read a letter received from Jeremy Berger dated August
22, 2022 objecting to proceeding with the Special Assessment Resolution No. 5.
Judy Walgren, 4397 Wilfors Dr.: Questioned why the culvert replacement delayed
the project for a year.
Terry Smith, 4446 Wilfors Dr.: Sought clarification on mailbox removal and the
width of the shoulder upon project completion.
Ann Cody, 4365 Congdon Dr.: Questioned if there were any remaining options to
consider, if there were other funding sources that could be utilized, and what
the road condition would be in years to come if the project was not completed.
She expressed her desire to see the project completed and valued the
perspective of the Project Engineer and Township Supervisor regarding next
steps.
Patty Wright (no address provided): Questioned if the Board could consider
another township road millage vote as an alternate funding source for road
improvements.
John McLaughlin – 4442 Congdon Dr.: Shared the road history of Red Cedar Manor.
Stated that there was a considerable base established when the road was
constructed and that it remains in good condition. He noted that the unstable
parts are at the entrance when you enter from Meridian Rd. To forego future
unknown cost increases and more road deterioration, he recommended that the
residents of the neighborhood move forward with the project.
Mannik & Smith Group Senior Project Manager, Corey Vincent, and Supervisor
Bloomquist responded to the Red Cedar Manor residents’ questions and
statements. Ms. Vincent explained:
how the road will feather into residents’ driveways and the projected longevity
of the work
timelines for optimal road construction
how wide the road would be upon completion of the project
possible construction impacts on resident parking
the competitive bidding process and the factors that are considered when a
business is awarded the contract
the implications of inflation for present and future road construction
projects, as well as the increase in demand for these services statewide
She provided context for what traffic controls, underdrains, slope restoration,
and mailbox removal means within the context of the project description.
Supervisor Bloomquist confirmed:
that the Drain Commission has not yet shared the cost of the culvert
replacement
the delay in the project due to the erosion and undersized culvert were
necessary and would have destroyed the road had construction moved forward
that Plan B is no longer a viable option due to timing.
She explained the project estimation process used by Ingham County Road
Department (ICRD), reminded residents that the original price was an estimate
from the prior director of the ICRD, shared how surrounding townships were
utilizing Federal Covid Funds (also known as ARPA), and recommended that any
future considerations for a Township Road Millage to fund road work would
require initiative from residents.
Both Ms. Vincent and Supervisor Bloomquist expressed their concern for
continued road deterioration and cost increases if construction did not
commence as planned. Future unknown variables such as interest rates, possible
financial bonding, material and constructions costs, and limited availability
of construction companies due to increased demand for their services would need
to be strongly considered should the project be rebid.
Trustee Creagh moved to close the public hearing.
Seconded by Trustee Eyster.
Motion carried.
Public Hearing closed at 8:20 p.m.
Special Meeting for Deliberation
Trustee Creagh moved the Township Board move forward with Alternative 2 of the
Red Cedar Manor Road Resurfacing Options 9-24-20 with the following three
conditions: the Township would determine the cost that would be subsidized for
the culvert replacement should the Drain Commission not cover it; the Township
strongly encourages Red Cedar Manor residents to personally remove their
mailboxes in an effort to reduce overall costs; the Township and Project
Engineers will work with contractors to find ways to save money on traffic
safety conditions and costs.
Seconded by: Treasurer Cutshaw
Discussion: 
Trustee Creagh expressed his appreciation of the comments shared and the
demeanor presented by resident participants. He shared his desire to pursue the
project with the understanding that it is an additional cost and burden
especially during a time of high inflation and financial struggles. He stressed
his desire to find ways to work with the residents, based on ideas presented,
to reduce the costs where viable and to consider the option of the township
subsidizing costs not covered by the Drain Commission’s culvert replacement
(once determined).
Trustee Duffy expressed his support of Trustee Creagh’s motion and that the
intent is to try to bring the cost back down to the costs before the drain
issue.
Trustee Creagh moved to amend the initial motion to include language that caps
the amount the Township would subsidize to “not to exceed $20,000.00.”
Seconded by: Treasurer Cutshaw
Clerk Cleveland shared similar concerns as Trustee Eyster regarding the impact
of future Special Assessment Districts if subsidization of the drain/culvert
work were to occur for Red Cedar Manor.
Supervisor Bloomquist shared that there are no drain issues in the Meadowdale.
Future drain issues would need to be addressed as they are determined.
Trustee Eyster expressed her concern for setting a precedent on estimates for
bidding. She reiterated that the possibilities of other problems arising in
other subdivision road projects cannot be predicted. She is concerned that we
are putting the township in a difficult position and that the Board cannot
guarantee that it will financially cover work that is unknown to project as it
occurs. She reminded the Board that it is often after engineering begins that
unknowns arise.
Trustee Creagh shared his appreciation for the caution and wisdom of Trustee
Eyster and viewed this Red Cedar situation as very unique. He reminded the
Board that part of the township road policy is roads, not necessarily drains.
He viewed this opportunity as policy setting instead of precedent setting. He
recommended that the board consider incorporating the exploration of drainage
issues into the petition process of future Special Assessment Districts.
Voice Vote
4 Ayes
2 Nays
Amended Motion:
Trustee Creagh moved the Township Board move forward with Alternative 2 of the
Red Cedar Manor Road Resurfacing Options 9-24-20 with the following three
conditions: the Township would determine the costs that would be subsidized for
the culvert replacement should the Drain Commission not cover it, at a cost not
to exceed $20,000.00; the Township strongly encourages Red Cedar Manor
residents to personally remove their mailboxes in an effort to reduce overall
costs; the Township and Project Engineers will work with contractors to find
ways to save money on traffic safety conditions and costs.
Discussion:
Treasurer Cutshaw shared concerns about property value will diminish if the
road was returned to gravel. She supports Trustee Creagh’s motion.
Clerk Cleveland shared concerns about moving forward, but was willing to
consider the amended motion.
Trustee Eyster suggested that consideration be given to stating that we set it
at no more than the excess of 10% or $20,000.00
Roll Call Vote:
Ayes: Treasurer Cutshaw, Clerk Cleveland, Trustee Eyster, Trustee Duffy,
Trustee Creagh, and Supervisor Bloomquist.
Nays: None
Motion Carried.

Red Cedar River Water Trail/Williamston Rotary Satellite Club Update
John Bollman, 4185 Meadowdale: Mr. Bollman provided the Board with an update on
the Red Cedar Water Trail efforts. He noted that the work is a combined
endeavor of the East Lansing, Okemos, Williamston Sunrise and Williamston
Satellite Rotary Clubs. They have a shared vision to create a local and viable
“up north water opportunity” for area residents. The updates included:
Launch site developments
Signage and logo efforts in conjunction with the Ingham County Parks Department
Grant sources that are being sought for information kiosks and floating docks
for access
Ideas on the utilization of the rapids for training and experience with river
boating
Developing maintenance programs that would include ascertaining blockages,
clearing log jams, and river traffic monitoring
Collaboration with the Boy Scouts on Eagle Scout Projects that included the
creation of a Boat Rack
How the development of this water trail could encourage patronage to local
businesses and restaurants along the route, as well as lead to possible
enhancements of the roadside park located on Grand River at Meridian Road
Mr. Bollman noted that the work has cultivated partnerships across many
municipalities, local organizations, and government agencies committed to
continue the progress towards making this river trail come to fruition for the
benefit of area residents.

Red Cedar Antiques Demolition – Request for Proposal
Treasurer Cutshaw moved the Township Board approve the request for proposal for
the demolition of the remains of the structure at 1435 E. Grand River Rd.
(parcel # 33-03-03-34-403-009). According to the Blight Ordinance under Section
20.01 and 20.02, the conditions on the property at 1435 E. Grand River Rd. is
considered a public nuisance and must be abated. (20.03) (20.08).
Seconded by: Trustee Steinberg
Discussion: Supervisor Blomquist noted that the current state of the burned
building is unsafe and is in violation of the Township Blight Ordinance.
Furthermore, she shared that there is no insurance on the property. There have
been several attempts of communication in multiple formats regarding the
property, including certified mail, but the owner has not replied or
communicated upon receiving these communications. The Board inquired about
repayment of the demolition fees to the Township. The Supervisor explained that
upon completion of the demolition, a lien would be placed on the property and
appear on the owner’s tax bill. Payment to the township would occur immediately
upon payment of the taxes. Supervisor Bloomquist also reassured the Board that
the upcoming actions by the Township, including the approval to seek an RFP by
the Township for demolition services as well as timelines for the work, would
be communicated to the owner. The RFP is due by September 28th so that it can
be finalized at the October Board Meeting.

Elections – Clerk Cleveland shared that the Election Department is gearing up
for the General Election in November. The August Primary has been certified by
the State. Both of Williamstown’s Precincts balanced without a problem, as well
as the Absent Voter Counting Board (AVCB). She was able to secure a Tabulator
from the City of Lansing for use as a second Tabulator for the AVCB in
November. It will be returned to them upon completion of the Election. In
addition, the AVCB location has been moved to the Forster Woods building at St.
Katherines this year. Clerk Cleveland expressed her appreciation of their
willingness to host our residents/precincts and share this additional building
with us for Election Day.
Summer Taxes - Treasurer Cutshaw shared that that the deadline for Summer Taxes
was today (9/14/22) at 5pm. The Township experienced a high rate of payment,
only 129 residents haven’t paid. That is the lowest number in years. Letters go
out residents who have not yet paid on Thursday, September 15th that will
include a 1% late charge. She noted that tax payments made directly to the
local banks have increased and gives residents options. Treasurer Cutshaw
commended the efforts of Deputy Treasurer VanErp in ensuring a smooth tax
season for both residents and the township office.
Red Cedar Manor – Supervisor Bloomquist shared that Ingham County Road
Commission notified her of the need to reschedule the road work for next May
2023. They confirmed that the price will not change. A letter has been sent to
the residents. She also noted that the Drain Commissioner is looking to get
Federal Funds for the culvert replacement. Once this becomes known, the
townships portion will be able to be determined.
Safe Routes to School – Supervisor Bloomquist updated the Board on progress of
this initiative. The goal is to create a shared pathway for bicycles and
pedestrians along Williamston Rd. to include the Maple Shade subdivision. The
stakeholder group of participants who are working on this will be submitting a
grant for Federal Funds to help pay for this project. Public input will be
sought before the grant application and routes are determined. The Board noted
that this supports our Strategic Plan for walkable communities.
Public comment for agenda and non-agenda items
Opened at 8:55 PM
Donna Tocarchick - 9605 Deer Tr.: Ms. Tocarchick shared her appreciation for
the answers she received regarding her questions. She noted that she is still
seeking information on the Railroad Quiet Zone and Neighborhood Road Policy and
confirmed that Supervisor Bloomquist will contact her regarding this.
Nancy Horton – 5632 Shoeman Rd.: Ms. Horton shared her concern regarding the
Township Code Enforcement position and its necessity, as well as funding. She
asked the board to consider a public review of the names of applicants and
their qualifications before hiring.
Closed at 8:59 PM

Seconded by Clerk Cleveland
Meeting adjourned at 9:00 p.m.

Damon Rd. Seasonal Display Board Discussion – Supervisor Bloomquist summarized
concerns from Damon Rd. residents, the process used in determining where the
display fits in relation to the Blight Ordinance, the role of the Township in a
situation such as this, and suggested solutions to the situation. Board
discussion ensued.
Letters/emails of concern were shared with the Board noting that traffic in the
neighborhood varied but peaked at 350 cars per night. It was noted that if a
health emergency arose, emergency vehicles would be unable to access the
neighborhood. There are times when there are no issues with the traffic and
there are times when issues are present.
Procedurally, when ordinance complaints are reported to the Township, they are
investigated with a letter sent if a violation is found. Supervisor Bloomquist
is not necessarily the person who would complete investigations, it could be
the Township Planning Assistant or Building Inspector. In this case, Supervisor
Bloomquist was the investigator. She had visited the display four to five times
after receiving complaints. Supervisor Bloomquist expressed a desire to be fair
and considerate. The purpose of the letter was to ensure Ms. Underwood
understood her rights with regards to the ordinance. She stated that no one
wants to regulate holiday lights, however the Township does regulate issues
within the blight ordinance.
It is advised that Ms. Underwood work with her neighbors regarding the display
so that the Township is not receiving complaints. Many of the displays are
interactive. Thus, it is not always a drive-by situation. Access could be
better if the seasonal display was placed in a non-residential area, such as a
fairgrounds or other public space where the ability to park and move around
safely is present, instead of a dead end street.
Trustee Steinberg stressed that this situation illustrates the difficulty of
meeting the needs of all people. He recommended reviewing Ms. Underwood’s
changes and determine if it would remedy the situation from the point of view
of the neighbors. He stated that the changes should be considered if they
remedy the violations of the ordinance. He questioned if there is middle ground
or a way to have the seasonal display safely? He supported that neighbors need
to be involved and make their voices heard to Ms. Underwood. It needs a
discussion instead of anonymous complaints. 
The complaints began in 2020 and it is Supervisor Bloomquist’s understanding
that the neighbors have expressed their concerns with Ms. Underwood.. 
He wondered if there could be a solution where the traffic flow kept moving or
if the Township could host it? He wondered if that could lessen the liability.
Supervisor Bloomquist noted that it would have to be a discussion by the
Board. 
Trustee Eyster noted that these seasonal displays, for both Halloween and
Christmas, are each 30 days – for a total of 60 days. That is almost 1/6 of a
year. She also noted that people visit for much longer periods of times over
the weekends (Friday-Sunday). She recalled how much the Planning Commission
struggled with determining how long things like fireworks could occur. The time
for Ms. Underwood’s display exceeds what would have been permitted in the
past. Trustee Eyster would like to seek confirmation on all the holidays that
have a seasonal display on Ms. Underwood’s Damon Rd. residence and a
calculation of the amount of days that each is available for public display/
drive-by. She noted that this situation should follow the standard Township
process. This gives residents who have direct exposure an opportunity to
express their feelings. Trustee Eyster reasoned that if you permit something to
occur – then you will have to allow it for everyone. This has more implications
than just one holiday display.
Trustee Duffy noted that there are other sizable displays in the area. He
questioned if those neighbors minded? He feels as though there needs to be less
oversight. Residents should be able to do what they want on their property.
Supervisor Bloomquist noted agreement, except when it affects one’s neighbors.
She stated that it is the reason why the Township has ordinances in general. It
is a balance between protecting those who want to do what they want and
protecting the rights of neighbors to enjoy their property as well. Supervisor
Bloomquist reiterated that Ms. Underwood needs to reach out to her neighbors,
propose a solution, and see if it is sufficient. Unfortunately, the proposed
changes were not discussed after the December 21,2021 letter was received. The
Township could have worked with the compromise had a decision been reached with
neighbors prior to now.
Supervisor Bloomquist noted that her next steps would include a follow-up
communication to Ms. Underwood that included another invitation to work with
the Township. The communication would also include the suggestion of reaching
out to her neighbors. She would also be seeking clarification from Ingham
County Road Department about the turn-around at the end of Damon Road to
determine if it is considered a cul-de-sac or part of a private drive.
Brenda Seelman – Clark Schaefer Hackett CPAs and Advisors – Presented a review
of the Williamstown Township Audit for the fiscal year ending March 31, 2022.
She noted that their report format changed this year and audit opinions are now
listed first. Ms. Seelman provided highlights of the report with regards to the
Township’s current revenue and expenditures, as well as the capital assets and
general fund balance. Additionally, she provided a summary of the Township’s
net position, which has seen an overall increase. She reported that due to the
implementations of last year’s recommendations, there are no recommendations
for this year.
Sgt. McCready for Chief Plaga – Meridian Township Police – Sgt. McCready
reviewed the quarterly report in comparison to this time last year. He
highlighted current and upcoming projects for the Meridian Township Police
Department including the Beard Fundraiser for charitable organizations,
Halloween Open House on 10/29, and the Citizens’ Academy. Williamstown Township
currently does not have any residents enrolled. The Youth Academy will take
place in February 2023. This event is for high school students who are
interested in law enforcement. He encouraged anyone in high school, with an
interest, to enroll. Sgt. McCready also updated the Board on department
staffing. Recently two officers completed the field training program and two
more have just begun. There are five officers currently in the Police Academy
who will then have to go into the field training program. The department has
recently reevaluated its pay structure to attract more people and hires, as
well retain them. They are authorized for 41 officers, and they are making
strides to get there.
Planning Commission (PC) Report – Chair Eidt shared a summary of the October
5th Planning Commission Meeting. The second public hearing on Event Barns was
held. Due to the federal case on the Peninsula Wineries, it was referred back
to the subcommittee where modifications were considered around alcohol, music,
event frequency and capacity. Deliberation on the modifications of the proposed
Event Barn draft ordinance language will occur at the November 2nd PC Meeting.
The Commission considered proposed updates to the Home Occupation Ordinance
regarding Telecommunications. After the discussion, the topic was tabled.
Further clarification and direction from the Board will be sought for future
inclusion or not. Proposed Medical Marijuana, under the Home Occupation
Ordinance, was also reviewed. McKenna will provide updated recommendations
based on the discussion held.. A Public Hearing on Farm Signs on Residential
Property was called. A Subcommittee for Capital Improvement Planning was
established and will work to make recommendations to the PC and Board. A
November 2nd PC Meeting was scheduled due to the Thanksgiving holiday. A second
subcommittee was created to determine the slate of officers for the upcoming
year. Board discussion ensued with Chair Eidt around implications of the
Peninsula Wineries case and telecommunications.

Event Barn Regulations – The Board reviewed the draft ordinance and commended
the work of the Planning Commission regarding Event Barn regulations. They
noted that the draft is very thorough and well done. Chair Eidt commented that
the hearings and resident input provided excellent feedback for consideration.
Additionally, the committee field trips to established event barns in
neighboring townships also informed the process, solutions, and decisions. The
Board considered questions around the review process that owners will
experience as they work towards a permanent special use permit, enforcement of
ordinance and penalties if the permit is violated, as well as considerations
should the property owners sell. It was noted that impact to neighbors was
strongly considered in informing the final draft. Action will be taken at
December Board meeting.
Farm Sign Regulations – Trustee Creagh noted that conversations ensued at the
Planning Commission level regarding sign size and increasing it so that it can
be seen from the road. Action will be taken at the December Board Meeting.

options for future planning.
Elections – Clerk Cleveland reported that overall things went well. Resident
feedback has been positive. There was 72.89% voter turn-out between the two
precincts. The Absentee Ballot Counting Board moved to Forster Woods, at St.
Katherine’s, for the General Election. The feedback on this change was very
positive. Additionally, the use of a second tabulator was immensely helpful to
the AV Board, as well as the increase in workers from 4 to 6 election
inspectors. Clerk Cleveland noted a tabulator issue occurred at Precinct 2 that
lasted approximately 2.5 hours on Election Day. It was determined that the
mechanical issue was caused by a voter using a gel pen on their ballot instead
of the markers provided in the voting booth. Clerk Cleveland continues to stay
updated on the legislative changes.
Roads – Supervisor Bloomquist noted that, aside from the projects that had to
be delayed, all other road projects have been completed for 2022. This included
the new four-way stop at Sherwood and Zimmer. She reminded the Board that the
2022 costs are significant and will draw down Township funds for road
improvements. She reported that the Pebblebrook neighborhood has shared a
letter of interest and is currently seeking neighborhood signatures for future
road improvements.
ICC-MTA – Supervisor Bloomquist reminded the Board of a Holiday gathering in
early December for the Ingham County Chapter of the Michigan Township
Association (ICC-MTA). She encouraged attendance, as it provides an opportunity
to meet and interact with fellow Boards and Townships. RSVP by December 1.
Resident Correspondence for Damon Road – Supervisor Bloomquist provided the
board updated copies of the letters exchanged around the Holiday light display
on Damon Road. It was confirmed that there are 12 homes on Damon Rd.. 
Public comment for agenda and non-agenda items
Opened at 8:52 PM
Jerry Eidt, Planning Commission Chair/Resident 4115 Vanneter Rd.: Mr. Eidt
commented on working as an Election Inspector in the 2022 General Election. He
commended the competence of the election staff and noted the level of
professionalism, intentionality, and desire to run a safe and successful
election.
Closed at 8:55 PM
Adjournment and Review
Trustee Duffy moved to adjourn the meeting.
Seconded by Clerk Cleveland
Meeting adjourned at 8:56 p.m.

Public Comment for agenda and non-agenda items

group.

Township Supervisor, Clerk, Treasurer, and Trustees. They recommend a $2,000
increase in the annual pay for the officers (Supervisor, Clerk, and Treasurer)
for the 2023-2024 budget with no additional increase for the 2024-2025 budget,
bringing their annual pay to $33,000. For the Trustees they recommend an
increase in annual pay to $5,750, from $5,400, for the 2023-2024 budget with no
additional increase for the 2024-2025 budget. Their recommendations are that
the per-meeting pay for Trustees stay the same as the current $65 per meeting
after more than two meetings in a month. Supervisor Bloomquist thanked the
Commission members for their service.

Nuisance Ordinance Draft Revisions – Board Member suggestions have been sent to

Further discussion ensued regarding the storage of building materials at
construction sites, odors and fumes, consideration of project work around
stipulated holidays, as well as the new title of the ordinance.
Neighborhood Road Policy – Supervisor Bloomquist updated the Board on the
recent edits to the road policy. She noted that the main changes included the
removal of definitions of different roads so that the focus could be on
neighborhood roads. The goal was to make it easier for residents to understand.
The Board discussed the petition process outlined by the state, the possibility
of fundamental site issues being determined prior to construction, the
recommendation of a second meeting upon completion of the petition process, as
well as overall improved communication and guidance regarding the special
assessment process. Supervisor Bloomquist will provide a revised policy at the
next meeting.

not meet within the last month. Consideration is still being given to the
township Harvest Festival. He noted that there will be additional planting of
approximately 68 trees at the park in conjunction with Earth Day.
Elections - Clerk Cleveland shared that the Bureau of Elections presented at
the recent Michigan Township Association 2023 Capital Conference and explained
that there will be an increase in election equipment needs, funding, and human
resources to fulfill the expectations outlined in the recent passage of
Proposal 2022-2. Clerk Cleveland noted that as more is learned and determined,
she will inform the Board. She also updated the Board on upcoming preventative
maintenance and upgrades to the township tabulators and Voter Assist Terminals
that will increase speed, accessibility, and security. 
Cemetery - Supervisor Bloomquist shared that an Eagle Scout project has been
approved for fencing adjacent to the garage at Summit Cemetery. Mapping out of
the Green Burial spaces continues. She noted that residents are expressing
interest in purchasing these spaces. Revisions to costs will be considered at
the next Cemetery Board meeting.
Board of Review Updates - Supervisor Bloomquist updated the Board on the
upcoming dates and times for the Board of Review. Residents are currently
scheduling appointments for review of their assessments.
Property Tax Updates – Treasurer Cutshaw noted that Winter Tax season recently
concluded. She also shared information on the Michigan Homeowners Assistance
Fund (MIHAF). MIHAF helps homeowners by providing funds to prevent homeowner
mortgage delinquencies, defaults, foreclosure, loss of utilities or home energy
services and displacements of homeowners experiencing financial hardship. She
continues to share this information with residents, when applicable, and noted
that two homeowners in Williamstown Township were assisted this year through
this initiative.

DISCUSSION ITEMS  
Rural Ready Community Grants – Supervisor Bloomquist updated the Board on the
grant guidelines and eligibility that must be established in order to be
identified as a rural area and therefore participate in the Rural Ready
Community Grant process. The goal is to be able to seek a grant to be utilized
for the potential development of a Joint Master Plan between the City of
Williamston, Wheatfield Township, and Williamston Township.
Safe Routes to School (SRTS) – Supervisor Bloomquist updated the Board on the
progress of this safety initiative. The community would be eligible for
$880,000 to utilize for improvements. Priorities include improving the
accessibility and reliability of a walkway at the wetland on Vanneter Rd, a
three-way stop at the intersection of Vanneter and Rowley Roads, and an off
road pathway from Bismark to Sherwood and rerouting the bus route in the
parking lot of Discovery and Explorer Elementaries. The Board commended the
process and final presentation. It was noted that it was a thorough collection
of information and data that is very helpful for planning and decision-making.

Elections – Clerk Cleveland reported that the state recently provided a model

the process, answer questions, and review the model agreement. If it is
determined that the parties would like move ahead with an early voting
partnership, the agreement would come before the Board at next month’s meeting
and shared with the state by late September.

School Letter – Township Board members shared their perspectives regarding a
letter dated November 6, 2023 sent to the Township from the Williamston
Community Schools Board of Education. The Board discussed the township’s role
pertaining to housing and development. It was noted that this topic was
included in their recent Strategic Planning Session. Additionally, with the
upcoming work on updating the Williamstown Township Master Plan, conversations
with community stakeholders to address housing needs will be timely. Supervisor
Bloomquist requested the Board of Education create a list of questions for the
Township to address before their proposed January meeting. This effort will
help to inform what the schools are looking for from the Township and what the
Township can provide to Williamston Schools.
 
Strategic Planning – Supervisor Bloomquist reviewed the summary from the
December 8th Strategic Planning meeting. She requested each board member share
their top three priorities for the upcoming year. These priorities will guide
the development of the 2024-25 budget.
 
23-24 Budget Review – Supervisor Bloomquist updated the Board on the 2023-24
Budget and planning for the next fiscal year. She will be meeting with each
department to prepare a budget proposal for the January Board Meeting. One item
that she would like to revisit in January is the implementation of the state
recommended Admin Fee as part of tax collection.
 
Reports – Departments and Committees
NIESA – Trustee Duffy reported on the November 9 th NIESA Board Meeting. He
noted that the 2024 General Fund Budget was reviewed. A detailed Treasury
Report will be provided at their upcoming December 14 th meeting that will
provide a further breakdown of each proposed budget. Conversation was reopened
regarding renovations to allow for full-time staffing at Station #62 Leroy
Township.
 
Parks Committee – Trustee Steinberg noted that an arborist worked with the park
committee members in early December to eliminate invasive species. Progress was
made in decreasing these plants. Supervisor Bloomquist discussed the plans to
apply diamond dust to the fields so that it can settle over the winter months
in preparation for the 2024 baseball and softball seasons.
 
Elections – Clerk Cleveland updated the board on upcoming mailings for the
Presidential Primary in February.. She confirmed that all election equipment
has arrived and that preparations are beginning for Election Inspector
training.
 
Roads – Supervisor Bloomquist updated the Board on the status of the three
subdivisions interested in road improvements. She indicated that petitions in
each of the subdivisions did not reach the necessary threshold and therefore
will not be moving forward with the process. The Board discussed revisiting
local road programs, the township’s Neighborhood Road Policy, and ways to make
the process easier for residents to navigate.
 
Cemetery – Supervisor Bloomquist is beginning to meet with contractors to seek
bids for the entrance bridge and shepherd’s wall at the new green burial site.
 
 
Public comment for agenda and non-agenda items
Opened at 8:15 PM
 
Sarah Belanger and Deb Wolf - Vice President and Trustee for the Williamston
Community Schools Board of Education respectively - shared that the WCS Board
of Education letter was intended to be informational and a call to action. They
said the Board of Education views the housing issue as a priority for the whole
community and they value the partnership with the Township in seeking solutions
in an effort to maintain enrollment, offerings, and quality staff. They hope
Township Board members will participate in the upcoming January meeting.
 
Sue Alchin, 3536 Burkley Rd. – expressed concern regarding the Christmas Barn
display in the pole barn at Wamhoff Farms. She shared her experiences as a
neighbor to this property and the impacts on her residence due to increased
traffic, lights, and noise. She is also concerned about environmental impacts
due to a recent parking surface application. Because this is a new display,
since the one at Halloween, she questioned if the process to address events
that do not meet ordinance regulations begins again.
 
Matt Ellsworth – 4514 Petoskey Dr. – expressed appreciation for his neighbors
working to improve the Pebblebrook Subdivision community and to the Township
Board for working hard to balance competing interests.
 
Closed at 8:25 PM
 
Adjournment and Review
 
Trustee Duffy moved to adjourn the meeting.
 
Seconded by Trustee Steinberg
 
Meeting adjourned at 8:26 PM

Meridian Township Police Report – Chief Grillo summarized the Police Report for
the first quarter.
He noted there was a slight uptick in calls for service for this period. He
updated the Board on current staffing levels with 36 trained officers. The goal
being 42. With the increasing staffing levels, they will be able to improve
their focus on roadway safety. Chief Grillo also answered questions about
Meridian Township’s Recruitment process and the recent damage at the Community
Park.
Planning Commission (PC) Report - Chair Eidt shared a summary of the March 27
th Planning Commission Meeting. A public hearing was held for the Accessory
Dwelling Units (ADU) revisions. The commission resumed their review of wind and
solar amendments and set a public hearing date for May 22 nd . A public hearing
was also set for the May meeting for parking requirements for multiple family
residences. The Planning Commission Meeting/Workship Schedule for fiscal year
2024-2025 was adopted. The Master Plan Opinion Survey was reviewed. He
expressed the Commission’s condolences for the unexpected death of Township
Planning Assistant, Jim Howard. The Board addressed the possibility ADUs as
rentals.
